PRELIMINARY FUND of £75,000. The object of the Lancashire Plateway Company is to cheapen and improve the Conveyance of Goods and Minerals in that portion of Lancashire lying mainly between the Ribble and the Mersey. It is not denied that railways and canals are numer- ous in the district, but the tratfc already- occasionally taxes seriously their powers. and is yearly increasing; moreover, the charges they have combined to make are so heavy, as to have been the subject of long-standing,and general dissatisfaction and hitherto unavailing remonstrance. These reasons, added to the necessity that our national indus- tries be not handicapped in their competition with foreigners, seem to constitute at once a cause and a justification for a new and cheaper system of inland conveyance. Besides the advantage of cheaper carriage, the Piateway Com- pany will be ab'e to convey goods in better condition, more conveniently, and probably, throughout Lancashire, in a:shorter period of time.

- If, therefore, lower charges, better condition, greater con- venience, and sufficient speed be realised, a fair basis for an im- portant public convenience is established, and also a probability of a good profit to the shareholders. It is desirable that the attitude of the present carriers towards the various industries of Lancashire should be plainly stated, to serve as a needful justification for offering them competition. It will hardly be found one that the trading public can be ex- pected to submit to, if escape be possible. The English system of allowing carriers to charge "what the trade will bear," as the phrase is, taken in conjunction with undisputed power of combination, has resulted in the abandonment of what would prima facie appear an equitable bssis of charge, viz.: cost, plus a profit. The carriers have recognised that trade is strong in Lanca- shire, and that, when combined, they have only to ask in order to have ; and that however traders grumble they pay, and that distant and often unremunerat lye portions of their systems can be conveniently supported by disproportionate charges over this vigorous district. The result is that it is difficult to And in the world, except in small and exceptional cases such as the Panama Railroad, equally high %rates or carriage; and as a mult of the-whole, it is believed that along the main line of Lancashire traffic, namely, that between Liverpool and Blan- chester, fifty years f railways have increased tLe cost of car- riage and not materially lessened the time of transit. Yet Lancashire is pre-emineutly suitable for cheap transpor- tation. The country presents no engineering difficulty, fuel and material are cheap, labour of every description good and abundant, and the stream of traffic flows both ways. It should be well understood that the complaint is not of a minute or small fractional overcharge. If the railways in Lancashire stood alone, and were not mixed up with other lines, they would probably only need ~to exact, for working and pr.-It, a sum considerably less than their present charges, and the plateway system contemplates even further and material reduction.

It is admitted that the fear of opposition on routes out of Lancashire by companies having no interest, or only a slight one, in Lancashire, has kept up excessive charges in that county. This arrangement has diverted goods from their Le.tural channels, and acquiescence by Lancashire traders in such an arrangement is hardly to be expected. The conveyance on the same line of both passengers and goods has increased the cost of the latter in a manner few would suspect. It has also diminished the cargo-carrying power of the line, by demanding a cons:derable interval be- tween the trains, and has caused needless and costly speed to the heavy traffic in order to clear the lines. These causes combined have both narrowed the capacity and increased the cost of carrying goods by rail. The proposed plateway will be constructed on land, acquired under Parliamentary powers, in such a way as to admit of wagons being at any point drawn on or off. Such wagons can be taken by horses to the point where drawn on to the plate- way, or from the point where drawn off along the ordinary roads to thrir final destination. Under this system cotton loaded at the ship side or manure loaded at the stable, will be carried along road and plaleway and delivered at its ulti- mate destination (whetner mill or farm) without change of vehicle.

A great difficulty of the present sys'em, and one that in Lan- cashire seems insepartple from it, is the necessity of removing the goods to and from horse-drawn carts at the stations. This is a somewhat costly process, by reason of the time lost by carters and their teams, and of the great station space and ap- pliances required for handling the goods. It has always been held to justify, under the nam3 " termina's" a considerable portion of the heavy charges. This on the plateway system it is hoped in great measure to avoid. Thus the present handling at stations would not take place, and many of the costly appliances incidental to the railway systeat will be rendered unnecessary. In thus differing from 'railways by avoiding handling, the plateway will have the advantage of not damaging the goods, and may therefore expect a preference for nearly every article of comme.ce. It needs no argument to show that a distinct money value attaches to the conveyance of bale goods direct from warehouse to ship, or of cotton from ship or warehouse to mill. This advantage of diminished handling will be noticed to apply to an extensive list of articles of varying values, such as coals, slates, bricks, fruit, liquors, glass, earthenware, &c., in fact, will in some degree affect all, except uninjurable articles, like timber and metals.

To the grain trade it will offer the advan'age of the aboli- tion of sacks. The heavy charge these involve will evidently be saved, when the article can be carrie I in bulk from the wharf or warehouse to the miller. The trade in coals for u,e in the towns will have the advan- tage that the actual cart or wagon delivering at the house or factory will have been loaded at the pit, thus cheapening car- riage and avoiding breakage sat,d loss of v eight. Branches of the system may be expected to spread over the agricultural district, and produce in time come to be loaded at the farm, drawn by horses to the nearest point on the pate- way, and thecee c_uiveyed at a low rate and without breaking bulk to the best market. The system promises a much-needed advantage to agriculture, which railways have only conferred to a very limited extent. The remoteness cf the stations at one end from the farm and at the other from the consumer, have weighed the p oduce with the cost and damage of hand- ling which, added to the high carge for simple carriage, have debarred the farmer from his fair pat ticipatlon in the general benefit. On the plateway system these disabilities may be ex- pected to disappear. - . -

From the moderate speed at which it is proposed to work the plateway, the cost attendant on an expen3ive system of signal- ling will be avoided. In fact, the plateway aims to be simply an improved high road adapted to steam traction. Termini near the centres of the towns, as have been obtained by the railways, wuuld only be sought as they were felt to be required. The facilities afforded by the wagons leaving the p;ateways at any point, and teing thence takea along roads and streets, greatly reduces the importance of having such stations. The saving in capital would be very cmsideratole.

ROUTES.

It is proposed, in the first instance, to seek powers to make lines over the following routes, subject to such alterations or omissions as may be found necessary as the work proceeds. Sonthern Section A.—Frans South end cf Liverpool to Oldham, via. Warrington, South side of Manchester, Ashton. and Staley Bridge. Central Section B.—Fr.dn North end of Liverpool to Oldham, yid St. Helens, Ashton-in-Makerfield, Bolton, Bury, Heywood, and Itochdale. • Northern Sectiur o.—From Ashton-in-Makertield on Section B to Burnley, viii Wigan, Chorley, Blackburn, Church, and Aceringt, n. D.—From Section 0 near Chorley to Preston. _ _ COST OF THE UNDERTAKING.

It is approxilf-ta-eliest-i;Zed'illiTtite—c7s-t..;;ith full equip- ment of rolling stock, will be about £.-5,000 per mile. Detailed estimates are in course of preparation. ESGINEERING OPINION. By Mr. Thomas Hawksley. CE., 30, Great George-street, Westminster, and Mr. Edward Woods, C.E., (in, Victoria- street, Westminster. (Copy) 30, Great Gebrge-street, Westminster, S.W., June 15th, 1882. Dear sir.—We have carefully considered the Lancashire Plateway project. In an engineering point of view it is per- fectly feasible, and in a commercial point of view it will be not only a great public convenience, but also as we believe, a pem- ntary success. We are, dear sir, faithfully yours, (Signed) T. HAWKS LEY, EDWARD WC.ODS. Alfred Holt, Esq. PRELIMIN&RY FUND. An undertaking of the magnitude described can only be set on foot by carefully and patiently going through all necessary preliminaries. For this a preliminary fund is required, mid it is estimated that £75,000 will suffice. The present object is to obtain subscribers to that fund. _ _

It is wanted for the following purposes :- 1. Complete survey, design, and parliamentary estimate of capital. 2. The preparation of such drawing and models as will serve to illustrate the mode of working. 5. The application to Parliament for the necesthy powers, followed, if those powers are obtained, by _
_ applications to the public for the capital. The mode proposed for obtaining this preliminary fund is as follows : •

Each subscriber will, if an Act be obtained, become entitled to have allotted to him at par an amount of stock equal to ten times his subscriptions, and the sum he has contributed will be taken as part payment for the same. There is no doubt that the bill will encounter opposition. A new system of carriage is not likely to receive legislative sanc- tion without searching and adverse criticism. This can only be overcome by submitting careful designs, accurate estimates, and clear demon tration of a public advantage. The surveys and estimates are so far advanced that they will be completed in time to apply :for a bill in the session 1882-3, when, if the Act be obtained, a public Company, with a reli- able amount a capital, will be announced, and the usual machinery for permanent management put into operation. The amount promised to the preliminary fund has warranted the making the surveys and other preparations for depositing a bill (all these are in an advanced state), but further assistance is required for meeting the expenses of carrying the bill through Parliament. A "preliminary committee "of five is proposed. The f glow- ing three gentlemen, with power to add two others hereafter, have agreed to constitute the nucleus of this committee. viz.. Mr. Thos, D. Hornby, Mr. John Greenwood, and Mr. Alfred Holt.

Messrs. Hawksley and Woods are proposed as engineers, and Mr. J. C. Rees as parliamentary agent; Messrs. Thornely end Dlsmore solicitors and secretaries in Liverpool, and Messrs. Bircham & Co. solicitors in London. The gentlemen named be:ow (together with others) are willing to provide about £35,000 to the fund for preliminary expenses. It is sought by this advertisement to obtain the remainder. Subscriptions to any amount are solicited. Any further information will be afforded by the Secretaries to Any applicant in person or by letter. TEIOBNLEY aLd DISMORE. Solicitors, 14, Water-street, Liverpool, Secretaries. SUBSCRIBERS. - - -•

THE AUTUMN WOODS. The autumn woods are glowing In robes of gold end red, The summer green is going. The leaves will soon be dead; And soon the winds will mutter Their sorrowful refrain, And down the leaves will flutter, Like showers of golden rain. AERIAL PHOTOGRAPHY.—The Municipal Council of Paris having voted a grant of 1,000 francs to the Academy of Meteorological Ascension for the purpose of nuking experi- ments in aerial photography, an ascent was made on Sunday by members of the Academy from the Carrefour de l'Obser- vatoire. They carried with them an apparatus for taking instantaneous photographs. This had six lenses pointing in different directions, so as to embrace the whole of the hori- zon and to produce a panoramic photograph. The balloon rose 200 metres. A telephone was afterwards fitted up in the car to enable the occupants to communicate with their friends below. • STOCKING ENGLISH LAKES WITH AMERICAN BASS.-Mr. Silk, the well-known pisciculturist, of Barghby Park, Stain- ford, landed in New York at the beginning of the month,on his way to Greenwood Lake and the Delaware, where he lintends to secure 2000, young bass to bring back to Eng- land. In 1878 Mr. Silk secured 240 bass, which averaged from three to four inches in length. In 1879 he took away with him over 1,100 bass, 812 of which survived the voy- age, and were in due time along with their fellows. The fist, which he took to England in 1878 and 1879 were placed in the Like Whitewater, near Stamford, on the estate of the Marquis of Exeter. The fish have always done well. Those I first introduced weigh from one and a quarter to one and a I half pounds, and the second lot have increased to three- quarters of a pound. The fish are breeding, and the expert- ment has been so far successful that it is to be repeated on a larger scale. Of the 2,000 bass with which Mr. Silk expects to be returning by the end of this month, some are for the Duke of Manchester, others for the Westminster Aquarium, the Lowestoft Acclimatisation Society, a reservoir at Wake- field, and several reservoirs near London. THE INTRODUCTION OF THB POTATO.—Solanum tuber- osum, the common potato of our fields and gardens, was first introduced by Sir Walter Raleigh, who brought the roots from Qaitto. and caused them to be planted in his own garden at Youghal, in Ireland. On the plants arriving at maturity Sir Walter's old gardener, availing himself of the privileges of his situation, gathered some of the fruit or "potato apples," as they are now called, and tasted them. Those of our readers who have eaten of this particularly unpalatable and unwholesome production will feel no won- der that the ire of the old man should have been raised. Breaking in unceremoniously on his master's studies, he ex- claimed, If this is your fine foreign fruit, I would not give it garden room, not I!" " Well," said Sir Walter, "if it is as bad as you say, dig it up at once; but if you find any roots worth looking at bring them to me." It is, perhaps, needless to say that the roots proved very well worth exam- ining. It was not, however, until about 1732 that regular potato crops wore cultivated in Scotland. Eogland followed the example set by the Scottish farmers, and grey the new root. So deep was the prejadice existing against this plant In the minds of the ignorant that when the R11i3i2621 Govern- ment issued seed potatoes to the native cultivators, with orders to attend to the increase of the crop, the new tubers were called the "Devil's apples," a name which, in sortie remote districts of the Oural, they still bear.—Cassell's Popular Educator. it is always safer to err in Lvour of others than of our- relves. Alpst of the sbadows that cross our path through life are carded by standing in cur own light. It is the diligent head_ alone that maketh rich in self. culture, growth in wisdom, and also In huilness. Take care to be an economist in protparity there is no fear of your being one in adversity.—Zi ionerman. Grief knits two hearts in closer bonds than happiness ever can; and common sufferings are far. stronger links than com- mon joys. Shame is a painful sensation excited by a consciousness of guilt, or having done something which inures repata- tion.—Dr. Webster. Wealth, after all, is a relative thing, since he that has little, and wants less, is richer than he that has much but wants more.—Colton. There are many things that are thorns to our hopes until we have obtained them, and envenomed arrows to our hearts when we have done so.

A physician gives f-a-dozen reasons why men grow bald. They all amount to about the same thing—it is because their hair comes out. A man should be virtuous for his own sake, though no- body were to know it; as he would be clean fo: h;s own sake, though nobody were to see him. True fortitude I take to be the quiet possession of a man's self, and an undisturbed doing his duty, whatever evil be- sets or danger lies in his way.—Locke. Always be good-natured if you can. A few drops of oil will do more to facilitate the movement of the most stub- born machineryithen rivers of vinegar. "Yes," said Morgan, "the gentleman you speck of is very agreeable as you say. I found him one of the most agreeable menl ever met. He doesn't say much." Nature is just towards men. It recompenses them for their sufferings; it renders:them laborious, because to the greatest toils it attaches the greatest rewards —Montesquieu. DI-humour is nothing more than an inward feeling of our own want of merit, a diseatiefaction with ourselves, which is always united with:an envy that foolish vanity excites.— Goethe. Depend upon It, that If a man talks of his misfortunes, there is something in them that is not disagreeable to him; for where there is nothing but pure misery, there never is any recourse to the mantis's of it.—Dr. Johnson. For the length of life there is no law. The weakest thread will draw itself out to an unexpected length, and the strongest is suddenly cut off by the scissors of Fate, who seems to take delight in contradictions.—Gathe. Daring a trial a judge called a witness. No one answered, and an elderly man arose and solemnly said, "He is gone." "Where has he gone ?" asked the judge in no tender tone. "I don't know; bat he is dead," was the guarded reply." Pride, 111-nature, and want of sense are the three great sources of ill-manners; without some one of these defects no man will behave himself ill for want of experience, or what, in the language of fools, in called khowing the world. Husband and wife should no more eruggle to get the last word than they should struggle for the possession of a lighted bombshell. Married people should study each other's weak points, as skaters look after the weak parts of the ice, in order to keep off them. By attention to this ap- parently small matter the COWS 3 of wedded life would run more smoothly, and thus happiness ensue. Some of the Chinese similes are said to be as pointed as they are sarcastic. They call a blustering, harmless fallow "a paper tiger." A man who paces too high a valuation upon himself they compare to " a rat falling into a scale and weighing itself." A spendthrift they compare to " a rocket," which goes of all at once, and a man who expends his charity on remote objects, neglecting his own family, is said to "hang up a lantern on a pole, which is seen afar, but gives no light below." A French lady recently died at the advanced age of ninety. Her will contained this provision :—I leave to my physician, whose enlightened care and wise prescriptions have made me live BO long, all that is contained in the old oaken chest of nay boudoir. The key of the cheat will be found under the mattress of my bed." The heirs were mach disturbed. The fortunate physician arrived. The chest was opened, and found to contain solely all the drugs and potions, still in.• which the doctor had given his patient for twenty years • back. TIINISTLN PaovEnus.—The foot goes where the heart iesda.—if the ass is invited to the wedding it is only that he may carry the wood.—Work for thy character until it be renowned, then it will work for thee.—Tire woman to whom fortune does not come says that her husband is bewitched. —He has no bread to eat and he is looking for a wife signi-

flee: Be not ambitious when your means —are limited.— It Is the crier himself who has lost his ask," is used in speak- ing of those who cannot do for themselves what they can do for others.—" What the grasshoppers have left the little birds have eaten," means that misfortunes never come singly.—" He went to the sea and found it dry," means that a cowardly man will always fail in his undertakings.— Hs fortune has turned into nails and straw," refers to a prodigal.—" He eats the fruit of the paternal garden and yet insults his ancestors," refers to ingratitude.—" One horseman does not make the dust cloud." This signifies that the work of one man cannot produce very great results. _A TURKISH Jusrwe's JUSTICS.—A poor Turkish slater, _ _ _ _

of Constantinople, being at work upon the roof of a house, lost his footing, and fell into the narrow street upon a man. Tne pedestrian was killed by the concussion, while the slater escaped without material injury. A. son of the deceased caused the slater to be arrested. The cad' listened atten- _ _ _ .

tively, and, in the end, asked the slater what he had to say in his defence. "Dispenser of Justice," answered the ac- cused," it is even as this man says.; but God forbid that there should be evil in my heart. I am a poor man, and know not how to make amends." The son of the man who had been killed thereupon demanded that condign punish- ment should be inflicted upon the accused. The cadi medi- tated a few moments, and finally said, "It shall be so." Then to the slater he said, "Thou shalt stand in the street where the father of this young man stood when thou didst fall on him." And o the accuser he added, "Thou shalt, if it pleases thee, go up on the roof, and fall upon the culprit, even as he fell on thy father. Allah be praised !" A Locomouvis ENGurE.---First let us have a look at the engine. It has a decidedly business-like appearance. Steam is up to fall pressure and is blowing off through the safety- valve with a fierce hissing sound. The engine is one of the most powerful that are made, and the driving-wheel is of Immense proportions. It is with no idle purpose that the driver and stoker examine the working parts, and pour oil _ _ _ _ _ _

upon all points of friction. There is the strength of a thou- sand horses embodied in this machine, and it is capable of conveying a load of 200 tons at a speed of 50 miles per hour. Its energy is generated in the boiler which occupies the cylindrical part extending from the funnel to the screen which shelters its driver and stoker. The boiler virtually consists of a large tabs having numerous small tubes tra- versing it from end to end. The ends of the small tubes are brought out through the ends of the boiler, and the use of the tusea is to carry heated air and flame through the water which surrounds them, and thus' cause it to be rapidly con- verted into steam. As the steam is generated it collects at a v high pressure in the large copper dome which very the boiler, and from that point it le conducted to the ear- mounts -cylinders through pipes The cylinders lie one on either side under the fore er,d of the boiler. When the steam is turned on it enters the cylinder, and camels a piston to move to and fro. The piston has a stout rod of iron attached to It which is connected wida a crank on the axle of the great driving-wheels. As the pistons Move from end to end of the cylinders they exert pressure on the crank and cause the wheels to revolve, aod so the train is drawn forward.—Fo,,s an article entitled" How we Travel by Railway," in " Little Folks' 11l .:,ne" for October

THE BULLDOG.—There is a considerable amount of 'igno- rance about this breed of doge, and it is cettain that his somewhat "uncanny" appearance has much to do with the prejudice against him. He is ens of the ugliest of all dogs, the broad, high, and large skull, the cheeks standing promi- nently beyond the eyes, the forehead tiat and much wrinkled, a peculiar indentation between the eyes, known as the stop; the short and wrinkled face, the turned--up muzzle, the flesh portion of which hiding the teeth; the nose black and large and well set back, the neck well arched, with plenty of dew- lap and great apparent strength; the deep, wide chest; the short back, the powerful-looking legs, between which the body appears to swing, all tend to give the animal a most peculiar appearance, and if we listen to the remarks passed by visitors to dog shows upon the bulldogs, we will find that they are not regarded with muck favour by the general pub- lic. It is true that the bulldeg is generally uncertain in temper, and the different varieties vary much in this respect. I Some are stupid and amiable, whilst others are very Zero- clone indeed—that is, to strangers, for, as a rule, this breed of dog is one of the most affectionate and gentle of the r whole dog race with those whom it knows. We have often been astonished at the way in which various specimens would bear knocking about by children or owners; but if anyone else offered to go near, the; instead of gentleness, there would be ferocity. They are not to be recommended as pets to be kept indoors, as the mere appearance of one of these dogs might seriously alarm a stranger, and their un- certain temper might also cause much mischief. If they are kept it should be in proper kennels whore they can he fas- tened up and prevented from doing any harm. The bull- dog is said to be typical of the British character in its per- tinacity, for when a good one gets bold of an opponent en I fastens its long fangs into it, then it will hang on until it either kills or is killed. Originally bled for the purpose of bull-baiting, this was a necessary qualification, and it was the dog which never showed the skits feather that was looked upon with most favour. To train young dogs, the best way is, let a couple each get hold of a piece of wood, and they will struggle over that long enough. We need I scarcely add that a bulldog is one of the best watchers that I can be kept, and no robber will venture near the place where one is—such gentlemen value their flesh too highly for that. VEGETABLES FOR DOGS.—A great mistake is often made by keepers of dogs in feeding them entirely on meat, or even meat biscuits, for dogs as well as all other animals need vegetables to keep their systems in order. Sporting doge, or such as have a very large amount of exercise, are able to throw off all the surplus heat, and can, therefore, be fed on the food already spoken of, the consumption of oil or fat, In consequence of their bodily activity, being sufficient. But for dogs kept in confinement, or as pets, or even those that have but a moderate amount of exercise, the result of feeding upon heating foods is to cause then to get fat and gross; they become indolent and inactive, and their skin is offensive, or internal diseases ensue. Tit-bits from the table cause more complaints amongst dogs than anything else, and these should be used very judiciously indeed. Every dog needs vegetables. Those working do not require them more than twice a week; but such as have very little exer- cise should have them every day, and, in fact, they should form, with wheaten bread or plain biscuits, the staple diet. , Messrs. Spratts, the well•known dog biscuit makers, have re- cently added beetroot to their cakes, and this is a valuable addition, sufficient for working dogs, but not nearly so for others, who should have vegetables in addition, if biscuits are used. This question of feeding is a very important one, and we shall return to it again. Firrneas FOR A PIGEON Lovr.—The first thing in fit- ting up a pigeon loft if breeding is intended, is to divide it Into two compartments, so that when young pigeons are about they can be separated from the older ones. If this is not done it will be found that the older ones will harass and annoy the others, if not absolutely injure them. Perhaps this may be thought to contract the space given to the birds, but as it is always advisable to avoid overcrowding the loft there need be no real danger of this, and the advantage is very much greater than any disadvantage, which will be more apparent than real. If the loft is a room with the window on one side the partition should run down the centre of the room to within three feet of the window' and a door hinged to the end of it, and so made that when it is thut at one side the birds can get to the aviary, which we may suppose iwill be outside the window, and one lot of birds will be shut in altogether. Then when it is thought desirable to let these out, the door can be shut on the other side to keep the Inmates of that compartment secure, and allow the others out. This is a very simple arrangement, but a very admir- able one. The pertitition should run to the top, bat the upper half will be better made of wire netting. If the loft Is an outhouse, so that the front of the house can be made with open doers, and the aviary be of fall size, then it is better to divide both loft and aviary into two, and there will be no need to restrict the birds, as would be otherwise neces- sary. The fittings of a pigeon loft will depend very largely upon the taste and pocket of the owner. The first thing in that portion which is to be devoted ta the breeding stock is to build a row of shelves, sty about fourteen or fifteen ioches apart, and twelve inches wide. The top row had better be wired in front, for use as preparation or matching pens; the others should be covered on the fronts, and so divided as to make a couple of nest boxes, slay twelve inches wide, with an open space between each of the same width. Thus, if a shelf is six feet long, it will make two pairs of nest boxes, one at each extreme end, and then open spaces, and two more back to back in the centre. Each nest box should he close at the front, one side and back, and two are given to each pair of breeders, as often there are young ones in one nest and eggs in the other. If the bottom shelf is kept , about two feet above the ground it will be all the better, as water fountain, food, or gravel boxes can be puthhere, and will be handy for the birds without being in the road.

CANARY daGi-Es.—We described the -breeding cage last week, but there is another form of cage which is most com- plete in itself, namely, the single one so commonly used. This has its own seed and water vessels, its little egg drawer can be readily handled, hung anywhere, and is easily cleaned outside as well as in—a by no means unimportant matter. But it is only a single cage, and no more. Yet it can be made into two, if large enough, by a movable partition, and thus it is useful either as a single or a double cage. The compartments can be used independently, or in connection with each other, when it is found necelsary to nse it as a nursery or for other purposes. By the adoption of varioaa kinds of sliding partitions, many convenient arrangementa can be effected s whisk It is obvious cannot be done in a

div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY' [ruuished bg Mr. E. J. KibPmckfte, 31, Tavistock-street London, TV.C., and a'epri'Ait.d.by perafission.] THE POWLETTS

As the present Duke of Cleveland calls himself Powlett, I suppose I ought to use that name ' • but, seeing that the family patronymic has been changed from Vane to Powlett, and from Powlett back to Vane, and from Vane back to Powlett again, perhaps some succeeding Duke may choose ' to resort once more to the illustrious name which his ancestors bore, and by which the family is best known. I may also explain at once that the present Dukedom of Cleveland is not the bastard Dukedom that:owed its origin to the adulterous connection of Charles 11. with Barbara Villiers, wife of the Earl of Castlemaine, who was created Duchess of Cleveland by her Royal paramour. That title descended to her eldest son by Charles 11., but subsequently ' expired. One of the Vanes, however, marriekt a female descendant of Barbara Duchess of Cleveland. The pedigree of the Vanes claims that they originally come from the borders of Wales; but at the earliest time of which anything definite is knows of them (Henry VI.), Henry Vane held the Manor of Hilden, in Kent. How it was acquired I know not, and it does not mucli matter, as it was sold not long after. At the beginning of the Reforma- tion, then, the Vanes were plain Kentish squires, and they appear to have been 'zealous supporters of the Reformed Faith. Sir Ralph, the son of Henry Vane, obtained a con- siderable grant of lands at Shipbourne, in Kent, formerly be- longing to the monasteries of Tunbridge and Dartford, which are, or at any rate were till recently, in the posses- sion of his descendants. Sir Ralph was one of the entourage of the Protector Somerset. Sharing in his prosperity, he shared likewise in his fall, and was finally hanged upon Tower Hill. If Burnet is to be believed, he was a man who merited a better fate. Though Sir Ralph died an ignominious .death, his lands passed to a kinsman who narrowly escaped a similar fate of his share in Wyatt's rebellion.

The next heir of the property was the real builder of the fortunes, if not of the greatness, of the house. Throughout the history of James I. and Charles I. the name of Sir Henry Vane^often occurs, though his fame has been altogether obscured by that of his illustrious son.* Clarendon speaks disparagingly of him; and, indeed, he deco not appear to have been anything more than a successful courtier. It was as a courtier that he rose to be a great landowner. Clarendon says that "his fortune was not great, but he found many ways to improve it," which is -quite true, as we shall see. In the reign of James I. Vane was appointed Cofferer to the Prince of Wales; after the accession of Charles he was Comptroller of the Household; and subse- quently Secretary of State. We must now go back a little. In the reign of Elizabeth, Charles Neville, Earl Of We.,lmoreland, was engaged in an abortive rebellion to release Mary Queen of Sects and-restore the old Catholic faith. Mr. Fronde represents him as rather driven into' rebellion by fear than any other cause. He escaped, and took refuge in the Low Countries; tut all his vast possessions were confiscated. After the accession of James, he pleaded hard to be restored to his lands, inasmuch as he had espoused the cause of James's own mother; but the King, who had plenty of favourites to provide for, turned a deaf ear to the unfortunate Earl. I believe some of the Neville estates were in Shrgpelsire—at Wem, for instances, where the Duke of Cleveland :new holds property; but the greater part of the property was in Durham. Raby Castle had been in their possession for ,tenturies; so ako had Barnard Castle, which, on the confiscation of John Balliol's English estates, had been granted by the King to the 13eauchamps, front whom it passed by marriage to the Neville!. The Bishop of Durham, who was almost a King in the county, had a legal right to such forfeitures; but, in spite of adverse legal decisions, the Nevilles held feat to their grant. After the flight of the lass Neville, Earl of Weatmorela the estates remained for a time in the possession of Crown,. but in 1613 they were granted to Carr, the IC-ng's favourite. A year or two after, on Carr's disgrace and • - feiture, Raby, Barnard Castle, and Brancepeth, were granted to trustees for the augmentation and support of Prince Charles for ninety-nine years. Almost immediately the trustees granted the remainder of the term to Vane, the Prince's Cofferer, and in 1626 he obtained the reversion in fee for £1,500 fine, to be held in socage under £5l 101. rent, the woods to be surveyed and valued separately, azsd the fees of the several officers, £52 Os. per annum, to be discharged. Just the kind of bargain which we might have expected to be driven by a courtier of that period. Sir Henry appears to have done an extensive business in land-jobbing. I find that he sold Hadlow, in Kent, which he had inherited, and bought Fairlawn and Wrotham in that county. Douhtleas he had other good bargains which have escaped my note. Considering the advantages he had derived front his position at Court, his conduct in supporting the Parliamentary party in the later years of his life certainly savours of ingratitude. But as he grew old he came under the influence of his son, the Vane—
Young in years, but in sags counsel old, of Milton's sonnet.

Of the younger Vane it is needless for me to speak at length here. There is hardly one of the heroes of the Common- wealth that has so stainless a record. The man whom Milton praised, whom Cromwell feared, whom Charles 11. dared not allow to live, needs no poor eulogy of mine. He had been appointed Treasurer of the Navy, and is said to have relinquished profits of £30,000 per annum for the bene- fit of the Commonwealth. Of all the leading Republicans of that ago Vane was the most consistent, the most philoso- phic, the most statesmanlike. Cromwell takes beyond ques- tion the first place among the historic Independents, but the second place among that noble band must be accorded to Sir Harry Vane. His death was the best testimony of his great- ness. He was the only man who died upon the scaffold for his share in the Great Rebellion who was not actually a regicide ; and he was executed because, as-Charles It. wrote, he was "too dangerous a man to let live if we can honestly put him out of the way." He died on Tower Hill "like a prince," as a Cavalier who was present testified—a patriot and a statesman well worthy to be associated with Sydney and Russell. Sir Christ,pher Vane, son of the great Sir Harry, was knighted by Charles 11., and created a peer by William 111., with the title of Baron Barnard. He married the sister and co-heir of John Holies, Duke of Newcastle. He appears to have taken no active part in public life, but, like Mrs. Craik's well-known hero of fiction, John Halifax, he aided in supporting public credit at a critical moment by paying large sums of money into the Bank. The third Lord Bar- nard, who married the daughter of the Duke of Cleveland, son of Charles 11, held the lucrative office of Paynaaster of the Forces, and gained two steps in the peerage by his elm tion to the Earldom of Darlington in 1754. The third Earl of Darlington, who was created Marquis of Cleveland in 1827, was one of those wise and s'atesmaelike nobles who so largely aided in saving the country from a revolution half it century ago. We are accustomed to indulge in sneers. at "the Whigs" in these days, and the debt of gratitude which the country owes the Whigs of 1832 is too often forgotten. For my part I would rather prefer to remember their virtues than their failings. Let us take the Marquis of Cleveland, for instance. He seems to have considerably increased his landed property by purchase. I have stated above that the Vanes have property in Somerset, Cornwall, and Sussex. A portion of this seems to have been acquired for political purposes, though, under the circum- stances, with a most laudable object. Tile Marquis com- manded no less than six borough seats, before the passing of of the first Reform Bill, namely, two each for Ilchester, Camelford, and Wichilsea. Of that Bill he was an ardent supporter. Taunted with being a borough-monger, the Marquis frankly declared that he had purposely, at great expense, obtained the control of his boroughs because such property was so often used for improper purposes, and there was no other mode of counteracting those who thus used it. A nomination borough he declared to be "a species of pro- perty, if such in any sense it could be called, that could be desired only for the sake of two objects—either for the sake of Parliamentary influence, or for the pecu- niary advantages to be derived from a sale of seats in the House of Commons; and, if such property was bad in one sense, it was bad in the other, and ther.fore it ought to be put an end to both ways." It is said that the purohast

div.head: RETURN OF TROOPS FROM EGYPT.
div.p: THE RETURN OF TROOPS FROM EGYPT.

The second detachment of Household Cavalry marched through the metropolis on Sunday, and were welcomed with of course, f " which hth c were popular ovation surpassing even that given on Friday to to the Royal Blues. They were preceded by three bands, viz, those of the Ist Life 'Guards, the Royal Horse Guards tunee was,nt Blue, and the Middlesex, which played alternately. Their first Cce most nclueritlgapilpreorporeiaotmeesin" the xul han;,-"rimz tepreSeniative detachment of troops whose courage and endurance in Egypt, as testified by the highest authorities, have never been surpassed in the history of the British Army. Although considerably bronzed, the men, like their horses, are thinner than when they left, whilst their scarlet jackets, faded and soiled, indicated the effects of the Egyptian sun and the inevitable ineiclent4 Qf war. At many points were displays of flags, banners, and mottoes of wel- come. Even where these were occasioeally wanting there was no lack of enthusiasm on the part of the populace. Among the onlookers in Piccadilly was the Prime Minister. .Mr. Gladstone stood at a window in the house of the Marchioness of Aylesbury, and was much cheered by the ourside crowd. The etreet decorations were especially pro- fuse at Knightsbridge. Within the barracks yard itself there was but a small company of spectators. The band of the Coldstream Guards was in attendance, and at a quarter past two o'clock played "God save the Queen" in recogni- tion of the arrival of the Prince aad Princess of Wales and their daughters, also of the Duke of Edieburgh, the Duke of Tick, the Princess Mary, and the Duke of Cambridge. At ten the Prince of Wales briefly addressed the troopers in the Riding School, and is said to have congratulated them on their military achieverneets. Among those present in the barracks, in addition to the royal visitors, were Lord and Lady Pembroke, Lod and 14,dy Browelow, the Marquis of Ormonde, the Hon. Cecil Duncombe, Lord Charles Bruce, the Hon. B. Fitzpat, ick, Asc. Having inspected the stables, the royal party drove off shortly before four o'clock, whilst the returned troopers went to dine or receive welcome from their rejoiced friends. The arrival of the Post-office Corps from Egypt on Tues- day caused great excitement in London. A hundred men joined the Post-office service, and over 40 were sent out, the rest being held in reserve. It was the first occasion that a volunteer force had been sworn in under full army regula- tions, and all the men rill be transferred to the reserve, re- ceiving reserve pay arid the Egyptian medal. The men reached Waterloo in the afternoon, under the ceemmand of Captain Sturgeon and Lieutenant Vial!, and were met by Colonel Du Plat Taylor. Headed by two two bands, they marched through an enthusiastic crowd to the General Post Office, where they were received by the Postmaster General and leading officials. The Chatham division of the Royal Marines returned to head quarters on Monday, from Egypt. The Duke of Edinburugh was at the docks to welcome them in an aldress, in the course of which he acknowledged the bravery of the Marines in action, and regretted the loss of sa many of their comrades. The troops were enthusiastically received in the town, and they will shortly be entertained at a banquet. On Tuesday evening, a banquet was given at Windsor to the 2nd Life Guards on their return from Egypt. The Mayor presided, and the guests, 500 in number, included the whole regiment, as also Prince Christian, Mr. Richard- son Gardner, M.P., Lieutenant-Colonel Ewart, cic. The Mayor, in proposing the health of Colonel Ewart and the officers and gentlemen of the regiment, alluded to the gal- lantry displayed by the troops, especially in the night charge at Kassassin. Colonel Ewart was received with prolonged cheers on rising to return thanks. On Monday afternoon the men composing the Plymouth detachment of the Royal Marines, returned from Egypt, were entertained at a banquet by the inhabitants of Stone- house at St. George's Hall. An immense crowd cheered the men on arriving at the hall, and the band played "See the conquering hero ',•comes." :The building was handsomely decorated, and the dinner was attended by the Mayors of Plymouth and Devonport, officers of the port and garrison, the borough members, Captain Price and Mr. Puleston, and others. The Duke of Cambridge wrote expressing regret at his inability to attend, as also did Colonel Howard Jones. labsent on service.

The banquet to the Royal Horse Guards Blue which was postponed in consequence of the marquee having been blown down, was given on Wednesday evening in the Town Hall, Holborn. A banquet to the Ist Life Guards was given on Wednes- day night, at Knightsbridge. Mr. Mitchell Henry, M.P., presiding, and the Duke of Teck and a distinguished com- pany being present. The toasts of the regiment having been very heartily drunk, Colonel Talhot and Colonel Keith Fraser responded, expressing the gratitude of the men for the hearty welcome home they had receifed.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

At the annual election on Monday, Colonel King-Harman (Her I%lajnty's Lieutenant of county Roscommon), was displaced from the poAtian of chairman of the Hoyle Town Commissioners, which he bad held for seven years. It is stated authoritatively that the Lord Lieutenant bas 13h2en pleased to commute the sentence of death passed on tke tad Michael Walsh to penal servitude for life. The,:e- priere of the young conorict hat given general satisfacti,an in Ireland. In one of the Nationalistic organs it is stated that Walsh is only in his timteentk year. An attack was made on Sunday night upon Patrick Dwyer, the postman who travels between Cullen and Tip- perary. The assault took ,place near Limerick Junction. Dwyer alleged that the men -seized him and knocked Lim to the ground. One of the mail bags was carried away. It wao subsequently found on the road, after having been rantacked. No arrests have been made.

Two men have been committed for trial charged with being the murderers of the farmer Browne, near Castle- island. The principal witness against them is a woman named Brosnan, a neighbour, who,, in her examination before the magistrates, said she did not tell at the inquest who the men were vriaom she had seen go into the fi-ld where the murder was committed, "because he would like to save them as they were neighbours." She afterwards told her priest that she had taken a false oath, and he bade her not de so any mere.

In opening the Dublin Commission, on Wednesday, Judge Barry commented on the extraordinary increase of crime in the city since the time when he was principal Crown Prosecutor. At that time the number of cases reached about 15, but on this occasion they numbered 75, and on an average amount to 50. Three of the cases to be tried are from other parts of Ireland under the Crimes Act, and of these the most important is the Maamtrasna murder, which, as the judge said, would be more justly described as a massacre, for five of the Joyces were killed and a sixth seriously injured, and, no doubt, left for dead. Ten persons, it will be remembered, are to take their trial for this terrible crime.

An incredible story is told in the columns of the Free- man's Journal. Some years ago a great sensation was caused in Belfast by the conviction of Dr. O'Hara, of that town, of forgery; and other unproven charges against him were that he had stolen a gold watch and chain, and caused the death of William M'Kee, of Grey Abbey, County Down. James Harvey, a recently liberated prisoner from Portland, now says that all these charges against Dr. O'Hara were false and the result of a wicked conspiracy, and the state- ment duly attested by a Catholic priest at Weymouth, has been sent to the Freeman for publication. It not only acquits Dr. O'Hara of all the knowledge of the crimes laid to his charge, but mentions the names of persons residing in the neighbourhood of Belfast who are said to have been in- volved in the conspiracy, and who really caused the death of 31Tee. No doubt the matter will be investigated, but, without corroboration, little credence will be given to it. Mr. Michael Davitt delivered a lecture at Clerkertwall on Monday night on the subject of the Castle Government of Ireland. Mr. Davitt said he' bad not abandoned the land question of Ireland, but would deal with it in Scotland dur- ing the coming week, and afterwards in Ireland, his deter- mination being to make it as hot as he could for the Irish landlords. He should persist in his agitation until not a single remnant of the existing infamous system remained. He denounced the unconstitutional manner in which Ireland was governed, and said there never could be peace so long as Englishmen placed Ireland in the clutches of such a Government. Regarding the question of the franchise, he complained that England and Wales had an unfair numerical superiority in representation over Ireland. If a direct-minded Englishman asked him to point out a just and feasible remedy for this everlasting Irish discontent he simply answered "extend the Irish people what you have extended to Canada; restore to the Irish people the right to make their own laws.". Till Irish landlordism was thoroughly destroyed, he would be its sleepless enemy. It will have been observed that in recent speecheseproml- nent members of the Liberal party have dwelt upon the evidences which are to be found of an improvement in the stite of Ireland. Such of their opponents as haVe been sceptical on the point can hardly refuse to give credence to the testimony of that most terrible of Irish resident magistrates, Mr. C:iffard Lloyd. That gentleman writes : —" A short time ago I was able to announce to the people that, owing to the immunity from mime in the baronies of Loualirea, Killartin, Leitrim, Athenry, and Dunkellin, his Excellency had been pleased, upon my recommendation, to direct that the tax for the extra police in those baronies, under the Crimes Prevention Act, should not be at present collected. The continued tranquility existing in that part of Galway has enabled me to ask his Exc,illency to revoke the proclamation issued under Section 18 of the Act, and this the Lord Lieutenant has now been pleased to do. I feel confident that the bles,,ing,s of peace and order, now in great part restored, will be fully appreciated by the people, and that for the future we may rely with some confidence upon their co-operation in preserving both."

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

~ HOUSE OF LORDS.—TITESDAY. Dont twenty-five Peers were present to-day when the Zunis met for the first time after the two months' adjourn- t.--.Earl GRANVILLE gave notice that he should on uraday moVe a vote of thanks to the army for the opera- te;o,l3s in Egypt, after which their Lordships will be asked to Journ until the 10th of /i)vember, when judicial business 1,711 be taken.—The Marquis of SALISBURY intimated that $24,1 the vote of thanks he shall ask a question with regard gtrie intentions of the Government as to the policy they -"*`*.tito pursue in Egypt.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIESDA.Y. 2rOr MEMBERFL—Mr Shaw took his seat for Halifax, Mr. Craig-Sellar for the Haddington Burghs. D 4y:ID R. CHURCHILL AND THE AUTUMN SESSION.—Lord Zeritriacimr. raised a question as to whether the holding adjournment of an autumn sitting is not a violation of .75titutiona1 practice. The hon. member, contending that course was a diminution of the ancient rights and rities of Parliament, moved the adjournment of the GrLADSTONE urged that if there was anything the principle contended for by the noble lord, his motion ould not be for an adjournment, but an address for a pro- s.,kgation The right hon. gentleman defended the course rE, en as the most reasonable and convenient, and justified ; on the ground of the unusual position in which the House `ellad itself in the discharge of its business. After a dis- 51on, in which Sir S. Northcote, Mr. Gorst, Sir W. Har- Van, and Sir H. D. Wolff took part, the House went to a Krision, and the motion for adjournment was defeated, the rahers being for the motion 142, against 209; majority vi.

ImpRISONMENT OP MR.
