div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

On Saturday the chainmakers in the South Staffordshire and East Worcestershire districts gave notice for an advance of 10 per cent, in their wages. At a meeting of the Board of Arbitration and Conciliation for the manufactured iron trade of the North of England, held at Darlington on Monday, Sir Joseph Pease was unanimously chosen on the suggestion of the men to act as arbitrator in the counter claims of masters and men—one being for a reduction of 7i per cent. and the other for an advance of like amount. _

THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—For the present, busi- ness in the iwn market, so far as new orders are concerned, seems to be atomparatively in abeyance. Although pig-iron makers have comparatively little or no iron to offer for delivery this year, there is a disposition to book forward orders at slightly under top prices, and Lancashire pig-iron could be bought at about 50s. per ton, less 21, delivered equal to Manchester; distinct brands such as Lincolnshire and Derbyshire, are also slightly easier in the top quota- tions, and in Scotch and Middlesborough iron there is very little doing. In finished iron there is some underselling, notwithstanding that makers have, as a rule orders in hand for the next three months. For delivery equal to Manchester the basis of prices is about an average of £6 15s. for bars, but there are sellers at as low as X 8 103., whilst in a few cases £7 par ton is asked. Sheet iron is in better demand than other descriptions, and is proportionately firmer in price. Tai LANCASHIRE COAL TEADE.—The coal trade has during the past week been in an unsettled condition in anti- cipation of the action of colliery proprietors with regard to prices and wages. As already intimated, an advance of 10 per cent. is being offered to the men generally throughout Lancashire, which is being accompanied by an upward movement in prices. In the Manchester district the ad- vance, which will be 101 per ton on round coal, and sd. on engine fuel, does not come into effect until the close of the month, but the West Lancashire colliery proprietors are already in some cases issuing notices of an advance ranging from 6d. to is. per ton. For the present prices are irregular, and can only be given approximately as averaging 10s. to lie. for best coal at the pit mouth, 3s. to 9s. for seconds, 7s. to 7s. 6d. for common hoase coal, 6s. 6,1. to 7s. for steam and forge coals 4s. 9d. to ss. 3d. for burgy, and 3s. 6d. to 4s. for ordinary slack. There has been a generally good inquiry for all descriptions of round coal during the week. Slack has been rather plentiful, with inferior sorts bad to move. The demand for shipment has been active, especially at Garston, and better prices have been realised. REVIEW OF THE GRAIN TRADE.—A week of almost un- broken wet,weather has put a atop to wheat sewing, except- ing on the soils which are light enough to work at any time when it is fine overhead. The weather has been against the threshing and marketing of wheat, and samples have come to hand in a very bad condition as a general rule. In provincial markets fine seed wheats have been raised is. per quarter, but in London the rates of the previous week have not been exceeded. Flour has met a very quiet trade at former rates, excepting that the value of London household declined 6d. on Monday last, and the condition of country flour has been such as to cause dissatisfaction. Fine malt- ing barleys have hitherto come forward very slowly, and prices have remained very steady. The demand for malt has been scarcely so good as during the previous week. For other descriptions of native produce there has been no change in values. The trade for foreign wheat on the spot closed very dull, and, if anything, weaker. Foreign flour has not come to hand quite so freely of late in London, and although trade is slow, prices have been sustained without elifficulty. Foreign barley has met a dull trade at unchanged rates.—Hark Lame Express. WAGES AGITATION IN THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE: GENERAL ADVANCE CONCEDED TO THE MEN.—As antici- pated last week, the action taken by the Manchester coal. owning firms in voluntarily conceding to the men an ad- vance in wages, aid which has led to similar action in the immediately surrounding colliery districts, has been followed by a movement in the same direction in the West Lanca- shire coalfield. On Tuesday a meeting of the West Lanca- shire Coalowners' Association was held at Liverpool, to take into consideration the application of the men for an ad- vance of 15 per cent., and it was resolved to offer an ad- vance of 10 per cent. Although this does not meet to the full the demands of the men, there isJitttle doubt that the favourable compromise offered by the employers will be ac- cepted, and that a stoppage of the collieries, which seemed imminent, and would certainly have been carried out unless the men had obtained some concession to their demand, will now be averted. This advance in wages will of course be accompanied by some advance in prices. Already some of the NVest Lancashire firms in anticipation of the action de- cided upon on Tuesday, have sent out notices of an advance of is per ton on round coal, and 5d per ton on engine classes of fuel, and this will no doubt be followed pretty generally throughout the district.

div.head: HEIR OF THE SALISBURYS.
div.p: THE HEIR OF THE SALISBURYS.

The coming of age of Viscount Cranborne, eldest son of the Marquis of Salisbury, was celebrated at Hatfield House, Herts, on Monday, and the festivities will be continued during the greater part of the present week. On Monday Lord Cranborne received several deputations, who presented addresses congratulating him upon attaining his majority. Among the addresses was one from the Mayor and Cor- poration of Hertford, which referred in complimentary terms to the connection existing between his lordship's family and the borough. Lord Cranborne signified his in- tention to sit for his portrait, to be subscribed for by the tenants on the estate. On Monday evening between eight and nine hundred tenants and other guests were entertained at a magnificent banquet, at which the Marquis of Salis- bury presided. Later on a ball of great splendour was given, nearly a thousand persons attending. The company included the Marquis and Marchioness of Exeter. Sir S. and Lady Northcote, the Earl and Countess of Galloway, Lord and Lady Rayleigh, tic. The house and grounds were illuminated in the evening by about for hundred elec- tric lights, and the adjacent town of Hatfield was also illu- minated.

Further festivities took place on Tuesday. The work- men and cottagers, with thdr families, were entertained to luncheon, and later on the chilOren attending the Countess Anne's School were provided with dinner. At dusk there was a display of fireworks. Owing to the unpropitious weather the athletic sports arranged for the villagers were post- poned.

div.head: SERIOUS STABBING CASE AT WIDNES.
div.p: SERIOUS STABBING CASE AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and E. K. Muspratt, a rough-looking and elderly man, named Robert Connor, was charged with cutting and woundinc, Patrick Howley, in a lodging-house in Oxford-street, Widnes, on the previous afternoon.—The prosecutor was in a very weak state, and had to be pro- vided with a seat whilst giving evidence. He said: lam a labourer, and lodge at a common lodging-house in Ox- ford-street, Widnes, kept by Joseph Mills. The prisoner is also a lodger in the same house. I was at my lodgings about five o'clock yesterday afternoon. The prisoner was also there, and bad been quarrelling with Mrs. Mills, the landlady, all day. I remonstrated with him, and told him to be quiet. Prisoner then got hp with an open knife in his right hand, and asked what was that to me. He then told meto leave the house, or he would take my life in less than five minutes. Prisoner afterwards sat down on the opposite side of the room to where I was sitting, and com- menced to sharpen his knife (which was a small black. hafted pocket knife with one blade) against the bench. Subsequently the prisoner came to my side of the room, and passed me as if he was going into another room, when he suddenly turned back holding the knife open in his left hand. As soon as I saw him coming to me I jumped, and qs I did so prisoner was going to "stiek " me in the stomach. The blow, however, caught me just behind the hip. I received a stab with the knife. When he stabbed me he muttered something to htmself, which I could not tell, and at once made for the door. Mrs. Mills locked the door and prevented the prisoner from making his escape. Cornelius Callaghan, a fellow lodger, was present when the wound was inflicted, and he went for the police. There was a wound made but it did not bleed very much. The wound gave me considerable pain at the time, but hurts me more to-day. I have been 'examined by Dr. O'Keefe, who dressed the wound, and I am at present under his care.—ln answer to the pri- soner, witness asserted that he did not strike him and knock his head, but merely pushed him away. Cornelius Callaghan gave corroborative evidence.—Dr. O'Keefe said: I was called in to attend Howley on the previous night. I examined him and found an incised transverse wound on his left thigh about one and a quarter inches in length, pene- trating nearly to the bone. The wound did not bleed much. I stitched it up and dressed it. It will take four or five days for the wound to recover before the man will be able to walk properly. It looked as if it had been stabbed, and was a very dangerous wound, as all stab wounds are. It was inflicted very near the femoral artery, and if the artery had been cut the man would have died in about five minutes.—P.C. Savery (672) said: From information I received I went to the lodging-house of Joseph Mills, in Oxford-street. I there Law Howley, who was bleeding from a wound on his thigh. He said Robert Connor had inflicted the wound. The prisoner was there at the time and heard what was said, and I took him into custody'. I and P.C. Skinner, who was with me, searched for the knife, and the latter found it in the prisoner's left hand pocket. I after- wards brought the prisoner to the police station, where I charged him with cutting and wounding Patrick Howley with a knife. He replied, "I know nothing about it." I then examined the knife, but fonnd no marks upon it.—Mr. Evans: What condition was the prisoner in ?—Witness: He had had some drink, but was not drunk.—The prisoner, who had nothing to say, was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

A most enthusiastic reception was on Wednesday night accorded to Major-General Drury-Lowe on returning to Bournemouth from the campaign in Egypt. The gallant officer was presented with an address of welcome and con- gratulation.

div.head: 4;çcr q'r 1 N'Tn THE EXAMINER"' SATURDAY, OCTOB
div.p: 4;çcr q'r 1 N'Tn THE EXAMINER"' SATURDAY, OCTOB
MISCELLANEOUS.

At Frome, on Tuesday, Phippon, who was charged with shooting two of his servants and attempting to take the life of a third, was committed for trial. Typhoid fever is prevalent to an alarming extent in the mining village of Silverdale, North Staffordshire. The dis- ease broke out some weeks ago in an old building in a low quarter, and now there are over a dozen cases in the village. The vicar is at the head of a movement to isolate cases and administer relief where required. A correspondent informs us that the Midland Railway Company Dave made overtures for the pureaase of the Furness Railway, whicli extends from Carnforth to Barrow and Whitehaven, and also has communication with Winder- mere and Coniston Lakes. It is stated that an arrangement has been entered into for the transfer. A remarkable illustration of Mr. Gladstone's popularity was furnished on Friday. The Pidorial World announced as its special feature a likeness and a biography of the right hon. gentleman, and within an hour of its appearance the issue was exhausted. The office was kept open until midnight in order to meet the extraordinary demand for the paper. Seven hundred and ninety-two students matriculated on Saturday, 688 being pensioners and 124 sizars. The latter include 85 non-collegiate students. Trinity beads the list with 177, St. John's contributes 103, and Trinity Hall comes next with 60. According to the annual statement issued by the university marshal, there are now 3,090 members of the university resideuts. Of these 1,407 are in colleges, and 1,683 in lodgings. NATIONAL FUND FOR SOLDIERS' FAMILIES. A short time since General Taylor arranged a military tournament at Drayton Hall to raise a fund for the relief of families of soldiers killed, wounded, or disabled in the Egyptian catn- paign. £5OO were thus raised, and it is now proposed to enlarge its original scope, and make the fund a national one. Lord Elcho presided on Monday over an influential meeting held at the residence of General Taylor Eaton-place, W., and on the motion of Sir Duncan Campbell, a committee was formed for the purpose of taking steps to provide funds. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A SON OF LORD DALHOUSIE.—On Tuesday a sad accident occurred at Brechin Castle to the second son of the Earl of Dalhousie, Patrick William Manta Ramsay, whose age is three years. The little fellow was playing in the breakfast-room, when be fell and broke the bone of his thigh about hall-way down. Two medical gen- tlemen from Brechin were soon in attendance, and chloro- form having been administered they set the broken limb.l The Earl and Countess of Dalhousie are at present in England. NEW POLITICAL ORGANISA.TION.—A new political move- ment, termed "The Northern Reform dab," has been started in the north of England, and has its headquarters in Newcastle. It has the four northern counties as the basis of its operations, and a request to extend the basis so as to in- clude North Yorkshire is under consideration. Its main ob- ject is the union of the various political organisations in the four northern counties far the propagation of Parliamentary and Land Law Reforms, and to bring pressure upon the Government to have them carried through Parliament. ARRIVAL OF MRS. LANGTRY IN NEW YORS.—Mrs. Langtry arrived at New York early on Monday morning. The manager, accompanied by the newspaper representa- tives, Mr. Oscar Wilde, and a band of music, went down the bay to meet her, and she received them on the deck of the steamer at seven o'clock. She was in excellent health and spirits. The voyage has been rough, but she was not sick, and enjoyed it exceedingly. After passing through the usual interviewing ordeal, she was driven to the Albemarle Hotel, Broadway and Twenty-fourth-street, where she will occupy the same suite of rooms as Madame Bernhardt had.

SIR MOSES MONTMORR.—This veneral and highly- esteemed gentleman, whose name is associated with works of charity in every quarter of the globe, attained the ninety- eighth year of his age on Tuesday. Sir Moses Montefiore has not been content to advocate and subscribe; he has laboured personally on behalf of those who suffered oppres- sion. Forty-two years ago he journeyed to Damascus. and by his efforts secured better treatment for the people of his race; and subsequently he visited Morocco and Roumania to obtain a like end. In his eightieth year he undertock and successfully executed a second mission to Morocco; and, when in his ninety-first year, went to the Holy Land, in order to secure relief for his brethren.

_ A PRAISEWORTHY ACT. - Considerable excitement was caused on the Bradford Exchange on Monday by an occur- ence somewhat rare in commercial annals. A Mr. Archibald. Winterbottom failed, some thirteen years ago, with liabili- ties amounting to nearly £50,000, and the estate paid a com- position of 103. in the pound. Mr. Winterbottom has just issued a circular, dated Manchester, October 20, intimating his intention of paying the remaining 105 to his creditors, and on Monday morninga number of Bradford firms received cheques for various amounts en that basis. One of these was a gentleman who was chairman of the creditors' com- mittee, and whose share of the proceeds amounted to over £I,YOO.

LIBERATION SOCIETY.—The local subscribers to the Man- chester and district branch of the Liberation Society, at their annual meeting on Tuesday, had submitted to them by, their committee a report which was considered of a satis- factory nature, but Mr. J. H. Crossfield, who presided, said that many of the agitators for disestablishment were grow- ing impatient at tke want of definite pregress towards the object they had in view, and he hinted that it may be neces- sary for the Nonconformists to break With the Liberal party and send them into the shady region of Opposition in order to arouse them to the necessity of dealing with the question. The meeting resolved to press forward the matter, and expressed the firm belief that the early introduction into Parliament of a motion dealing directly with the Church of England would be a valuable means of testing and educat- ing the opinion of the country in regard to disestablish- merit.

Tun ALLEGED RITUALISTIC PRACTICES AT SHEFFIELD. —Great uproar arose at an indignation meeting held at noon on Monday at Sheffield to protest against the ritualistic practices at St. Matthew's Church in that town. The room was crowded, and included a number of the High Church party. The chief speaker was Mr. Wynn, the parish warden, who denounced Mr. Omtnanney, the vicar, as a Jesuit in the church; as a man who, whilst eating the bread of the Church of England, was doing the work of the Church of Rome; a man who was false and unfaithful. He expressed his in- tention of never resting until the plague spot of Ritualism had been removed. Mr. Bindley endeavoured, on behalf of the Ritualists, to show that Mr. Ommanney was acting according to the Prayer Book; but he was greeted with great uproar and cries of "No Popery." A resolution was passed, amid great cheering, condemning Mr. Ontmanney's practices, and asking the Archbishop of York to put them down. THE MANCHESTER UNITY.—The intricate calculations necessary to ascertain the financial position of the Man- chester Unity every year have just been completed for 1831. The Order numbers 452 districts, comprising 4,158 lodges, having altogether 547,909 members. The capital on the Ist January last was £5,043,277, an increase during the year of £198,285. These figures relate only to sick and funeral funds ; but, including widows and orphans, juvenile so- cieties and other collateral funds, the total capital of the so- cieties, is £5,291,890, or nearly £9 15s. per niember. The income during the year was £761,649, of which £185,025 was interest on funded capital. The payments for sick benefits amounted to £420037, an average of 15s. 4fl. per member, and £13,000 in excess of 1881. Besides this, £111,279 was paid on the death of members and members' wives, making the total paid for ordinary sick and funeral benefits £531,334. TIER BISHOP OF LIVERPOOL AND THE SCOTCH CHURCH. —Speaking at a meeting of the British and Foreign Bible Society, on Monday, at Waterloo, the Bishop of Liverpool said he was glad to meet ministers of other denominations in order to show to the sneering world that all their differ- ences of opinion did not prevent them meeting on a com- mon ground in order to make them wise unto salvation. He was amused at the furious attacks made upon him while in Scotland. Finding no Church of England, he did not feel the smallest hesitation in working in a Presbyterian Church. The clergyman asked him to take the service and preach for him, and he aid so. He took the whole service and con- ducted it according to the custom of the church. He wished he did nothing worle than that—(hear, hear)—and be was not aware of any law he had broken. There was no Church of England place to go, and he had a perfect right to worship in a church where the Queen worshipped while in Scotland. He had that respect for the Queen and Crown that he was not ashamed to testify his respect for the Church of Scotland by taking part in the services while there.

GREAT &roux. Throughout Tuesday morning there were heavy falls of rain and snow, accompanied by a gale of wind, in the Midland, southern, and western counties, and the result recorded is an immense destruction of property. In Leicestershire, particularly, the floods were very disas- trous, and accounts from that district speak of railways being several feet deep in water and of streets in towns and villages being converted into rapid streams. A bridge on the Great Western Railway near Dorchester was washed away, and one of the carriages of a train fell into the gap. Fortunately the carriage was empty, and the other carriages, which contained passengers, remained on the line, and but little personal injury was sustained. As we have stated, the storm has already done great havoc, but it is feared that the mischief is not fully known. On Tuesday night many of the rivers were rising. Strange to say, the less of only one life is mentioned. A Bristol baker was drowned while out delivering bread in his cart. MR. WARTON AND CONSERVATIVE INGRATITUDE.—The Conservatives are treating Mr. Warton, says a London cor- respondent, with a base ingratitude. Under the advice of the Carlton Club, the Conservatives of Bridports have resolved to throw over their present member, and to support another candidate at the next election. Now, so far as the Liberal party is concerned, the removal of Mr. Warton from the House of Commons would be a great gain. He is simply a stupid and fanatical obstructive. He blocks bills which he has not even read, and he seems to think that it is the first duty of a member of Parliament to grevent all legisla- tion. Even under the new rules a person of Mr. Warton's ideas will possess considerable power, and the Liberals therefore will regard his abandonment by his politieal friends without any regret. But Mr. Warton has been eminently useful to his party. He has done fork for them which other members would scarcely care to perform. Whenever it was desirable to obstruct a bill, and it was advisable that the Conservative party should not be held responsible for the obstruction, Mr. Warton was ready to undertake the task. He is a Parliamentary oddity, and it was easy for his party to repudiate any complicity in his tactics. Mr. Warton thusdid his friends great service in the general business of obstruction, and he is naturally indignant at being thrown aside by tie leaders of his piny.

Mr. John Pearson, Q.C., has been sworn in a judge of the High Ccurt of Justice before the Lord Chancellor. Mr. Philip Currie, C. 8., of the Foreign Office, has been appointed Assistant Under Secretary of State, in succession to Sir Julian Pauncefote. The boot and shoe factory of Mr. Colin Grant, Arbroath, was destroyed by fire on Tuesday morning. The damage will amount to £12,000. _ _ _

The anniversary of the Balaclava charge was celebrated on Wednesday night by a banquet at Willis's Rooms. General Sir Edward Cooper Hodge, K.C.8., presided. Lord Stanley of Alderley has given notice that he will ask Her Majesty's Governmeht if they will now reinstate the name of Colonel Valentine Baker in the Army List.

An express train on the Great Eastern Railway, running between Spalding and Sleaford, ran off the rails on Wed- nesday afternoom at Kirkby Laythorpe. None of the passengers were killed, but two were badly hurt and others seyerely shakea. An action has been raisd against Mr. Alsop, solicitor, the London agent for the Balcarres family, by Philip, the person arrested on suspicion of writing the " Nabob " letters. Mr. Alsop's luggage has been detained at Edinburgh pending the trial of tile action.

Mrs. Gladstone opened a bazaar at Hackney on Wednes- day afternoon, held in aid of the school enlargement and vicarage building fund in connection with the parish of All Saints', Clapton. Mr. John Holms, M.P., presided. Mrs. Gladstone was accompanied by the daughter of the Bishop of Bedford. Loss OF A FISHING BOAT AND FOUR LIVES.-0110 of the boats belonging to Nairn port has baen missing since Mon- day, and the intelligence is confirmed that she foundered the same afternoon during a squall. Part of the wreckage has been picked up by boats which have returned from the spot where she was last seen. Her crew of four men have perished. The deceased were Alexander Main, who leaves a widow and five children; Hugh Hain, leaves a widow and five children; and Hugh Downie, leaves a widow and daughter; and Hugh Sergeant, unmarried. THE EXPENSES OF THE PRESTON GIIILD.—The treasurer of the Preston Corporation has just issued the financial statement of the recent Guild Festival. The amount paid by the Guild Committee towards the expenses of the cele- bration was £l,OOO. The receipts for balls was £3360, and for concerts £3,083, making, with other receipts of the week, £8,156. The expenses leave a balance of £626, which it is proposed to hand over to the Infirmary. The expenditure on the balls was £1,971, and on the concerts £2,785. The highest sum paid to any vocalist was Madame Albani, who received £367.

- THE Dux ECM' 011TRAGE : VERDICT AND SENTENCE.— The evidence and speeches of counsel in the charge against Charles Soutar, for removing the body of the Earl of Craw- ford from the vault at Dun Echt, having been concluded on Monday, Lord Craighill proceeded to sum up on Tuesday He reviewed the evidence at great length, and in doing so. pointed out that it was probable that more than one person was engaged in the removal of the body; but whatever num- ber were engaged in the work, if the prisoner at the bar was aiding and abetting, his guilt was the same as if everything had been accomplished by his own effort and skill. The jury, after half an hour's absence, unanimously returned a verdict of guilty, and sentence was passed of five years' penal servitude. IMPORTANT DECISION TINDER THE LICENSING LAWS.— At the Cardiff Police Court, on Wednesday, the Stipendiary heard a case involving an important point of law. Richard Jones, proprietor of the Coffee Tavern, was summoned, under the Licensing Act of 1874 and the Welsh Sunday Closing Act, for keeping his house open last Sunday for the sale of refreshments. After hearing the lengthy arguments of Mr. Vachell, who appeared for the defendant, the magi- strate held that as wine was not sold by the defendant, bat refreshments merely, the Acts did not apply. If he had sold wine, he would have come within the limits of the Sunday Closing Act, which referred to houses where intoxica- ting liquors were obtainable. The case was therefore dis- sikissed. - - -

On Monday Mr. W. E. Forster attended a meeting in Lon- don called for the purpose of forming a committee to en- lighten the ratepayers as to the questions which they will have to decide at the coming School Board election. The right hon. gentleman pointed out that London compared unfavourably with the provinces in the matter of school accommodation, and he contended that the rates ought not to be studied when the education of the children was con- cerned. Education was now more a necessity than it was in 1870, and the loss of it to a child was now a calamity. It was therefore a duty to nsake the means of education as efficient as possible. The question of free schools would have to be dealt with, as would also higher board schools. THE Vatan 01 A GREYHOUND. •—• There may very legitimately be a considerable difference of opinion as to the value of a greyhound, but a case at the Court of Pas- sage, Liverpool, on Monday, developed a divergence of views between the jury and a gentleman who claimed damages for the poisoning of his dog which somewhat surprised the court. Mr. John Donnan called at a butcher's shop and had his greyhound with him, bat seeing no one inside he turned to the door a minute or two, and his dog availed itself of the opportunity to eat some meat which had been 'poisoned for the purpose of killing vermin. He therefore claimed £2O damages, but the jury awarded him only Li; and when the clerk exclaimed" How much ? "the foreman stolidly replied, "Li—the value of the dog." To make matters worse for Mr. Donnan, the Judge, the damage being estimated at so low a sum, refused to allow costs; and as counsel was employed the death of the dog would be a dead loss to its owner.

A NICE QUESTION.—TWO Brighton ladies, one a dress- maker and the other a lady by whom she had been em- ployed, have imposed upon the judge of the Brighton County Court a somewhat difficult duty. The case arose through the lady refusing to pay the dressmaker for work done, because the dress did not fit. The dressmaker, however, indignantly declared that her customer had no figure, and as she was suffering with her liver she could not be squeezed, and consequently if was perfectly impossible to make her look like a Venus. No doubt the dressmaker's temper stimulated her tongue when she uttered these offensive remarks, but to settle matters it was decided that the learned judge should s2e the dress upon the lady, and judge fo, himself. This exhibition took place in the judge's robing room, the result being that his honour pronounced the dress to be not according to model, and the work very indifferently done. He therefore gave judgment for the defendant, which was some cpmpeilsation for the insult she had received.

IMPUDENT JEWELLERY ROBBERY ic MANCHESTER.—A few evenings ago a daring and temporarily successful rob- bery was committed at the shop of Mr. L. Beaver, jeweller, Cross-street. Soon after six o'clock, a well-dressed young man entered the shop and asked Mr. Beaver to show him some diamond rings. Suspecting nothing, the proprietor handed a case of rings from the window, and the young man after some delay, selected a handsome " dead-set " ring, value £2O. Instead of producing the necessary cash for payment, however, he turned and ran out of the shop, closely followed by Mr. Beaver. A long chase ensued, and the thief was finally overtaken by his pursuer on the further side of Deansgate. Thera a struggle took place, but Mr. Beaver succeeded in obtaining his property from the man, who, in the absence of any policeman, and backed by the sympathy ef a rough crowd which had collected, made his escape. After regaining the ring, Mr. Beaver went back to his shop, and informed the police of the occurrence, but the thief has not, up to the present, been further heard of. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT A MEETING: FALL OF A FLOOR: MANY PERSONS INJURED.—A terrible accident, by which a large number of persons were seriously injured, some it is feared fatally, occurred at Hanley on sunday evening. A short time before the hour appointed for the usual evening service at the Imperial Circus in connection with the "Sal- vation Mission" under "ox-Captain Gipsy Smith," who a short time ago was the cause of a split in the Salvation Army, a preliminary "holiness" meeting, attended by about 300 "soldiers" of the congregation, was held in an 'ante-room adjoining the building, and over a part of the circus formerly used as cineus stables. Suddenly the floor gave way, precipitating all present into the lower storey. This produced a terrible panic. Many person had their legs and arms broken, and all the others were bruised, shaken, or terrified. Many of the femals fainted, and lay as if dead until rescued by people who came almost im- mediately afterwards to the evening service in the circus. A fund is being raised for the relief of the sufferers.

THE EYANOEIIICAL ALLIANCE AND THE "HOLY CAR- PET."-At the Evangelical Alliance Conference at Leicester on Wednesday, it was decided to forward a memorial to the Government with respect to the participation of the English troops in the procession of the " Holy Carpet." It was re- presented in the memorial that the incident was seriously calculated to grieve all Christians, and amounted to a humili- ation inflicted in the name of England on those who con- sistently maintained the Christian faith. The Conference also gravely protested against the use of the English armies to render public service to the religion of Mahomet. It re- garded the plea that the troops were displayed only to do honour to the Khedive as not seriously advanced, and as being calculated to cause the populations of the East to re- gard us as a nation capable of adding levity to the disregard of our own religion, and of feigning respect for one hostile to it. The Conference lamented the violence done to the consciences of officers and men, and regarded as illusory the hope that any advantage would be gained by it. In conclusion, they asked the Government to take such steps as would prevent a repetition of such an incident. The Alliance also protested against the Sunday labour enforced upon English officials in Egypt.

ANOTHER EGYPTIAN Bum Booir. Another blue book of 343 pages on Egyptian affairs has been issued, which brings the correspondence up to the 17th of August. The correspondence deals principally with •the negotiations for the conference at Constantinople and the repeated invita- tions to ties Porte to send troops to Egypt. On July 4th Lord Lyons telegraphed to Lord Granville reporting a con- versation with M. de Freycinet who said Lord Dufferin had suggested to M. de Noaillea that they should join in propos- ing to the Conference that if Turkish troops went to Egypt two commissions, including representatives of all the Six Powers should be formed—one to superintend the oper- ations of the troops, and the ether to control the Egyptian administration. This M. de Freycinet authorised M. de Noailles to agree to. On the following day, however, Lord Lyons again telegraphed to Lord Granville, stating that M. 'de Frevcinet having been informed of the instructions given to the English Admiral at Alexandria felt himself unable to instruct the French Admiral to join in warlike operations. The French Government, M. de Freycinet ex- plained, considers they could not take part in offensive hos- tilities in Egypt without violating the Constitution, which required the previous assent of the Legislature, while if they , applied for the sanction of the Chamber they did not feel eonfident of obtaining it.
The Scotch fishing boats in the North Sea are safe. The miners at Low Beechburn Colliery Durham, returned to work on Thursday morning, after having been on strike over two months.

After an incarceration of nearly four days the two men entombed at the Gelli Pit, in the Rhondda Valley, have been brought to the surface. The &ods are subsiding at Trowbridge. Hundreds of persons have been thrown out of work at Bradford-on-Avon in consequence of the inundations. The schooner Comet, of Hull, from Sunderland to Teign- mcuth, foundered in the North Sea on Tuesday. The crew have been landed at Yarmouth.

The Senatus ileadentieus of Edinburgh University has resolved to confer the honorary degree of LL.D. on Lord Rosebery when be delivers his Mictorial address on the 4th proximo. The Press Association is informed by the owners that the hired transport Persian Monarch, with cavalry and troops front Egypt, arrived at Bombay on Thursday morn- ing all well. At the meeting of the Preston Town Council on Thurs- day morning, a letter was read from General Ponsonby on behalf of the Queen, accepting the Guild medal which the Council have resolved to forward to Her Majesty, and tendering her thanks. _ _

On Thursday morning, at the Preston Police Court, Martin Clarke was charged with breaking into a spirit ware- house through the roof, and also with breaking into Mr. Cooper's coal office, and robbing the drawers. He was com- mitted for trial.

The Irish party has not yet decided what course they will pursue upon the closure division. The general feeling is that they should oppose all restrictions on liberty of s'peech, but if the gag is to be applied it should be applied in such a manner that it will be felt by others besides the representatives of Ireland.

At a meeting of the Bristol Sanitary Authority, oa Thursday, it was stated that three thousand persons had been rendered nearly destitute by the floods, and that many small tradesmen have been ruined by the destruction of their stock. The medical officer reported that a large number of hoases have been rendered unfit for human habi- tation.

The Preston Town Council on Thursday passed resolu- tians in favour of the purchase of the Ribble Navigation by the Corporation for the sum of £72,500. The Ribble Navi- gation Company have offered to sell their undertaking for £75,000, but it is thought the present proposal of the Cor- poration will be accepted. The technical Education Commission has now resumed its daily sittings in London, and is engaged in the examina- tion of the executive chiefs in the Scieuce and Art Depart- ment, as well as in classifying and arranging the informa- tion and materials already gathered on the Continent and in Great Britain.

Regarding the Palmer missing expedition, an official tele- gram has been received at the Foreign Office stating that the remains of Captain Gill and Lieutenant Charrington have been found and identified, but nothing certain has been ascertained as to Professor Palmer.

Mrs. Langtry has secured clever managers for her tour in the United States. The auction sale of the seats for her first performance realised prices higher than any that have been obtained since Jenny Lind's time. The Prince of Wales has telegraphed to Mrs. Langtry his good wishes for the success of her tour.

On Wednesday night, whilst the Salvation Army proces- sion under the command of " Gipsy " Smith, was passing the local section of General Booth's army in the Market- place at Hanley, an old woman named Emma Gibbons sud- denly fell down dead. The cause of death is unknown. The event caused considerable excitement arnong the Sal- vationists.

An extraordinary shooting case is reported from Dundee. Quarreling was heard in the house of a family named Whyte, and firearms were discharged. It was afterwards found that two members of the family were suffering from bullet wounds—one of them being in a dangerous state— and their youngest brother, Hume Whyte, 18 years of age, an iron turner, was arrested. The 7 Birmingham magistrates on Thursday morning dis- charged with a caution a gunsmith named Walter Roberts for attempting to hang himself. Prisoner attempted self- destruction through a money lender, who had advanced him £7 at over CO per cent, interest, refusing to receive an ia stalment tendered a few days overdue, and Ecizing under the bill of sale instead.

At a conference of nut and bolt makers at Darlaston, on Wednesday night, it was stated that thousands of females worked at the forges in the same way as men in making nuts and bolts, They worked with the men, and frequently worked seventeen hours a day. The forges Ns ere never visited by the inspectors of factories, and the women were thoroughly demoralised. It was resolved to make further investigations, and afterwards to bring the matter before Parliament.

At an inquest held on Wednesday night at Wednesbury, respecting the death of Ann Holmes, who had committed suicide, it was shown that the deceased, after drinking for several hours, procured some vermin-killer, and, in the pre- sence of her son, attempted twice to take it in some tea. Whilst he went for some assistance, the deceased found the poison, which had been hid, and drank it, and shortly after- wards expired. -Verdict, "Suicide during temporary in- sanity." Reynolds, one of the Englishmen who was lately tried and acquitted at Berlin on the charge of being concerned in the Reichsbank robbery, has now been liberated, and has vanished with all due expedition from Berlin. His less fortunate companion, Berner, who was similarly acquitted, is stid in custody, and as soon as the necessary formalities have been gone through will be handed over to the English Government, which claims him on the charge of having commitled some large jewel thefts at Carlisle. The result of a ten days' Gospel Temperance Mission in Reading has been that over 2,500 new pledges have been taken. It is estimated that over 20,000 persons attended the meetings, toth the new and old Town Halls being crammed nightly. An official return by the temperance party shows that a quarter of the entire population of Reading have llscome total abstainers. There are to be further meetings at no distant date.

The agricultural returns for Great Britain for 1881, issued ou Tuesday, show the total quantity of cultivated land re- turned as under :—All kinds of crops, bare fallow, and grass amounted to 32,313,000 acres, or an increase of 100,000 acres over latt year. The whole of this increase was in England and Wales, Scotland showing a smaller cultivated area than last year, their being several instances of decrease caused by the conversion of sheep runs into deer forests. Peter M'Culloch, Liverpool, merchant, was charged on remand, at Liverpool, on Thursday, with smuggling 2,8001b5. of tobacco. Since the previous hearing the prisoner's brother lad been arrested, and the Commissioners of Cus- toms had determined to take the Case to a higher court, as they had power when large sums were concerned. The prisoner was therefore discharged by the stipendiary, but immediately rearrested in court by a detective, and he will be sent to London.

At Accrington, on Thursday morning, Edward M'Cor- mick a Furness man, was again charged with causing the deathe of John Bury, labourer, at Church, on Sunday week, under the circumstances previously reported. Dr. Buttle said death was caused by effusion of blood in the head, the result of the rupture of a blood vessel, which might have been brvught on by a violent blow or by excitement. There was no mark of violence. The prisoner was committed for trial at the Manchester Assizes, bail being allowed. Writing to a London j)urnal, a correspondent asks some interesting questions as to the present price of bread, meat, and fish. He says: " Wheat is now 93. per quarter cheaper than at this time last year. Bread remains unaltered. Who, then, pockets the difference and robs the public ? Foreign meat in carcases is largely imported and highly spoken of. What becomes of it, for it is never seen on sale here ? Twenty-five tons of Hudson's Bay salmon were quite re- cently imported frozen. Has anyone been able to buy some? I asked for information at a swell fishmonger's, but no one would admit ever hearing of it. The salmon for sale was styled 'Dutch.' " The memorial status of Thomas Carlyle erected on the Chelsea embankment was unveiled on Thursday by Professor Tyndall. In the course of his isaugural address, Professor Tyndall recalled the time of the bread riots in Lancashire in 1842, and Carlyle's words of sympathy evoked by those oc- currences. The condition of his toiling fellow countrymen oppressed him like a nightmare. Carlyle saw clearly the iniquity of the Cern Laws, His powerful advocacy of public education was prompted by his perception of the vanity of expecting political wisdom from intellectual ignorance. He eulogised Carlyle's many virtues, his lovo of truth, his humour, and his imagination! Mr. J. K. Cross, M.P., addressing a meeting at Bolton on Saturday night, claimed from his knowledge and his busi- ness relations with it to be able to speak with some authority on the Egyptian question. He said the troubles began in 1877 or 1878, when the Conservative Government passed over the insult offered to their servant, Sir (then Mr.) Rivers Wilson. Moreover, a good deal of the discontent had arisen from the abused power of the Joint Control, the creation of the Conservative Government. He therefore re- pudiated the blame thrown upon the present Government for the state of affairs in Egypt. At the Birmingham Police Court, on Thursday, Albert Woolf, aged twenty-three, tailor, was committed for trial for attempting to murder Lizzie Holland, his sweetheart. The prisoner and the young woman had been engaged for the past fifteen months, but owing to the former's jealousy the latter returned him all his presents, including the wedding- ring on the 10th inst. Next evening, according to the young woman's statement, the prisoner asked her to renew the engagement, but she refused. He thereupon seized hold of her arm, but she broke the grasp and ran away. Prisoner pursued her and stabbed her on the right side of her face, rendering her insensible, and she was carried to the Queen's Hospital, where she remained till Thursday morning from the injuries sustained. THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER AND MR. GREEN.—We (London Guardian) hear with much satisfaction that the Bishop of Manchester, undismayed by the obvious difficul- ties lying before him and by the defiant tone in which his communication to the patron of Miles Platting was received recently at Derby, is about to make a formal application to Lord Penzance for the release of Mr. Green. He has, it appears, been definitely advised that the living is now vacant under the provisions of the Public Worship Regulation Act. This vacation of the living may, we can see, be open to some legal question; and if it be so open it is at least highly probable—in fact, after Sir P. Heywood's impassioned declaration, it seems all but certain—that the question will be raised. But the bishop naturally acts on the opinion of his legal advisers till that opinion is proved to be erroneous; and, assuming that Mr. Green, having vacated his living, is no longer in a condition either to obey or disobey the moni- tion of the court, proceeds to apply for his release.

div.head: FOREIGN I NTFLUGVNCE, THE STATE OF EGYPT.
div.p: FOREIGN I NTFLUGVNCE, THE STATE OF EGYPT.

- ARABI PACHA : HIS TRIAL. • The Times correspondent has reason to believe that the entire proceedings may be stopped by a decree of exile against a ringleader and a general amnesty to the rest. Arabi expresses his intention of making a "clean breast" of everything, and some startling disclosures are anticipated. He says that events have proved to him the folly of hoping in any further national movement or of trusting to the Sultan, and that Egypt's future happiness necessitates the virtual government of the country by the English. The result of Arabi being accorded efficient legal advice is immediately apparent. A large trunk full of Arabi's papers has been recovered by Mr. Broadley, which is said to com- prise the complete correspondence with the Sultan and others from the commencement of the movement until the date of the arrest. These documents, which were secreted In all sorts of extraordinaiy places, have been collected by Arabi's son and negro servant under orders from Arabi. The documents are believed to be most important, and cer- tainly to contain a sufficient number of signatures to com- promise the whole of Islamism, but they have yet to be translated. _

—Mr. B r-o-adley and Mr. Napier the European counsel who have been detained for the defence of Arabi have now been admitted to an interview with their client. The prisoner is giving them full details and instructions. It is now con- ceded that counsel may call any witness, confront him with the prisone:, and cross-examine. This is perhaps the greatest concession, because hitherto Arabi had not known on what evidence the prosecution went, and had not the English Government interfered would have been convicted withont a chance of knowing his accuse's. Secondly, it is allowed that witnesses may be calle4 from foreign countries as well as Egypt, or their evidence be taken by commission. Thirdly, counsel may address the Court and have the right of final reply. Virtually the investigation will commence de ?tor°, but will not begin before the end of the Bairam holi- days. It is now admitted by counsel for the prisoner that all the elements of a fair trial are secured.

A late telegram from Cairo, which, however, needs con- firmation, gives currency to a rumour that the Sultan has given orders for the proceedings against Arabi to be stopped. In another telegram it is positively stated that the Egyptian Government has no intention to throw any obstacles in the way of a fair trial, or of doing anything to prevent the pro- ceedings from following their due course, whatever may be attempted by the Porte in that direction.

THE CHARGES AGAINST THE BRITISH TROOPS. Further evidence, if any were needed, has been given in contradiction of the allegations against our troops by the Cologne Gazette. These charges were in all probability manufactured on the banks of the Rhine. Baron Von Hagenow, the German attache at headquarters, declares himself perfectly convinced of the utter falsity of the charge, adding, "Your great fault was over-humanity, for you ceased firing when the enemy turned their backs. In our army we should have considered it the moment of harvest, and have continued firing." As regards miner charges, M. de Boissy, the correspondent of the Temps, foolishly picked up and wore a helmet belonging to one of the Black Watch. The Highlanders, not the Indians, mistook him for a spy, and roughly treated him. Colonel Methuen recovered all his effects except his revolver and glasses, and expressed his regret, which was perfectly well received. This same, M. de Boissy discovered that our troops had entered Tel-el-Kebir with "a golden key," and not by sheer fighting. THE REORGANISATION OF THE EGYPTIAN ARMY. Baker Pasha's proposals for the re-organisation of the Egyptian Army are now published in detail, and are very easily understood. Accepting the fact that the officers of the late Army are unreliable, he proposes that non-com- missioned officers should be recruited from among Bosnians, Albanians, awl Bulgarians, and that half of the superior officers should be Englishmen engaged for two years, the other half being selected from loyal P,gyptian officers. Half the proposed regiments would have English and the other half native officers, and in this way an advantageous rivalry would be created, The Army, be thinks, should consist of 0,000 Infantry, 1,000 Mounted Infantry, 500 Cavalry, 600 Horse and Field Artillery with 24 guns, 1,000 Garrison Artillery, 100 Engineers, 1,400 Gendarmerie, and 300 men attached to the Commissariat, &c., making in all a force of 10,900. The Staff would be composed of an equal number of English and Egyptian officers, and the total annual cost of the Army would not exceed £36B,ooo—the amount formerly set apart as Army expenditure. In approving of Baker Pasha's scheme for the reorganisa- tion of the Egyptian army, the Government of the Khedive made only a few slight modifications, the most important of which is that providing that British offcers shall be ap- pointed as instructors to all regiments commanded by native officers. TROUBLE IN THE SOUDAN.

Arabi's insurrection has been quelled, but Professor Schweinfarth, who is a great authority on Egyptian affairs, is of opinion that his rebellion WAS a small matter compared to the trouble that is brewing in the Soudan. There the false prophet who has so long been spoken of is still to the front, and is gathering strength and fame. There is a belief, too, among Mahommedans, that the new prophet will be revealed on the 12th Novinnber, and this, coupled with the news of the false prophet's successes, causes great excite- ment. In June last 6,000 soldiers are reported to have been surrounded .2 and massacred, and the important town of Khartonm:is expected to be attacked as soon as El Obeid, the sapital of Kordojan, which has long been beseiged, is captured. Should Khartoum fall into the hands of the prophet, Professor Schweinfurth believes that the whole of Upper Egypt will rise in his favour. Another report of the war against the false prophet in Sonthern Egypt gives a more serious account of the situa- tion than that already published. It is now said that an Egyptian force of 12,000 men, led by Yusseff Pasha, was in July surprised in the Gadir Mountains and massacred, only one officer and twenty-seven soldiers escaping. The report of this incident has taYelled a long way, and has no doubt grown as it progressed, but there can be little doubt that the false prophet is by this time a formidable personage.

div.head: JOINT CONTROL.
div.p: THE JOINT CONTROL.

The Cairo correspondent of the D-7711—y- Telegraph states that the following important modifications in the Joint Control are now under consideration by the Egyptian Ministry. It is proposed that the two Comptrollers shall be replaced by one Councillor of Finances, with full power to obtain all information. He will have no direct communica- tion with the Khedive, but will report annually on the state of the finances, and his appointment rand dismissal will be regulated according to the terms of the decree of November 18, 1870. The new councillor will not be entitled to advise on administrative questions not connected with finance. Though he will have a seat at the Council of Ministers, he will have a consultative voice on questions of finance only.

MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS. The English council have thanked Sir E. Malet for the assistance he has rendered them in gaining admission to the trial. Arabi Pasha has expressed his satisfaction with the re- vised arrangements fir his trial, and his confidence in the decisions of British Government. On Friday Sir G. Wolseley took up his quarters on board the Iris despatch boat, and on Saturday the victorious General with his staff left Alexandria for Trieste en route for England. The Snitan has received from the Khedive a telegram of congratulation on the occasion of the Bairam Festival, hnd it is conceived in unusually respectful terms. Lord Dufferin's reply to the last Note of the Porte has not yet been sent, but the belief exists in Turkish circles that a satisfactory arrangement with England is on the point of being proposed. In spite of denials, the statements of the ill-treatment of prisoners are absolutely correct. Some of the chief prisoners were beaten with slippers, others were spat upon. Arabi him- self did not escape from insults. In Alexandria, a correspondent there telegraphs, all the rumours concerning the ill-feeling of the Arabs and their intention to attack the Europeans proved absolutely with- out foundation. A Constantinople correspindent telegraphs that the an- tagonism between Said Pacba and Mahrhoud Nediin, who has taken the lead of the reactionary party, is still increas- ing. It is believed that one of them will have to leave the inistry. The Constantinople Hakikat, alluding to the prospect of an understanding between England and Turkey, remarks that it is for Lord Dufferiu, rather than the Porte, to bring this about by putting an end to the delays which retard its realisation.

The Russian Council of State has decided to recommend the restoration of a considerable number of estates which had been confiscated in Poland and elsewhere on account of the " disloyalty " of their owners. IMPENDING GREAT STRIKE IN PARIS.—A strike of unpre- cedented magnitude is impending in Paris. The workmen in the furniture trade have given notice to cease work unless they receive a considerable advance of wages, with a reduction of hours of labonr. It is feared that 20,000 men will be on strike in the very heart of the revolutionary quarter of the French capital. The masters are seriously thinking of a general lock-out. MoNsioNoN ClTNL.—Monsignor Capel, who has for some tine past been engaged in an appeal to Rome on cer- 'tain matters in dispute between himself and his superiors in the Roman Catholic diocese of Westminster, has, the Ifors- isg Post says, obtained judgment in his favour. The differ- ences arose out ef the conduct of the late Catholic Univer- sity, of which Monsignor Capel was rector, and the matter, it will be remembered, resulted in Monsignor Copal's bank- ruptcy. He ii now engaged in preaching in various towns in Italy, and purposes wintering at Rome prier to resuming his clerical functions in England. Loss OF A STEAMER AND SEVERAL HUNDRED COOLIES.— , A steamer bound from Hong Kong for Victoria with several ' hundred coolies on board has been lost a few miles to the north of the Straits of Juan de Fuca. None of those on board are known to have been saved. The Straits of Juan de Fuca are situated between Vancouver Island and Wash- ington territory. It is stated that the coolies were on their way from Heng Kong to Victoria, the capital of Vancouver , Island, where they would have been employed on the great railway works recently commenced there. , AN ErmosisN CIGAR.—A strange but well authenieated story comes from Szeged. Muller, an engineer employed in the works of reconstruction, bought on Sunday four cigars. When he had smoked about one-half of the second be laid it on his writing table, when all of a sadden it exploded,

throwing him off his chair and wounding him on the cheek, the ears, the lips, and the left hand. Fortunately the room in the schoolhouse where ha and his companions had been working was large. Inquiry showed that there had been a glass tube inside filled with nitro-glycerine. The Transvaal Government appears to be committed to a struggle with the chief Mapoch, who has refused to recog- nise'the authority of the Rvublic or to surrender the mur- derers of Seccocceni. A force of 2,000 Boers is to be sent into his territory. A desilpieh from Teheran states that the city of Herat is now govßijaed by a son of the Ameer Abdurrahmsn. There have been some disturbances in the neighbourhood of Cabal, probably arising from some petty acts of oppression by the local Governor, who has been killed by the rioters. TYPHOON' AT 144ANILL : SIXTY THOUSAND FAMILIES HOMELES3.—An official despatch received at Madrid from Manilla, dated the 21st inst., states that the typhoon which swept over that city destroyed all the wooden and thatched houses, and carried away the iron and tiled roofs of the other houses. Sixty thousand families have been rendered homeless. The barracks, hospitals, Government Offices, and factories have been destroyed. The loss of life is, however relatively small. Molacanan and Boulacan have also been devastated.

Chief John Dunn protests against the restoration of Cee- wayo to Zululand without any previous consultation with hiinself;and wishes it to be understood that in Lis opinion the Government's conduct will be most injurious to the prestige of all Englishmen in Africa. No doubt the restora- tion is a very serious matter for Chief Dunn, who profited much by Cetewayo's dethronement, as he had previously profited by his friendship, but it will require much more than his interested protest to convince English people that the return of Cetevrayo is not both just and politic. The celebration of the "bicentenary of Pennsylvania " on Tuesday afforded a spectacle which is said to have been "inexpressibly grand." Hundreds of thousands of visitors, added to the usual population of Philadelphia, were massed in the streets and along the wharves of that great city, and the representatives of William Penn landed, oddly enough, amidst the thunder of cannon and the shrieking of innu- merable steam whistles, and were received by a naval and military force. A great attraction of the show was supplied by the presence of 3,000 peaceful American citizens got up for the occasion as red men." The Times correspondent states that these men belonged to a "pepular secret benefit society, which is based on Indian customs." ATTEMPT TO Swocer KING MILAN.—The Bergin capital has been thrown into a state of intense excitement by an attempt to shoot King Milan. His Majesty had just returned to Belgrade after paying a visit to Roum-lia, and was en- thusiastically received on his arrival. When, however' ac- companied by the Queen, be at a late hour visited the Cathedral, a lady, the widow of an officer who was executed in 1875, attempted to shoot him. The shot did not take effect, and the King entered the Cathedral, but the Queen fainted and had to be at once removed to the Palace. On the populace learning what had happened intense excite- ment prevailed, and a cry was raised to lynch Madame Markowitch, but she was taken care of by the police. There is some reason for attaching political significance to the event, but, on the other hand, it is stated that the widow has been very melancholy since her husband's death, and is scarcely responsible for her actions. E`TTRAOILDINLEY EXPLOSIONS IN A FRENCIIEESTAURANY. —At two o'clock on Monday morning two explosions occurred in the restaurant attached to the Bellecceur „ Theatre, Lyons, in which about 200 persons were seated partaking of refreshments. The detonations appeared to proceed from beneath one of the tables, and caused the greatest alarm, most of the persons rushing precipitately .to the doors. Immediately afterwards a third and more formidable explosion was heard, which shattered the tables, woodwork, and mirrors of the restaurant, and seriously in- jured three persons, a number of others being more or less hurt. A judicial inquiry has been opened. The explosions are stated to have been caused by small bombs left under ' one of the tables by three men who entered the restaurant ten minutes before the occurrence. • MURDER OF A LOVER BY AN OFFICER : TERRIBLE TRAGEDY.—Another terrible drama was enacted at Berlin as a sort of pendant to the tragedy which lately lifted the veil from a painful part of the social life of Berlin. In the latter case a mistress shot her lover and then poisoned herself. But now the roles are reversed. lb lover pis- tolled his mistress and then blew his own brains out. The affair has caused all the more sensation as the murderer and suicide was a Prussian officer, Captain Feeiher von Schtotter by name, attached as teacher to the Military Gymnasium at Berlin. Nothing more is known of the motive of the crime, except that the unfortunate officer had lived for several years with his victim, described as a young woman of considerable refinement and education, by whom he had a daughter; that wranglings between them had been frequent of late; that their servant was awakened in the night by an uproar in their chamber; and that on Monday morning they were both found on the floor stone dead, the mistress with a bullet through her heart, and her lover with one through his head, and a revolver at his aide. GREAT EETOLUTIONARY CONSPIRACY IN FRINCE.--aA Paris correspondent telegraphed from Paris on Wednesday night :—There are various conjectures hazarded to-night as to the motives of the Government in bringing about the sudden suspension of the trial at Montceau on the ground that judge and jury alike were not free to act in conse- quence of the receipt of nemerons threatening letters. The affair is now put off for three months, and naturally in some quarters the Government is severely blamed for prolonging the uncertainty of the public and the discomforts of the preventive detention among the prisoners. The true reason _ seems to be given in a long statement published by the Paris _ (Gambettist organ) to-night, according to which an organi- sation has been discovered for starting a revolutionary move- ment throughout France. In every city, village, and com- mune, there is a group of members of this conspiracy. These in their turn send members to a federation which represents the department, and all the federations select a delegate to the Central Committee, which meets once a month at Geneva. All the dynamite cartridges lately seized are of Swiss fabrication. The Government is believed to have put off the trial in order to get more information about the plot by the secret examination of the prisoners. AN ENGINE-DRIVER'S HEROISM: SIX HUNDRED PAS- SENGERS SAVED BY ONE Alete.—A Daily News telegram from New York says :—An engine-driver on the Pennsyl- vania Railway on Monday saved the lives of six hundred passengers by an extraordinary act of heroism. The furnace door was opened by the fireman to replenish the fire while the train was going thirty-five miles an hour. The back draught forced the flames out so that the car of the locomo- tive caught fire, and the engine-driver and the fireman were driven back over the tender into the pascenger car, leaving the engine without control. The speed increased, and the volume of flame with it. There was imminent danger that all the carriaees would take fire and the evhole train be consumed. The passengers were 'ethic-stricken. To jump off was certain death, to remain was to be burned alive. - The engine-driver saw that the only way to save the pas- sengers was to return to the engine and stop the train. He plunged into the flames, *limbed back over the tender and reversed the engine. When the train came to a standstill he was found in the water tank, whither he bad climbed with his clothes entirely burnt off, his face disfigured, his hands shockingly burned, and his body blistered so badly that the flesh was stripped off in many places. Weak and half •onscions he was taken to the hospital, where his in- juries were pronounced serious, with slight chance of recovery. As the train stopped the flames were easily extinguished. The unanimous testimony of the passengers is that the engine-driver saved their lives. His name is Joseph A. Sieg. FRANCE AND Ttnets.—A statement made on Monday that a draft treaty had been concluded between France and Tunis was promptly followed by a semi-official cotnmunica• -- tion to the Paris press, which asserts that the details pub- lished in the newspapers are "wanting in accuracy," and adds, "when the arrangements neceeeitatecl by the develop- ment of the French position in Tents are finally settled they will be submitted to Parliament." The story told by the Paris correspondent of the Time: was that a draft treaty was concluded on the 10th of July between the Bey of Tunis and M. Cambon, the French Resident, which was sent to Paris to be translated and approved by the Government as a preliminary to ratification by the Chambers. The fall of M. de Freycinet interrupted its progress. According to this treaty France, recognising the difficult and equivocal posi- tion which the Bey now occupies especially in respect of the collection of taxes, undertakes to become responsible for the payment of the Tunisian debt, which amounts to about five millions starling. The immediate consequence of the transfer is that the Commission charged with the Con- trol falls to the ground. It is further provided by the treaty that a new French tribunal shall be organised in Tunis, to which France shall have the right of sending all suits of whatever nature or nationality. The correspon- dent states that "as corollary to the foregoing stipulations —that is to say, to the compulsory transfer of the debt, to the abolition of the Financial Commission, to the estab- lishment of the tribunal substituting a simple judical pro. cedure for the existing capitulations and suppressing the latter—France has the right to organise or reorganise the administration of the public property, and to supervise an& direct in the Bey's name the collection of the taxes. The treaty, besides, provides a civil list of 700,0001 a Year for the Bey, and further allowances for the princes to the annual amount of 1,300,000 f. The treaty constitutes not a simple protectorate, but a kind of diplomatic annexation, and the Parliamentary ratification may be deemed a fore- gone conclusion."

The Rev. Dr. Ward, present won of Durham and rector of Ryten, died at his residfetanc?d, EVton near Newcastle, somewhat suddenly, on Thursday, aged 55;from congestion of the lungs. A conference of members of the Farmers' Alliance was held on Monday at Westminster Palace Hotel. Mr. James Howard, M.P., presided. Tbe chairman having reviewed the objects of the alliance, moved a resolutir urging upon the Government to introduce early next session bills to se- cure to tenant farmers the whole value of their improve- ments. The resolution was passed, as were also..resolntions in favour of the abolition of the law of distress in England, another embodying a memorial to Mr. Gladstone to introduce bills to give absolute and complete secueLy to capital in- vested by English and Scotch tenant farmers in improve- ments.
