div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, OCTOBER,2B, 1882,

THE House of Commons reassembled this week for the purpose of reforming its rules of procedure, and the numerous attendance of members testifies to the importance attaching to the subject. Contrary to general expectation,the opening night was not marked by any of the wranglings which we had been led to anticipate, or which the oratory of the two previous weeks seemed to foretell. Mr. Bradlaugh was within the House, yet he remained technically without its precincts, awaiting, no doubt, his own opportunity for pressing his claims; Mr. E. D. Gray,the recentl - imprisoned member for county Carlow, was in atten- dance, and a debate on his confinement was completely disarmed by Mr. Gladstone's prompt declaration of the intentions of the Government on this very ques- tion; and though Sir Wilfrid Lawson was present and seemed to be in excellent trim and willing and anxious to fight the Government on the Egyptian question, be was obliged by the nature of Mr. Gladstone's motion respecting the campaign to reserve his attack upon the Government until Thursday evening. Lord Randolph Churchill, we are happy to observe, was i . again n his place, recovered from his recent illness, and if we may judge by his speech on Tuesday even- ing, his sojourn in the sick chamber has rather quickened than otherwise his ntellect. Scarcely had the Speaker taken the chair than Lord Randolph was upon his legs and at his old game of moving the ad- journment of the House, though it must be confessed that in this instance he had some show of reason for so doing—what he has not had on many previous occasions. During the noble lord's enforced retirement from Parliamentary warfare he has evidently been searching the pages of Haseard, and he has discovered that Mr. Gletler,one, in calling members together after the Ap•

div.head: EXAMIN
div.p: EXAMIN
THE

propriation Bill received the Royal Assent, has beea violating the Constitution. The contention of the member for Woodstock is that Parliament should in August last have been prorogued instead of only ad- journed, and that it should have been summoned afresh for the present sitting. This of course means it would have been necessary to have relinquished all the progress that had been previously made with the reform of the procedure rules, and it would have in- volved the observance.of all the necessary formalities attending upon the opening of'Parliament—a Speech from the Throne and an Address—the very things which it was the object of the Government and of the House to avoid. It is a remarkable thing that it should have been reserved for the noble lord to make this wonderful discovery, and it must be a matter for regret that he was not able to be present in his place in Parliament, so that he could have saved the Constitution and preserved the freedom of members and a controlling inluence over this wicked Government. To say the least it is not very creditable to Sir Stafford Northcote and his colleagues of, the front Opposition bench ,that they were not able to avert the great calamity which the noble lord so graphically depicted. After all, however, the mem- ber for Woodstock only discovered a "mare's nest," and though his speech in disclosing his prial was somewhat ingenious, it lacked the quality of having anything in it. Lerd Randolph contends that there is no precedent for the course now being followed by the Government, and in support of this contention he quotes from records as far back as the reign of Henry IV. But, as Mr. Gladstone showed, the noble lord had not been sufficiently indestriourin his search or he would have discovered that in the year 1120 the House adjourned and met no less than three times after the passing of the Appropriation Act, with the object of passing a Bill of Pains and Penalties against Queen Caroline. One hon. member was bold enough to say that this was not business—the passing of a Bill of Pains and Penalties—but to the majority of people we think it. will be recognised as very important. It having, therefore, been shown by Mr. Gladstone that there was a precedent, and a very strong one, too, in favour of the Government, the noble lord's ground was completely cut from under him, and all the as- sistance he received from the titular leader of the Op- position and from several members of the Fourth Party failed to muster a force sufficient to obtain an adjournment of the House. The division showed a majority in favour of the Government of 67. It seems to us the noble lord's mancouvres served only one purpose, and that was—to effectually waste valuable time. This matter having been got rid oc, Mr. Gladstone at once turned to the imprison- ment of Mr. Gray, and it will be a satisfaction to the country to know that the Government con- ' template bringing in a bill at an early period dealing with the question of imefisonment for con- tempt of court. As the law at present stands the judges are vested with enormous powers, which are not always exercised discreetly, and any measure which will tend to improve the law will be gladly welcomed by the judges as well as by the public. Mean while a committee is to be appointed for the purpose of inquiring into the circumstances attending tha hoprisonment of Mr. Gray, who, we are told,will be satisfied if what he has undergone should be the means of attracting public attention to the anomalous state of the law. Interest in the first night's pro- ceedings was naturally centered in the new rules of procedure, and Mr. Gladstone's statement thereanent; and there must be a general feeling of relief that the Government has decided to abide by the first resolu- tion in its main proposition, that of closing debate by a simple majority. This, as we have frequently said, is the only safe course to adopt; and if the resolution errs at all it is, as Mr. Bright says, on the side of not being sufficiently stringent for the evil it is intended to cure. The wording of the resolution may be altered, but its essential conditions are to be adhered to. In some of the other rules, however, there are to be modifications inserted which will, we believe, be welcomed on both sides of the House. At the present time great inconvenience arises from frequent motions for the adjournment of the House being made. By the second rule, as originally framed, it was proposed that no such motion should be made except by leave of the House, before the orders of the day or the notices of motion have been entered upon; but in order to provide for emergencies, it is intended to modify that rule considerably. Again, it is frequently found that the "half-past twelve o'clock rule " operates too stringently. By it no opposed measure can be taken after half-past twelve, and by its aid Ur. Wharton and such like mischievous mesabers has been able to block many useful measures. The Govern- ment, however, propose to exempt from the operation of this rule motions for leave to bring in bills, and also bills which have passed through committee. These, after all, are minor matters compared with closure by a simple majority. It is on this the great fight will take place, and that it is to be a bitter one is shown by the tone and temper of Ur. Chaplin, Sir W. Barttelot, Mr. A. Bartlett, and other members of the Opposition. We hope that the Liberal party will remain loyal to the Government and to its leader, and that the first resolution will be carried by a decisive majority. The Conservatives are very much afraid of thb Closure, but they surely forget that it will operate to their advan- tage when in power as much as it will to that of the Liberals at the present time. The violent opposition of the Conservatives can only be suticiently explained on the hypothesis that they do not expect to be in power again; and certainly, seeing that they make so bad use of their innings, they do not deserve to be.

Mu. G. W. LLTILLII, of Sandbach, is by no means a new exponent of tenant farmers' grievances. His opinion on the Land question, as expressed during his candidature for the representation of Mid-Cheshire at the last general election, and on numerous more re- cent occasions, are well-known to the readers of The Examilter. Few, however, of Mr. Ltthatn's con- tributions to this important controversy will be read with greater interest by Cheshire tenant farmers, and the advocates of land law reform generally. than will be his brief but telling speech at the meeting of the members of the English and Scottish larmers'Alliance, held at Westminster Palace Hotel on Monday. Mr. Latham seconded the adoption of a resolution proposing that a memorial be presented- to the Prime Minister urging upon the Government the desirability of introducing, early next session, bills to give "absolute and complete security to the capital of English and Scottish tenant farmers, in- vested in the icaprovements of their holdings. Mr. J. Howard, M.P., and Mr. Barclay, M.P., who were the previous speakers, dealt with the question from a tenant farmer's point of view. The position taken up by Mr. Latham was widely different and somewhat unique. Speaking, not as a tenant farmer, but as a Cheshire landlord, he expressed hiraself perfectly certain that unless free sale and free cultivation, together with security of tenure, were conceded to We tenant farmer, English land- lords would soon cease to exist. If rents were to continue being lowered, as they inevitably must if the present system of land tenure were not altered, it would, said Mr. Latham, become impossible for inglish landlords to continue to live under the shadows of the old oaks of the old mansions which had been left them by their forefathers. Tenant farmers would be driven from the country, and the landlords would be compelled to hide them- selves in the metropolis. How is this gloomy prospect to be brightened? How is the English country gentleman to maintain his present social Position and to continue to dwell in the manorial halls of his ancestors? In Mr. Latham's opinion the only way to avert the over-shadowing calamity is to trust the tenant farmer. "Let the tenant farmer," _remarked Mr. Latham, " be allowed to cultivate hid laui as lie liked, and not according to

div.head: 'RDA Y,
div.p: 'RDA Y,

the crochets of some old fogy in Lincoln's Inn; or the whim of a stupid land agent." It is to be feared that Mr. Latham represents but a very small pro- portion of the English land-owning class. Tenant farmers seem to have little to hope from Whig or Tory landlords. The proceedings in the committee rooms in conneetion with the two bills appertaining to tenant farmers, which came before Parliament early in the present session, show conclu- sively that the landlords as a body are de- termined to concede as little as possible of what they deem to be their rights and privileges. Be that as it may, two large and powerful sections of the electors are now making it manifest that some serious changes will have to be made ere long. Despite the apathy, and, in some cases, tne opposition to the movement on the part of Chambers of A griculture, where the landlord and land agent influence, if it does not predominate, has considerable sway, tenant farmers are beginning to make it evident that they are really in earnest in their agitation, and press their demands 'with Rauch rigour. 01 all sides voters in the largo urban constituencies are evincing their interest in this question of land reform. They are beginning to see that it is not merely a question which only seriously affects the squire and the farmer. As recent as Saturday last there was issued from Newcastle the manifesto of a new organisation which has for its main object the confederation of the various political associations in the four northern counties for the prop3.oinn of parliamentary and land law reforms. Similar na)vements, too, are being initiated in various parts of the country. While expressing no opinion on the book itself, but merely calling attention te the fact, as showing the wide- spread interest which new centres in the English land question, it may be stated that no less than 20,000 cheap copies alone of Mr. Henry George's " Progress and Poverty" have been purchased within the last two or three weeks, mainly by dwellers in towns. This in itself shows that an, intelligent spirit of enquiry animates the voters in the borough consti- tuencies, and is a powerful argumen; in favour of the matter being early brought before the attention of Parliament. The Farmers' Alliance does not desire that the Agricultural Holdings Bill should be made compulsory. They tegard that measure of the Beaconsfield Administration as complicated, insuffi- cient, and unduly restrictive. They contend that were that almost enttrely non-effective Act made compulsory it would fail to secure to tenants the whole value of their improvements, even when they quitted their holdings; while the measure does not even attempt to prevent the confiscation of a tenant's improvements by renting him upon them if he stays in his holding. The tenant farmers ask that any legislation on their behalf shall not only be permanent, but that it shall not be even semi-permissive. In short, they ask for legislation which neither landlord nor lawyer can set aside, as suits their convenience or caprice. Apart from tke influence which will be brought to bear on the question by voters in manufacturing constituencies the tenant farmers of themselves have a strong claim on the Government. There are doubtless many obstacles to be surmounted, but if ever a Government was able to deal with the question, the Government of which Mr. Gladstone is now the trusted head is in a position to do so. It is to be hoped that the farmers' anticipations will not be altogether disappointed.

We would direct the attention of our readers to the im- portant prospectus in another colnran of the Lancashire Plateway Company. The object of the scheme shadowed forth by the Company is to break down the enormous rates now charged by the railway and canal campanies in Lanca- shire for the carriage of goods and minerals, and every effort put forth in this direction is bound to secure, as it deserves, a fair amount of support. Tne commereial com- munity is entirely at the mercy of these companies, whose charges, as WAS once pointed out by the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, are often unauthorised, and the only way in whish the public can protect themselves against them is by expensive and extravagant litigation, a state -9f things which ought not to exist. For want of legitirnate com- petition the carriers combine, and the consequence is, as stated in this prospectus," it is difficult to find in the world, except in small and exceptional cases, such as the Panama Railroad, equally high rates of carriage." It is almost incredible, yet there seems good ground for the belief, "that along the main line of Lancashire traffic, Remaly, that between Liverpool and Manchester, fifty years of railway have increased'athe cost of carriage and not materially lessened the time of transit." This the Plateway Company intend to remedy, and with that view, they propose, with the sanction of Parliament, to construct through the country a net-work of railway or a " plateway," in such a way as to admit of wagons being at any point drawn on or off. These wagons can then be taken by either horses or a slow loco- motive to the point where drawn on to the platewar, or from the point where drawn off, along the ordinary roads to their final destination. It is contended by this means that cotton loaded at the ship side, or manure loaded at the stable, will be carried along road and plate- way and delivered at the mill or :farm without change of vehicle, without the expense attending " handling " on the railways at the present time, and with much less liability to damage. For the purposes of the plateway, the high- roads of the:county are to be utilised. It is proposed in the that instance that from the south end of Liverpool a plate- way shall be constructed to Oldham, the route taken being through Warrington, touching the south side of Manchester, through Ashton and Stalybridge. From the other end of Liverpool will be constructed another line, also to Oldham, which will pass through St. Helens, Ashton-in-Makerfield, Bolton, Bury, Heywood, and Rochdale. From Ashton-in- Makerfield there vrill.be a third line through Wigan, Cheater, Blackburn, Church, and Accrington, on to Burnley; and another from Chorley to Preston. Thus, the portion of Lancashire lying mainly between the Ribble and the Mereey Is to be covered. te It is estimated that the cost of the plate- way, with full equipment of rolling stock, will be about £35,000 per mile. In order to make the necessary applica- tion to Parliament a sum of £75,000 is required, of which £3i,000 is already promised, and the promoters are sow appealing to the public for the remainder. Each subscriber Ito the preliminary fund will, if an Act be obtained, become entitled to hare allotted to him at par an amount of stock equal to ten times his subscriptions, and the sum he has contributed will be taken as part payment for the same. It is impossible to close one's eyes to the fact that the ple'e- way, feasible as it is, will be a rival to the ship canal pro- ject; but if from the two schemes one can be evolved which, while conciliating all parties, will at the same time result in a great public convenience and a pecuniary gain, then the efforts now being put forth will not have been in vain.

The meeting on Sunday closing, held last Friday week in the Public Hall, was a success in more aspects than one. The resolutions proposed were accepted with a hearty enthusiasm, which left no doubt as to the feelings of the large audience on the subject of the closing of public- houses on Sunday; but the proceedings were especially noticable for the speech of the Rev. J. Billington, who made what I may call his first public appearance in Runcorn. Although he has been ministering in the town for a period of about 18 months he has not,! believe, addressed an audience outside of his own congregation, and the vigour with which he pourtrayed the temptations oflered by the grog shops, and the mental struggles of the not utterly bad drunkard, interspersed with a humour which appeared well suited to his listeners, was a complete surprise to all assembled. His abilities were fully recognised, and the speech created quite a " talk" in teetotal circles. Bat Mr. Billington, I believe, is also a not ineffective speaker on politics, and it is to be hoped that Runcornians will have other opportunities afforded them of listening to a speech from that gentleman. Now that we have found what a "shining light" we have in our midst, it ought no longer to be allowed to remain hidden under a "bushel."

The Bishop of Peterborough, Dr. Magee, is not ene of those who entertain a holy horror of reading rooms being open on a Sunday, yet there are few persons, if any, who would question the right rev, prelate's sincerity or doubt his Christianity. Speaking the other day with reference to the opening of these rooms on the Sabbath the Bishop is reported to have said that he can go into his library on Sunday and read, and why, he asks, shoifld not the poor man go into his at the public reading-room and do

likewise? On many a wet Sunday, he added, readable books or newspapers would be a perfect godsend to thousands of people who have not libraries at home, and even on fine Sundays there would be large numbers of readers. These words of wisdom I commend to the attention of all those who are opposed to such harmlefis recreation as the Bishop advocates. The arguments used by the Bishop are the very same that have been used over and over again by those who are in favour of the opening of libraries and museums on Sundays, and for which.they have been denounced as Atheists. I suppose by a parity of reasoning Bishop Magee must now be reckoned as belonging to the„ungodly !

Mr. Errington, the member for Longford county, is again at the Vatican, and the suspicions of Sir H. D. Wolff are zaturally aroused. He has intimated his intention of ques- tioning the Prime Minister on the subject of Mr. Errington's second visit, and as a consequence the Press Association has been furbishing up information, and is enabled to state, on the best authority of course, that Mr. Errington has no official position, nor has he received any Ministerial corn_ mission whatever on his present visit, nor does he bear any credentials from any member of the English Government, or from any ecclesiastical dignitaries. Is that sufficiently explicit for the worthy baronet ? It is understood that the rope, as well as Earl Granville, is favourable to the appoint- ment of a British representative at the Vatican, while Mr. Gladstone is stattid to be personally inclined to the recep- tion of a Papal agent to the English Government; and whatever some Liberals and Radicals may say to the con- trary, I believe the idea is a good one, and would be Imo- ductive of good. But I think it scarcely likely Mr. Erring- ton will be deputed to carry out the negotiations; and it seems to me a pity that gentle.nan's visits to his Holiness should be disturbed by the itnpertinences of the member for Portsmouth, whose bigotry does not do him any credit.

The Conservative policy at the present time appears to be one of obstruction solely. Lord Randolph Churchill set the ball rolling at the meeting of the Commons on Tuesday Sir IL D. Wolff followed suit on Wednesday, and there is every probability now that the reform of the rules of pro- cedure will occupy the attention of the Commons till very nearly Christmas. At a meeting of the party at the Carlton on Tuesday Sir Stafford Northcote was called over the coals fo allowing the debate on Mr. Gladstone's motion asking for precedence for the rules to close at an early hour, and as a consequence the worthy baronet and his colleagues on the front Opposition bench are for the future to be led by the Fourth Party, and to give their countenance to all its esca- pades. Au attempt has been made to enlist the sympathy and support of the Irish members in these obstructive tac- tics, but these have so far failed. Verily, the Conservatives members are only providing a rod with which to break their own back. They are giving unanswerable arguments for putting down obstruction. There is very little exciting in the news from Egypt this week. Interest still centres in the trial of Arabi, who is to be defended by Doggish counsel, and arrangements have been made whereby, it is generally adraitted, the rebel leader will have fair play. Arabi's correspondence has been discovered. The documents are believed to be very important, and it is said they contain a sufficient number of signatures to corn- promise the whole of Islamism. Probably it is this fact which bas caused the Sultan to wish for the trial to be quished and the rebels exiled. Though the insurrection led by Arabi has been quelled, I am afraid the end of our responsibilities in Egypt is not yet come. It is clear troubles are brewing in the Soudan, and in view of the suc- cesses of the false prophet and the probtbilities of a new prophet being revealed soon, it behoves us to keep a firm grip of the country. APVLICATION TO CLOSE A. WELL LT HA.LTON. —At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr John Brundrit, Mr. Farrington, sanitary inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, applied for a summons against either Mr. Wm. Stokes, the occupier, or the Marquis of Cholmondeley, the owner, of Prospect Farm, Halton, to close a certain well situated in the back yard of the farm. The water was supposed to be polluted with sewage. It had been submitted to the analyst and found to be impure. Water from the Water Works Company could be obtained at the top of the lane, a distance of 150 yard's from the farm. The Bench granted a sum:nons against, the Occupier. THE DOWNWARD STEP : TREF r BY A RUNC3BN Womeer.—At Runcorn Petty Session, on Monday, Ellen Hampson was charged on remand with feloniously stealing a skirt of the value of Is. 93., the property of Horatio Syred, pawnbroker, Church-street, Runcorn. It appeared that on Friday the woman entered the shop to which Thomas Hicks, the assistant, was attending. A few minutes after the departure ef the woman, Hicks missed the skirt, and he went to the Feathers' Ina in search of the prisoner. He found her there with the skirt in her possession.—P.C. Wallace deposed to apprehending the prisoner in Cooper-street, at eleven o'clock on Friday night. He charged her with stealing the skirt and she replied " I did not mean anything when I took it."—Mr. t uaerintert- dent Williemson said the prisoner wee a n rtive of Runcorn, but had not been previous:y before the court. She was a married woman and very fond of drink, and it was no doubt through the latter that she had c attnitted this offence.— The Bench said they would give the prisoner another chance, and fined her 103. and cesl-s £l, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. ALLEGSD ROBBERY raoet A CLPEIIN AT 111.13C3RN Before Mr. John Brundrit, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Mary Cox, a woman of bad character, was charged with stealing a parse and £2 103., the property of Griffiths Roberts, a master mariner, living at Dinorwich From the evidence adduced it appeared th itatiout 9 o'clock,' on the previous night, the prosecutor and another c tptain went into the tap-room of the Clarendon Hotel, Church- street. Shortly afterwards the prisoner and another woman entered. The prisoner represented that she was in want, and asked Griffiths to relieve her. He gave her a penny, and afterwards a shilling and a glass of whiskey, when the prisoner went and sat besides him. In a few minutes he discovered that his purse Ind been abstracted from his trousers pocket, and he acquainted Mrs. Lee, the landlady, of his loss. Mrs. Lee despatched a messenger for a police constable, and held fast the door of the room, where the pri- soner was seated, until his arrival. Whilst doing so, the prisoner " fought at her," and endeavoured to escape, but finding her efforts of no avail she leave Mrs. Lee 7s. 0.1. to allow her to go. Mrs. Lee refused, and P.C. Noden arriving on the scene took the prisoner into custody. Asked if she had any money, the prisoner replied "No ; this is all the money I have," throwing at the same time Is. 43. on the table. With the assistance of P.S. McMichael, the pri- soner, who was very violent, was conveyed to the police station, where the sergeant found the purse, containing two sovereigns concealed up the sleeve of her dress. The female searcher subsequently discovered a further sum of 7s. 7d.; and P.C. Noden received from Mrs. .1:?e the 7s. Gd. given to her by the prisoner. When charged with the theft the pri- soner declared her innocence, alleging that it was a "made up" affair between Mrs. Lee and the prosecutor. She was committed to Knutsford Sessions to take her trial.

A NEIGHBOURLY SQUABBLE AT RUNCORN. THE BATTLE ov THE BELTSIIES.—On Monday, at the Rnncorn Petty Sessions, before Mr. Wm. Bankes and Mr. John Brun- drit, Margaret Boyle, a married woman, was summoned for assaulting Jame Hardcastle, an elderly worn an, dressed in mourning.—Mr. Burton appeared for Mrs. Boyle.—The parties are neighbours, and live in Cambride-street, and the complainant alleged that on Wednesday morning, the 18th inst., Mrs. Boyle brushed the dirt on the road on to the parapet, and before her doer, as she usually did. Com- plainant west to brush the dirt away, and called Mrs Bavle a "dirty beast." The dirt was brushed backwards and for- wards several times—first before ?AM Hardcastle's door and then before Mrs. Boyle's door—and then complainant washed it away with a pail of water. Mrs. Bayle brushed the water into the face of Mrs. Hardcastle, who went inside and let the former" brush away."—Cross-examined by Mr. Burton: She had tried to ," stove" Mrs. Boyle out by but fling sulphur in the bedroom, but she could explain that. She had never spat at Mrs. Boyle, but the latter had "blown her nose "at her. (Laughter.)—Mrs. Bazley deposed to seeing Mrs. Boyle throw water at Mrs. Hardcastle, saying, as she did so, " You shall have it all old dame: You shall have it all." Mrs. Boyle swept the "itch " from the gutter before the complaint's door.—Mrs. Hill, Mrs. Besley, and Mrs. Faulkner gave evidence.—Mrs. Hardcastle was then charged with haying, on the 18th_ October, used abusive language towards Mrs. Boyle, calculated to commit a breach , of the peace.—Mr. Burton said he regretted that the time of ' the Bench should be taken up with a case of this kind. Re thought be could satisfy the Bench that some motive existed for Mrs. Hardcastle's conduct. On the 21st August Mrs. Hardcastle wasfirted 10s. and costs for assaulting Mrs. Boyle's child, and since that date she had been unneigh- baurlv. Every time Ale had met Mrs. Boyle she had made use of some epithet or abusive language, and occasionally she had spat at her. There had been a feeling of spite and maliciousness on the part of Mrs. Hardcastle, who now came to the court seeking to punish Mrs. Boyle to gratify her own spiteful and malicious feelings. On the day in question dirt had been brushed against Mrs. Boyle's back door by Mrs. Hardcastle. Mrs. Boyle brushed it back, and then the defendant threw some water, which went upon the clothing of the former.—Mrs. Boyle was called, and said she was the wife of Joseph Wilson Bc.yle. When she brushed the dirt back in the direction of Mrs. Hardcasie's door, the latter said "You bitch, you shall have it all back agaie' " and after some little further disturbance she said, " Youfaggot ; I cmld split your skull open for you and dash your brains out." at the same time holding her brush in a threatening position.—The evidence of Ellen Inglestield. Mrs. Williamson' and Mr. Powell having , been heard, Mr. Banks said the 13..nc1l were of opinion there I was fault on both sides—six of one ant heilf-a-lozeu of tip other—and both the cases tvould b dismissA.

IMPROVEMENT CLASS, Ruscon)l.—At the usual meeting of this class held on Mon- day evening last, an essay on Sabbath observance was read by Mr. Edward Jones. The essayist contended warmly for a stricter observance of the Lord's day, and stated that, nationally, as well as individually, the people would be benefited by it. A lively and interesting discussion ensued, in which the Rev. J. Billington, Messrs. Kirkham, Raiford, Parry, and Jeseph Marlow took part, and it was decided to continue the debate at the next meeting of the class. There was a good attendance of members, the chair being occupied by Mr. E. Gandy, the president of the class.

STEALING A HORSE'S NOSE•BAG AT HALEWOOD.-At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans and E. K. Muspratt„ an elderly man named Hamblett Taylor was charged with stealing a horse's noss- bag, the property of James Wright, Ramsbrook Farm, Hale- wood. The prisoner had been employed by prosecutor as a labourer for about a month. The nose-bag was safe in the stable between six and seven o'clock on Tuesday morning, and was missed on Wednesday morning. The prisoner went to Mr. Ashton's beLrhouse at.Garston on the 18th inst. and offered to sell the bag. Mr. Ashton told him be had a good bag, when prisoner asked if it was worth a glass of beer, stating in reply to a question that he had found it on the road.—The Bench committed the prisoner to gaol for a month withjbard labour.

YOUNG ROBBERS AT WIDNES.—On Thursiay, at Widnes Police Court, two boys, named James Hynan (9) and James Brannon (7), were brought before Messrs. J. Brock and Hol- brook Gaskell, jun., to answer a charge of stealing two pigeons, the property of Wm. Harrison, from a cote in a back yard in James-street. On Tuesday evening the prose- cutor saw the pigeons safe in the cote, and locked the door, leaving, however, the key in it. It was shortly afterwards discovered that the pigeons and the key had been taken; but on Wednesday morning, the pigeons, which appeared to have been roughly handled, came back to their cote. Subse- quently Hynan's sister delivered the missing key to P.C. Thompson, who then apprehended the prisoners. The pri- soners pleaded guilty, and the Bench ordered each of them to receive six strokes with the birch red.

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON Tint POLICE AT RUNCOHN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. William Bankes and Mr. John Brundrit, a man named John Jones, having the appearance of a labourer, was charged with having, on Saturday, been drunk and disorderly in Percival's-lane, Runcorn. He was also charged with assault- ing P.C. Noden, and further with assaulting James Crank, a billposter's assistant.—P.C. Noden said about half-past five on the day named the prisoner was drunk In Percival's- lane, and wanted to fight with another man. He (witness) asked him to go home, but he became still mere noisy, and said he intended to be locked up that night. Noden re- plied that he was acting in the right way to obtain hio desire, and took him into custody. The prisoner struck him on the aide of the face, kicked him, and became very violent. —Crank said he saw Noden alai the prisoner struggling on the ground, the latter kicking very wildly. He went to the assistance of the officer, when the prisoner knocked him down on the road, and whilst he was lying on his bock he bit his (witness's) little finger at the joint. He also threatened him.—Mr. Banks said the prisoner was no doubt a violent character, and he must learn that he could not do what he liked. For being drunk sad disorderly he was fined 10s. and casts and for the assault on the constable £1 and costs, and a similar penalty for the assault on Crank. In default, he was committed to gaol for 42 days, with hard

Owen, Yorkshire-street, Burnley, plumber. AMR:LOSE CHURCH, WIDNES.—The annual tea party in connection with this church was held on Wednesday evening, when about 200 persons sat down to tea. The following ladies presided over the tables :—Mesdames Bond, Riley, Bullough, Newton, Latham' Gerrard, Neil, Valentine, Knowles, and Messrs Cooper, Lougton, Hurton, Forster, Davies, and Hultne. Subsequently a concert, over which the Rev. George Bond, vicar, presided, was held, and there was a large audience. In opsning the proceedings the Chaitinan informed the audience that the peal of bells at Fan worth had been thoroughly renovated, and nothing could be more liarmoni rust than the "liquid ditty" which floated from their iron throats. There was one point in regard to S. Ambrose district upon which he desired to turich. He did not think the attendance at the Sunday morning service Was what it aught to be, and he appealed to them to make the necessery exertion to attend both services. , Sunday, no doubt, was a day of rest; but above all it was a day of rest for the soul, and nothing could be more sooth- ing than the beautiful morning service of the Church of England, including as it did the sublime lit.ny. (Hear, hear.) He thought every one ought to make a point of attending church twice a-dew. Dessenters could do it, and why not they? How could area, expect their children to at- teall church in the morning and school in the afternoon, if they themselves only attended divine service once during , the day. Their attending two services would show that they took a genuine interest in the church work, which was the I very thing the church reople were wanting in. The Dissznters being a small body did not fall into their error, but were compelled to work in order to keep themselves alive; but the Church of England, being a numerous and p merful body, thought it was not so necessary to pay much ' attention to these small matters. In conclusion, he re- marked that there were several difficulties in the way of St. Ambrose district being made into a separate parish. It would probably be two years before they could get the name of the intended parish on the Ecclesiastical Commissioners' list. The concert was then proceeded with. The St. Ambrose glee party also rendered several pieces of music. Mr. Banks was the accompanist. The usual votes of thanks concluded the pro- ceedings. HOW WIDNES WITNESSES ARE TREATED.—Sobn Halllloll, ' a strong, rough looking fellow, was brought up on warrant at Widnes Petty Sessions, en Wednesday, before Messrs. W. L. Evans (chairman) and E. K. Muspratt, charged with assaulting Patrick Keogh.—Superintendent Barker remarked thlt the case was in his opinion one of unlawfully woand- ing, and that of a very aggravated nature. In August last a number of persons were committed in that court for trial, and the prisoner was one who would have been committed for trial on that occasion, but he absconded, and kept out of the way until the 14th inst. The parties who were com- mitted fur trial for wounding John Norton, on the Old , Marsh, were all convicted except one, and Patrick Keogh was a witgiess against them. On the 21st inst. the prisoner Hannon was in the Grosvenor Hotel, and Keogh bad not seen him since the assault took place on Norton until then. When in the Grosvenor the prisoner told him to be get.ing out, and immediately afterwards said to a man, who was standing near him, that he would do nine -- stretches for a man like him. In consequence of being threatened prosecutor left the pint of beer he had paid for, and was making his way out of the vault, when the prisoner struck him on the right temple with his fist, and knocked him against the wall, and then on to the floor of the vault. As he was getting up, Hannon a second time dealt him a violent blow on the right cheek, which felled pros,cutor on to a form; and whilst lying on the form the prisoner again struck him on the jaw with such violence that he rolled over on the floor. Some person then got hold of the prisoner and told him to keep his hands to himself, as it was a shame. Whilst prisoner was being held Keogh got out of the vault and found that he bad two teeth broken, and spat one out as he was emerging from the door, and another c‘me out on Monday. As soon as he left the vaults ha went to the police station and:gave information. He lost a considerabla quantity of blood, his upper lip was cut, his face swollen, and his right eye discoloured. He never gave the prisoner any provoca- tion whatever. There was no doubt that the assault was committed because the prosecutor gave evidence at the assizes, and he thought it was a case that ought to be sent for trial. Witnesses could not come to that court to give evidence without being interfered with and abused, and there was no getting them to cone—The prosecutor and John C. Armstrong gave coefirmatory evidence; and Dr. O'Keefe described the injuries the prosecutor had sustained. —lnspector Barnett stated that a warrant was taken out against the prisoner for aiding in the assault on John Norton on the last week in July, and the prisoner was taken into custody on the 14th inst. On the 10. h inst, he was brought before the magistrates, but as Norton refused to prosecute he was discharged. Keogh was a very important witness against the prisoner ia that case.—P.S. Clarkson spoke to :apprehending the prisoner on the 23rd inst. He charged him with wounding Keogh, and he replied "I did not strike blot—The Chairman: You are a most violent cbaracter, and you will be committed to take your trial at the next Quarter t.iEtsions at Liverpool on the 3lst inst.

A MUCII MAE.RIED COUPLE AT RUNCORN.—A rather curious wedding was celebrated at St. Paul's Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday morning last, when a man 69 years of age led to the bymenial altar a bride of 66 summers. They were a" much married "couple, for the old lady had been four times left a widow, and the man bad led three previous brides to the altar. They were heard to remark as they tripped to the vestry that there was " not too much of a good thing," so that it would seem that in their matri- monial bargains they had not been like the pair described by Tom Hood, who were " paired, not matched." The bride, whose name:was Mary Lightfoot, and the bridegroom, whose name is Samuel Hayes, are comely, active old people, and possessed of a fair share of this " world's goods."

lALLEGED THEP', OF I HEN AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, !at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. John Brock, Sarah Ann Grayson was charged with stealing a hen, belonging to George B ill ington.—Mrs. Billington stated the hen produced was her husband's property. She missed it and a brood of chickens on the 26th inst. The brood afterwards returned but the hen did not, and she asked the prisoner, whom she knew, if she had found a hen. Prisoner replied in the nega- tive, adding that she knew nothing about it. The hen was worth a half-a-crown.—An officer stated that from informa- tion received be visited the prisoner's house in Edward. street, Halton View, and asked her if she bad any hens. She said she had three, which were her own, and he went into the backyard to lock for them, but found the cote locked. The prisoner very rduct.ntly gave up the .key of the cote, which, when opened, was found to contain only the hen produced. The prisoner's hens were rambling about.—The case was remanded until Wednesday, the prisoner being admitted to bail.

DECEASE OF A WIDNES LOCAL BOARD OFFICIAL.—It IS with regret that we record the sudden death of Mr. James Scott, one of the collectors to the Widnes Local Board. On Monday last Mr. Scott appeared to be in his customary health and fulfilled his ordinary duties. No signs of illness made their appearance when he retired to rest at nialt, but about six o'clock on Tuesday morning he broke a blood vessel, and expired in a few minutes. Mr. Scott was 51 years of age. His health had been in a delicate state for some time past, but he had, nevertheless, discharged his duties in a most satisfactory manner. For many years, the deceased held a situation under the London and North- Western Railway Company, and was appointed collector to the Local Board so recently as April 1850. The remains of the deceased will be interred in Ardwick Cemetery, Man- chester, to-day (Saturday.) WIDNES PARISH CHURCH ENTERTAINMENT.—The second entertainment of the present season took place in the Water- loo-road schools, on Tuesday evening. The Rev. J. Wright- Williams presided. The programme opened with the glee "Blow gently gales," which was given in good style by the glee class. Mr. Walker contributed " Why rouse the British lion ?" Tne quartette, "England," which was contributed by Miss Farley, and Messrs. Bate, Large, and Wilkinson, was particularly good. and desrvedly won an encore. Mrs. White was very successful in the humorous "Be quiet, do, or I'll tell my mother," and was encored. Mr. Hart gave a Lancashire reading "Donny at Hick's Woife's buryin," which elisited roars of laughter. Mr. Mason gave " Erin-go-Bragh," and was followed by Mr. W. White with the song, "Reuben Wright and Phcebe Brown." Mr. White was encored. The glee class displayed their customary correctness and harmony in the "Bells of St. Michael's tower," which was loudly applauded. Mr. W. Walker sang with spirit in the " Holy Friar." The next item was a recitation, "Thee and me," which Mr. Hart gave in very good style. Mrs. J. White sang with sweet- ness and felicity of expression in "Sunshine on the sea." The cater. "Chairs to mend," was happily interpreted by Messrs. Large, Wilkinson and Walker, and was vociferously encored. Mr. W. White's comic song, "Camomile tea," caused infinite amusement, and was encored. The pro- gramme concluded with the glee, "Night, lovely night,' to which the glee class did full justice.

WIDNES SCIIOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Thursday at the Board's Offices, Victoria-road. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were also present the Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. Jo.'in Brock, H. Wade-Deacon, Robert Shaw, and J. Holden Davies. The minutes of the District Education Committee, which were adopted on the motion of Mr. H. W. Deacon, stated the cases summoned before the committee were the following i—Applications for payment of school fees 60, for contravention of the Education Act 216, total 282. Fees were recommended to be paid in 56 cases, refused 10, number of prosecutions before magistrates 15, convicted 15.—The managers of Simms Cross Board Schools recommended that Mrs. M. E. Morgan be appointed head mistress of the infants' department of that school (vice Miss Henderson) at a salary of £B5 per annum. They also recommended that, at the parent's request, the indentures of Mary E. Robinson, a pupil teacher at Simms Cross Board school, be cancelled at once. The managers of -West. Bank school recommended that the resignation of Miss B. Brake, assistant mistress, be accepted.—The recommendations were adopted on the motion of the Rev. Father Finegan. The half-yearly report of the architects of the Board was sub- mitted, and it was decided that the external repairs con- sidered necessary should be. The repairs were most needed at Simins Cross School.—The Finance CL.mmittee recommended the payment of accounts, amounting to £483 15s. Sd. In moving the confirmation of that recom- mendation, Mr. Shaw said the overseers were drawing the last half of the poor rate, and he thought the Board might soon expect some relief from them.—The Chairman explained that accordiag to custom it would be their duty to appoint committees for the ensuing year. The present committees, he thought, had worked very well, and if the gentlemen who were on them would consent to occupy the position again, he was sure the Board would feel very much indebted to them. He, therefore, begged te move that the committees be reappointed.—Mr. Brock seconded the motion, which was carried, and the Board rose.

AMUSING SCENE: KEEPING COUNTY COURT BAILIFFS "IN POSSitSION."—On Thureday, last week, a somewhat singu- lar and amusing scene occurred at a dwelling-house situate in Crow-lane. Two bailiffs connected with the Warrington County Court were instructed to make a seizure at the house in question, and in duty bound entered in possession. The occupant—a female—unconcernedly stated that if they were the bailiffs, and would remain for a short time, she would find the necessary funds to release her goods from custody. They consented to wait, and took a seat as the lady left the room. The door was pulled to, but to their dismay, the officers of the law heard a fumbling at the lock, and a familiar click clenched that they had been locked in the dwelling-house, thus virtually keeping them prisoners in the house of which they had come to enter in possession. The lady who had turned the key on her prisoners did not return quite as soon as was expected, and the men in possession manifested some concern as to their mode of exit. After waiting for a considerable length of time, the younger of the two "bums," now that they had got inside and found they were likely for being kept in, determined upon making his escape in some way or other. The front door was locked and the key gone—there was no door to let them out at the back—and therefore he could only gain his liberty by getting through one of the windows. Either from compulsion by the fear of ridicule through being seen escaping from a front window, or from choice, he forced himself through a remarkably small aperture at the back and after some difficulty found himself in the free and open air once more. He at once visited the Newton Police-station and sought the assistAnce of the kind an obliginr: Sergeant stationed there. Together they returned to the heuee, the sergeant being imploringly appealed to to break opeu the door as a seizure—and a capture toe—had been made. But that gentleman refused to do this, adding that the bailiff outside might do so if he chose. Eventually the latter decided to this, and armed with a•formidabie weapon ia the shape of a borrowed iron hammer of massive propor- tions, commenced an attack on the house by battering at the front door. As could only be expected a consi&rable number of persons gathered round who were much amused and interested with the proceedings. Thedoorultimately gave v,av, and the unwilling prisoner was s rehlhoused Asemlolemhost the r immediately afterwards the tenant o appearance, and was considerably surprised at th,e !lateoef affairs. Going up to the bailiffs s she vehemently . tnern.nd ed to !snow "Who has bad the audacity to break into my house in that wa ?" The younger bailiff replied, ' I broke the y door open," to which her ladyship responded with " You had a good cheek." She was, however, quickly told of the seriousness of locking up bailiffs after they had taken possession, and thinking that discretion was the better part of valour even to females, she very willingly banded over the required amount, and the bailiffs retired leaving the heroine with a pleasant smile of satisfaction upon her features. .

THE HARE IN LITERATURE.

Sir,—Some young folks I know have dug out the follow- ing remarks anent the hare, from a volume entitled "False Beasts and True," by Francis Power Cobbe. It is one of the series of the country house library of standard authors, published by Messrs. Ward, Lock, and Co. . The extracts are taken from the chapter entitled "Animals in Fable and Art ":—" The animal which has been, perhaps, more mis- represented in fable than any other, is the hare. She is I the type of senseless timidity and likewise of idle boastful- ness. At one time the hares rush to drown themselves in a pond, till, seeing they have frightened the frogs, they think better of it, and agree to live, since they have found crea- tures more faint-hearted than themselves. At another time the hare makes a wager with a tortoise, and loses the race by lying down and going to sleep. And lastly, there is the piteeo story of The hare wh,,, in a civil way, Complied with everything—like gay; Her care was never to offend, And every creature was her friend. And who yet in her extremity implored in vain the aid of the horse, the bull, the goat, and the sheep, and received from the calf the polite farewell— Excuse me, then, you know my heart; But dearest friends, alas ! must part; How shall we all lament! Adieu! For see, the hounds are just in view. Ifvw the fact seems to be that the hare is not a helpless foal by any means; nor can it be said that mere terror and misery would be likely to drive her to suicide. On the contrary, she is a remarkably playful little beast in her sunny hours, both in freedom and when domesticated (everyone remembers Cowper's hares), and in her hour of adversity she displays marvellous coolness and presence of mind, making her bolts, and swervings, and doublings with consummate skill, and hiding herself as cunningly as a fox under a wall, allowing the greyhounds to leap over her. A gentleman in Lancashire having tried in several cases to save hares, after a severe run from the fate which some- times overtakes them, of perishing at night in their forms from cold, and who left them in a warm room with provi- sion of food, invariably found that their fright had by no means spoiled their appetites, but that they had partaken of a good supper or breakfast before the morning's release." The book also contains an amusing account of some geese and young pigs that were observed playing or enacting a kind :of game of prisoner's base, the porkers getting clezidedly the worst of it.—l am, sir, &c., ANGLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, October 22.
THE REV. CANON BNRCLAY ON THE CHURCH MISSIONARY SOCIETY.

Under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay, MA., the annual meeting of the Runcorn Branch of the Church Missionary Society was held in the Holy Trinity Girls' schoolroom, and amongst those present may be mentioned the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., the Rev. R. Palmer (deputation) and the Rev. D. Llewellyn. There was a good audience. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening address, said missions were of two kinds—Conservative, whose object was to pre- vent Christians from becoming heathens; and aggressive, whose object was to turn people from the power of satan unto God. It was the province of the Church Missionary Scciety to carry on the latter sort of missions—to send mis- sionaries wherever an opening occurred in order to turn men from heathen darkness tie Christian light. This was the object which the society had been pursuing for the last four score years, and to which God had given them an abundant measure of success. During this period it had wonderfully increased in the number and character of its promoters, and the funds which had been entrusted to the disposal of the society last year exceeded £200,000, notwithstanding the depression which had existed in the agricultural interest for the last year or two. In IEO4 there was only one missionary station on the pestilential slacres of Western Africa, with only two missionaries employed there, and these men of foreign extraction, who were not even mem- bers of the Church of England, and now there was a society having on its roll 460 ordained missionaries, be- sides 3,550 catechists and teachers. When they remem- bered also that in the 1,617 schools and seminaries sup- ported by this society instruction was given in 40 languages to upwards of 68,000 scholars, and also that the' society had enrolled nearly 180.000 professors of Christianity, the majority of them converted from heathenism, they had reason to thank God and take courage. "(Applause.) These converts were not men of one class. They belonged to every rank and clime, and were of every shade and colour' from the half-naked eavage of the southern seas to the highly educated Chinese. There were those who professed every form of refined or degraded superstition, and who worshipped in every variety of form such as the heathen did. When he said that the aggressive missions were the particular province of the Church Mis- sionary Society, he did not think he was quite right, because so much had God blessed its labour that in Sierra Leone, the iirst scene of the society's labours, there was now no lonsser a mission station. It could now be considered a centre, from which the light and truth of the Gospel might pene- trate into the interior. In that country there were 18 of what he might call parishes each worked by its parish priest. In each of these parishes there were one or two churches, where there were many worshippers. In these churches the very same prayers, the same psalms, and the same canticles were offered up, though very often with greater unction, as were offered up in the cathedrals and parish churches of 'their dear old England. In close proximity to the mission church they might always find the school, attended not merely by children, but by adults, in order that they might themselves be able to peruse the word of God. When they considered that in these schools there were upwards of 40,700 scholars, and upwards of 5,000 communicants, he thought they had cause for thankfulness. (Hear, hear). It showed that in that particular case the mission was conservative as well as aggressive, in preventing people from falling back through their many temptations. Remember, too, that these persons were not many years ago thrown on the shore, a band of thoughtless savages, just released from the noi- some hold of he slave ship, and now the colony presented the aspect of a Christian country. But the importance of Sierra Leone chiefly arose from its relation in the interior of Africa, a country, which on account of its pestilential climate was closed to all attempts at evangelistic effort. But in these liberated Africans, God had marvellously opened up a way for the conversion of the native tribes in the interior. The sons of Ham had learned to know and fear the God of Isaac, and they were now anxious to carry the glad tidings to their kindred. Strength to enter its feverish and fatal damps and zeal to carry on the enterprise were here united, and in the liberated Africans they saw con- siderable hope for the conversion of the people in the interior. Where could they find a nation which had made more sacri- fices than England had done for the poor African? If they had done so much to emancipate them from the fetters which galled their limbs, might they not make still greater efforts for the emancipation of these same Africans from the tyranny which the tyrannizer of the human race had imposed upon the sons and daughters of Africa? (Hear, hear.) Let each one do his best to introduce them into that noblest of freedoms, namely, the liberty with which Christ makes His people free. (Applause.) The Rev. WM. PRESTON read the report of the Runcorn bran& ,sshich showed that £63 3s. lid. had been remitted to the parent society. The Rev. R. PALMER gave an encouraging account of the work of the society, and referred to the recent munificent donations to the missionary society of Mr. W. C. Jones, of Daresbury, by which, he said, they had been enabled to develope and spread their organisation in China and Japan. On the motion of the Rev. D. LLEWELLYN, seconded by Mr. SEFTON, a vote of thanks was passed to the deputation; and a similar compliment baying been paid to the chairman on the proposition of Mr. PALMER, seconded by Mr. Poturr, the meeting terminated.

On Saturday, a seaman of the transport Marathon, named Palmer, was makii3g fast the foresail, when he fell from the yardarm on to the deck, and when picked up he was quite dead. In a letter on the subject of the proposed new rules of procedure, Mr. John Bright says the only fault to be found in them is that they are not sufficiently stringent for the evil they are intended to meet. It is proposed to erect a memorial to the late Dean of Windsor in St. Georae's Chapel, and a committee, of which the Prince of Wales has been pleased to consent to act as president, is being formed for the purpose of carrying this design into effect. The Conservatives of one of the districts in Finsbury have implored Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote to take heed lest the victory achieved by our troops in the field in Egypt be reversed in the council chamber. In reply the Marquis of Salisbury concurs with the Finsbury Con- servatives in "thinking that there is considerable danger lest the advantages which have been gained by the va!Our of our troops should be lost in negotiation."

CONGREGATIONALISM AT CADISHEAD. The foundation stone of a Congregational school chapel for Irlam and Cadishead was laid at the latter place, on Saturday afternoon last, by Mr. Zia Armitage, J.P., of Warrington. Congregationalism first obtained a footing in Cadishead in 1875, under circumstances described below, but the congregation has grown too large to be accommo- dated in the old shed in which the members have worshipped since the above date, hence the erection of a new chapel. The building, which will be in the Gothic style of architec- ture, is about 40 ft. long by 25 ft. wide, and will accommodate about 200 persons. There will also be an intermediary class-room capable of holding 60 or 70 infants. Fixed seats will be placed up the middle of the edifice for the congre- gation, and movable seats up the sides for Sunday school purposes. Tbe chapel will be built of gray bricks, with red bands, and Yorkshire stone dressings, and will cost about £5OO. The architects are Messrs. Tate and Popple- well, Mosley-street, Manchester, Mr. George Wallington, of Warrington, is the builder, and Mr. E. Auckland, of War- rington, is supplying the stonework. The weather in the morning was unpropitious, but in the afternoon the sun , broke out and lent its countenance to the ceremony, which was performed in the presence of a large number of persons. Besides Mr. and Mrs. Armitage there were also present the Revs. A. Mackennall, 8.A., of Bowdon T. Willis, Man- chester; J. Yonge Warrington; W. Place, Patricroft ; R. Dillon (Wesleyan), Cadishead • W. Woodburn, Partington ; Messrs. J. S. Garland, W. Wallington, James Kenworthy, B. Farrar, Warrington; E. B. Scott, I. M. Davenport, S. Riley and W. Robinson, Cadishead; R. B. Taylor and Wyatt, Urmson ; &c. After the hymn, "Sabbath schools are Eng- land's glory," had been sung, and prayer offered by the Rev. W. Place, The Rev. A. Menensreram, delivered an address. He said he must in the first place express the very great satisfaction which it gave him to be present that day. Mr. Yonge knew a great deal of the later difficulties he knew in connection with the securing of that piece of land, and of the carrying out of the work which had so far advanced as to demand their presence there that day; but he happened to know some of the earlier difficulties, and in the remember- anca of those, he cordially congratulated Mr. Scott, and other gentlemen associated with him, and all those who were interested in the work that called them there. Some few years ago it seemed an almost hopeless thing to secure a piece of land on which they might erect a House of God for Congregational:worship. The difficulties were many, and when they seemed to be overcome they where only landed face to face with a greater diffiuculty, with a per- plexity even of a more trying character than those which before they had met. He was sincerely glad the faith and patience of their friends had not been wanting; that they remained a company of worshipping people until this time. Those of them who knew the building in which they had met for worship must have surely recognised that those who could gather together from Sunday to Sunday in a place of worship such as that must have been men and women of unusual earnestness and unusual determination. Since the early Christians gathered together in dens and caves of the earth, he scarcely thought a more ungainly place had been used for public worship than the little meet- ing-room in Cadishead. Dis ,he would rather nieet In dens and caves of the earth than in such a shed as that in which had been gathered the people who worshipped there. They had come together to witness the laying of the foundation stone of what promised to be a very commodious and neat place of worship. He was glad it was on that site. Looking round upon the way in which the population was settling down there, he was inclined to think that site was a superior site to any of those which a few ago were coming under their notice. Having said this much with respect to the former difficulties of the place, he should like to say a few words to them in reference to that Congre- gational mode of church government which would be ob- served in connection with the church that was to come to- gether there. They were calling their friends to meet with them, and they were inviting to associate with them mem- bers of other communities to their own, and the inhabitants of Irlam and Cadishead might fairly ask what was their position in relation to those minor matters which distin- guished Christians from one another—what it was that dis- tinguished them as Congregationalists. Let him in the first place say the distinctive feature of Congregationalism was not the demand that Church and State should be separated one from another. They held that, and held it with great tenacity; it would be impossible for them to bee Congrega- tionalists if they did not hold that; but Presbyterians and large numbers of Methodists held that doctrine with as firm a tenacity as themselves, and yet they did not meet for worship as Presbyterians or as Methodists. Let him say again that the old Calvinistic type of doctrine which dis- tinguished the Congregational churches could not be said to distinguish them now. The Calvinistic type of doctrine, though it still existed among them, had nevertheless given way to an evangelical type of doctrine. He might say again the essence of their church polity did not lie in the right of the congregation to choose their own minister. , They believed that, and a great deal more than that. There I were two principles—he did not know which to place first and which to place second, but he would name them as nearly together as the powers of human speech would enable him. The essence of Congregationalism lay in these two principles—first of all, that the church of God was a community of men and women animated by a common per- sonal faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, and owning supreme allegiance in all things to His will; and that community, that was so constituted and bound together by a living faith and supreme purpose, had not only the right but had also the duty to manage its own affairs. Those were the two pillars that supported their Congregational conception of church government. Ha had spoken of the right and duty of such a community to carry on the work of the cburch in its own way. If they were asked what the work of the church was, they were remirded that the work of the church was, first of all, the building up of its own members especially in faith and piety, as Christian men and women; and in the second place, it was the extension of tlie kingdom of God. And who but earnest Christian believers,—who but those who had the living faith and supreme purpose towards Christ, were able to do either one or other ef these works ? The edifying of Christian believers, and the enlargement of the kingdom of God could not certainly be a work to be committed to the Houses of Parliament, where some were professedly un- believers in Christ, were others were simply professedly believers their faith having no power over them, and where only a very small number indeed admitted Christ to the supreme place in their thought and feeling, and obeyed Christ in all things. They were bound to see that those who did the work of God should be men and women of God; and it was in order to secure that that they bound them- themselves together in little fellowships of this character. They believed where men and women of that sea were gathered together Christ would fulfil His promise, and be in their midst. They might ask help from others, they might ask kindly consideration from others, and they would do all they could to commend themselves to others in the sight of God. Those who would gather together in that place when it was erected would be put in de- fence of those two principles. The necessity of main- taining the spirituality and purity of Christ's Church was, one principle, and the other principle with the defence of which they were charged, was the conducting of all affairs of that little Christian community: in accordance with the will of their Master, Christ. They would have to seek His will in reference even to the minutest matters of their com- munity, and in reference to the largest matters they would likewise ask His direction with the unfailing certainty that it would be granted. They were entering upon a very large work—not in the matter of expenditure ; they were not building a large chapel. There were others besides themselves in that village and district, and they were glad there were other congregations to gather in those who perhaps might not be affected by the teaching there. But the work they, were carrying on was large in this sense—it concerned in- timately the honour of their Redeemer, and concerned inti- mately the purity of life and growth in grace of the meta women, and children, whom they would gather together into their fellowship there. Large as the work was, they yet rejoiced it was not beyond the power they could command. He earnestly hoped on no consideration whatever those who were associated with that place would ever trifle with the parity of Christian fellow- ship, and on no account whatever admit and continue and allow to continue amongst them men in whose Christian character they had no confidence. He again congratulated them, and expressed his personal thanks to Mr. Yonge. who at a time when it was no longer possible for the congregation Ito which he (the speaker) ministered to continue the over- sight of Cadishead, kindly undertook to add that to the other Christian labours which he was fulfilling. He also stated how earnestly the church at Bowdon desired the pros- perity of that little community. They should never forget that it was to one of their own missionary agents the begin- ning in that place was due; and for the sake of Mr. Fielden, and in thee name of the church which em- ployed Mr. Fielden, and with which it was, his joy and honour to be associated, he should always feel called upon to render any service which was possible to him to the little congregation of Independents at Irlam and Cadishead. (Applause.) The Rev. Joan; YONGE said before proceeding with the actual ceremony which had called them there that day, it had been suggested to him that it would be right and fitting that the simple facts which had led to their existence and presence there that afternoon should be laid before the meeting. Their friend, Mr. Mackennall, in the closing part of his address, referred to those circumstances; but per- haps he might be permitted just to make a further reference to them. The simple history, then of this movement, might be said to be this: The preaching of the Gospel in connection with the Congregationalists in that neighbour- hood was first brought about by the settlement in that locality of a few families who in their previous place of abode had been accustomed to Congregational worship. That was about the year 1875, if he was correctly informed. It was then the late Mr. Fielden—whose name, he believed, was held in grateful memory by the people there, and who worked under the Bowdon Rural Mission, which was associated with Bowdon Congregational Church—first began the movement there. He was aided by a gentleman whom they were glad to have with them that afternoon, and who, he believed, was well known in that neighbourhood—Mr. ?lichens. The only available room discovered for preach- iFnigeldwas that which was still in use. That room Mr. instrumentali a in o t tfin thee' scene en at o t af m and work, and faithful preaching of the -Gesaorsanpieleseto Swtulaln.uWansyd ayd t had be po t h When it was closely packed the Cadishead Cathe- dral. as some people called it—(laughter)—would hold 70 or 80 persons; but when 80 were within its walls it was closely packed indeed. Notwithstanding all the physical discomforts under which their friends were working they

had held so well together, and Christ's work had so pros- pered in the school, that they had felt compelled 4o seek a larger and more comfortable place in which to carry on their work. The proceedings of that afternoon were the outcome of patient waiting and unceasing toil. It was felt there was ample room in that locality for a new place of worship. Within reach of that spot there was a population of more than 2,000 people. He believed he was correct in saying their Wesleyan-friends were the only other denomination in the village of Cadis- head, and that township, perhaps somewhat singularly, was unable to boast of any parish church of its own. Its in- habitants either had to go to Hollins Green, a mile and a half on one side, or to Irlam, a similar distance on the other side. Seeing that Irlam was likely soon to become a growing suburb of the city of Manchester, it had been felt all the more desirable to secure a site for a chapel. The merits of the case were testified to by the Lancashire Con- gregational Union, which granted an annual sum towards the maintenance of preaching there, and by the Lancashire and Cheshire Chapel Building Society, who had promised the sum of £lOO towards an expected outlay of £6OO, which the building would cost. They were already promised more than half—L33o—towards that amount. The friends on the spot had given more than £5O, and friends round about thei locality had given £l5O, and of these he might specially mention the firm of their friend Mr. Armitage, who gave £6O, and Mr. Jesse Howarth, who contributed £25. (Ap- plause.) Mr. E. B Score then, in the name of the children, teachers, and congregation who had been accustomed to worship in the building which was known as " Cadishead Cathedral," presented to Mr. Armitage a silver trowel with which to lay the foundation stone of their future chapel. Mr. Anectrada proceeded with the ceremony in a work- manlike manner, and, amid applause, declared the stone to be "well and truly laid." Addressing the assembly, Mr. Armitage said they had listened already to two addresses, one giving them the history of the cause in connection with that place of worship, and the other pointing out what the distinctive principles of Congregationalism were; and It was not part of his duty to attempt to enlarge upon those speeches. To be permitted in any capacity to take part in the erection of a house for the worship of God in accordance with the principle, and teach- ing of the New Testament was a privilege which he had learned to value highly. (Hear, hear.) At the same time he should have been more than content to have taken a far less prominent place in that ceremony than that which had been allotted to him. There were many persons pres .nt who had taken their fair share in the work of reviving that interest, and to them was due the honour of having supported this work and having brought it to its present very hopeful position. The duty which they had called upon him to dis- cbarge would have conferred upon anybody whom they might have selected a very honourable distinction, and he accepted it with gratitude and thankfulness. They would always regard that day as the starting point of a new era in their history, and he hoped the future would be all they hoped and more than that. He desired above all things that the records of the church would give to those who followed them a history uf true spiritual progress, and that the place shoula become a centre of light and usefulness in the neighbourhood so that great good might be done in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Applause.) The Rev. T. WILLIS gave a brief congratulatory address, and the ceremony concluded, as it began, with praise and prayer. A well attended tea meeting afterwards took place in the Wesleyan Day Schools, and following this was held a public meeting, over which the Rev. J. Yonge presided, in the ab- sence of Mr. P. N. Ford, of Stretford.

The rev. CHAIRMAN said he could not forbear expressing the hearty pleasure he had in the look of things that day. He was sure the Cadishead friends felt in good spirits, and, he felt confident the future of that Congregational move- ment would be a very prosperous and happy one. He took that oppoetunity of expressing his sense of gratitude to the friends who had allowed them to assemble in that room, and assured the Wesleyan brethren the Congregationalists had not come into Cadishead with any intention of making things worse for the Wesleyans. They believed there was room for both of them, and he hoped the future would sea them working together in full brotherly sympathy. Addresses were also delivered by the '..Rev. T. Willis, Mr. Nichols and Mr. J. S. Garland, the Rev. R. Dillon, Rev. W. Woodburn, Rev. Rogers (Lancashire Independent College), Messrs. R. Farrar, W. Wallington, James Ken- worthy, G. Wallington, C. B. Scott, I. M. Davenport, Jac. During the evening selections of music were given by mem- bers of the Wycliffe Church choir, whose performances were much appreciated.

Prosecutor and Burgess then ran away, and witness went to P.C. Rigby, and informed him of what had taken place.—ln reply to the Bench, prosecutor said Bradshaw did not inter- fere with him at all, but he was dressed-np as a woman.— George Burgess was then called, and his statement agreed with prosecutor's up to the part relating to who was [dressed up in a woman's clothes. He said he was prepared to take a "solemn oath" that it was William Bate who was dressed in a woman's clothes, and not the other man. He was quite confident of that.—Mr. Greenall: Well, prosecutor has taken his solemn oath that it was the other man, so what can I make of the two ?—The Assistant Clerk (Mr. Brown) said he was afraid no jury would convict on such evidence.—Mr. Greenall said he quite concurred with Mr. Brown.—P.C. Rigby deposed that he met the prisoners on Sunday-night at the time named coming from the direction of the spot where the robbery was alleged to have been committed, but neither of them wore women's clothes.—Mr. Greenall reminded Burgess that the prosecutor had sworn quite contrary to him as to which of the prisoners was dressed in women's clothes —Burgess : Well, he has made a mistake.—Mr. Greenall: But people who take oaths should not make such mistakes. Under the circumstances he felt he could aelopt no other course than to discharge the prisoners, as no jury would convict upon such evidence.—The prisoners, who I stoutly denied having been concerned in the aftair at all, • were then set at liberty.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY ADVENTURE ON WIN WICK-ROAD.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY ADVENTURE ON WIN WICK-ROAD.

1 At the Occasional Court House, Winwick-street, Warring- ton, on Monday, before Mr. E. Greenall, two men named W. Bate, wiredrawer, and Wm. Bradshaw, employed at Dal lam Forge, were charged with committing a highway robbery on Mr. Alexander Boyle Gibbon, assistant master- of Winwick Grammar School.—The prosecutor stated that en Sunday morning, about ten o'clock, he arrived at Warrington from Ireland, and went te the house of a friend in the town, where he stayed until half-past ten at night. He then proceeded to walk home, and as he was going on the way to Winwick he was stopped by the prisoner Bate, who was closely fol- lowed by Bradshaw. Bate said to h:rn "Have you got much money about you 2" and he replied "I have net." Prisoner then left him for a few minutes, and went into a house, and he proceeded on his way with a man named George Burgess, wheelwright and coachbnilder, Newton, whom he met. They had not got very far, however, before the prisoners overtook them, and passed and re-passed them several times. He (witness) then noticed that Bradshaw had changed his clothes, and put on a woman's clothes. When they came near the Corporation Longford Depot, Bate caught him by the collar of the coat, and said he must go hick with him. Prosecutor replied, "I am going on to Winwick, and I must get there to-night." Burgess said to Bate "Let him alone. It is of no business to you where he goes. He can go where he likes." Bate thereupon struck Burgess on the chest with his fist. Bate then again demanded money from both of them, saying he must have a shilling. Prosecutor said he bad no money to spare, but before he would stand prisoner's blows and knocks he would give him all he had. He then caught prosecutor by the collar and threw him down in a ditch, and prosecutor gave him all the money he. had, arnotnting to 10d. Bate then snatched his umbrella from him, and he had not seen it since. It was worth ss.

FRODS HAM.

FRODSHA3I DEBATING SOCIETY.—The first of a series of lectures, in connection with the above society, was given in the Girls' School, Frodsham, on Monday evening. The lecturer on the occasion was the vicar—Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A.—the subject being "The life of Dr. Samuel Johnson." The rev, lecturer gave a brief sketch of the leading inci- dents in the career of Dr. Johnson, and a vote of thanks was passed at the close of the meeting, on the motion of Mr. Thomas Riley, seconded by Mr. Henry Tiley. WWI:RYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS: SBRILONS AND ANNETAL MEETING.—On Sunday, two sermons were preached in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham, on behalf of Wesleyan Foreign Missions by the Rev.
