M. Bamford read extracts from' the annual report, and stated that the income of the Parent Society for 1881 amounted to £141,72.2 18s 7d, and the expenditure to £140,754 is id, showing a deficiency on the year of £5,031 2s ad, which, added to the deficiency of previous years, made a present debt of £.32,266 13s lid. The amount contributed by the Frodsham circuit was MO ss, or an increase of als 4d over the previous year. The Rev. Thomas Rippon, of Warrington, and the Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn, attended as the deputation, and addressed the meeting at corsiderable length. The total collections amounted to £l4, or an increase at the rate of £5 per cent. over the previous year. A hearty vote of thanks was ac- corded to the collectors and committee on the motion of the Rev. F. P. Edmonds, seconded by Mr. Moss, and a vote of thanks to the chairman was carried by acclamation, on the motion of the Rev. J. M. Bamford, seconded by Mr. R. H. Turner.

div.head: OVER.
div.p: OVER.

A Rand of Hope meeting was held at Over, in the Mission Room, Deiamere-street, on Monday night. There was a good attendance. Mr. Maudsley occupied the chair, and was supported by Messrs. John H. Massey, J. Hough, and other friends, all of whoa spoke very earnestly. The choir did their part well. Somin.—The Young Men's Society connected with the Marshall Memorial Schools, Over, held a soiree on Wed- nesday night, when Edward Leigh, Esq., presided, and a fairly good attendance listened to the music, essays, recita- tions, and the "Trial scene from Merchant of Venice," all of which passed off very well.

div.head: WEAVER.
div.p: WEAVER.

The anniversary sermons of the Free Methodist Church, Weaver, were preached on Sunday last by the Rev. W. T. Symons, of Winsford, when the church, in the afternoon especially, was well filled. The rev, gentleman spoke in his usual earnest and faithful manner. Great cause of encourage- ment was felt by the preacher and office-bearers, and pros- perity was expected to crown the efforts of the little church in the future more than for some time in the past.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

- DISTRICT MEETING.—The autumnal meeting of the Free Methodist Churches for the district Liverpool and North Wales was held at Winsford, in the High-street Chapel, on Tuesday and Wednesday last. Nearly 30 representatives from the different circuits came up for the conference, the greater portion of whom were ministers. The chairman of the meeting was the Rev. W. T. Symons, the superintendent of Winsford knd Sandbach circuit; and the secretary, the Rev. T. Naylor, from Crewe. Tuesday was devoted to credential work and hearing the state of the churches finan- cially and religiously, which may be spoken of in hopeful terms. A public tea was prepared, but the unseasonable weather' hindered many from attending, and the provisions were utilized for a second or society tea on the Wednesday. After the tea a public meeting was held under the presidency of Joseph Slater, Esq., of Woodford Hall, the mayor of Over. After a hymn, "Head of the church," had been sung (Mr. Buckley presiding at the organ), and prayer bad been offered up by the Rev. D. Brook, of Liverpool, the chairman said he regretted so small a meeting for Wins- ford, and especially with such great speakers. He thought they had reason to be glad that they had had an increase of 47 in the Winsford circuit of the Liverpool district rather than a decrease; though there had been a decrease of more than 100 on the whole district, which was matter of great regret. The Rev. Hy. Holgate was next called on to speak. He said a grand era was before them. The country was rising. Never were there so many Christian men and women in the world as at the present time. Education had become a power for good, but it did not accomplish all that some expected of it. It required to be sanctified by God's grace. Some took an optimist or hopeful view of things while others took a pessimist view and regarded things in the worst light. They ought to rejoice and be glad that they were what they are.--The Rev. Thomas Sherwood related a story illustrating the business aptitude of some of the Wins- ford brethren.—The Rev. Tho.-nas M. Booth set forth how the church should act with regard to its young. The chil- dren were the hope of the church, circle them by holy living, good example, and godly training. Keep them in, after bringing them to the church, that when they are old they may not depart from it.—After a few observations from Richard Lloyd, Esq., Liverpool, the Rev. David Brooks spoke of the influence of education.—The best thanks of the meeting were given the speakers and chairman, and the doxology terminated a pleasant gathering.—On Wednesday, a chnrch meeting followed the tea, and addresses by circuit ministers, Revs. IT. T. Symnos and James Wright, and other friends caused a very profitable time to be spent.

div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
Dr. Fox reports to the Nantwich Rural Sanitary Authority that the death rate of the district during the quarter ended September 30th was 16.5.

Municipal nominations have already been lodged at Ches- ter, which ensure stubbornly fought battles in most wards. On this occasion the struggle will turn entirely upon the Parliamentary Improvement Bill, to which there is a very great opposition.

An inquest was held at Chester on Monday, on the boily of Colour-Sergeant Mills, who died on Saturday morning in the barracks. He enticed his youngest son into the parlour and got him to pull the trigger of a Martini-Henry rifle. A verdict of suicide whilst in an unsound state of mind, was returned.

A stoker, named John Minshall, living at Pendleton, Manchester, was passing from an engine tender at Nortbgate Station, Chester, on Sunday, when he stumbled and fell, his bead corning in contact with a pointed lump of coal. lie was picked up in an insensible condition, and removed to the Chester:lnfirmary, where he now lies.
WIGAN. Representatives of miners of the Wigan district met on Thursday, and agreed to accept the 10 per cent. advance offered by the masters.

div.head: LYNN SE VVERAGE SOFIEME.
div.p: LYNN SE VVERAGE SOFIEME.
RATEPAYERS' MEETING.

On Monday evening a meeting of the ratepayers of Lymm was held at the Plough Hotel, to consider the new sewerage scheme. Mr. Cameron, chairman of the Local Board, presidea, and most of the members of the Board were present. There was a large attendance of ratepayers.—The CHAIRMAN explained that Higher-lane, from the Thrasher to Bleak House, all Eagle-brow, and the Top-lane district, part of Cherry-lane and Newfield, are drained; but the sewage is in no case dealt with in accordance with legal requirements. What the Board proposed doing by this scheme was to dispose of the whole of the sewage of the district in a permanent and efficient manner, and how they proposed to do this was by securing 13 acres of land in Statham Eye; carrying the pipes over the pool road on the now almost historical bridge, leading from thence in nearly a direct line to the corner of the road below the :station. But before getting so far a branch sewer would be cut to drain Statham and the well-known Oak Tree district. The drain discharging from Newford, near Mr. Rogers', would also be picked up by the way. From the corner the sewer would run up the road about half way towards the cross- ing, and then turn off at nearly right angles, and parallel with the railway some little distance, past the first bridge from Lymm station. It would then pass under the railway, up through the dam bank, valley tunnel, under the canal, arid pass along the bottom end of gardens Owned by Messrs. Brown, Evans, Taylor, and others, and on to where the present Eagle-brow discharges. So far, ex- cept with regard to the land, what he described was pretty much the scheme which was laid before the inspector at the unfortunate enquiry on the 30th November last. At that enquiry Mr. Harrison instructed the engineer to extend the proposed works very considerably, stipulating that Rush Green sewer should be joined into the sewerage system, a new sewer to be made along Pepper-street in order to pick up the Higher-lane and Oughtrington sewerage, and sanitary pipes to be laid in Eagle-brow, where at present there was only a tunnel through the rock. These instructions had been carried out in the amended plans. But there was another point which the Inspector recommended for con- sideration with which they had been unable to comply, and that was taking the outfall works to the glebe land. The , engineers found that the levels would not admit of the '

[Board going there, besides other serious objections to that site, even if the level were favourable. He might say that the scheme was unanimouedy adopted by the Board.— Mr. HOORRS referred to the difficulties regarding glebe lands and said there was no doubt whateYer that the most snit- able place to be found was in Statham Eye. There was no place east or west that could be adapted for that purpose without pumping, and he was sure the ratepayers would not like them to go into such an extravagant course.—ln reply to Mr. Hall, the CHAIRMAN said they had examined all the fields that were feasible, and the engineers and professional officers came to the conclusion that the Rector's land was not suitable at all.—Mr. HALL said it appeared to him that the time had come when the ratepayers of Lymm should have some information given afC to the proceedings taken latterly by the Local Board. Referring to the bridge which it was proposed to make in connection with the scheme, he said there was not the slightest doubt that if the canal scheme went on there wouM be no floods in the meadows, and he thought it would 'col very ridiculous if in the future they had to look back to a bridge over a couple of dry holes. The name would then ho changed from Pool's Bridge to Fool's Bridge. (Laughter.) He observed that the sewage would go into Laskey Brook,. which was in the parish of Thelwall, and they would find themselves up to the eyes in litigation for contaminating the brook with their sewage. He asked the cost of the bridge.--The CHAIRMAN said it would be about £23o.—Mr. HALL said the estimate was once at £75, but apparently it had grown considerably. The scheme itself had grown from £2,000 to an estimated cost of nearly £B,OOO, and he was told by a good authority that it would be more like £9,000.—A RATHPAYHR asked how much-had been spent on sewerage before.—The CHAIRMAN said about £3,000. A RATRPATHR said that would make a total sum of about £ll,ooo.—Mr. HALL hoped that the ratepayers, when the Commissioner came down, would be present with him, and show him by their determination that so large an amount of money was not necessary to be spent. There had been, be was glad to say, a petition sent to London signed by nearly every tradesman and shopkeeper in the Parish.—Mr. TAILOR said he had been single-handed throughout the fight. The schemes were laid before the Board and hastily considered.—Mr. SMITH said it appeared from the minutes that had been read that instead of the time and attention of the Board having been devoted to the consideration of this important matter, which would cost in the aggregate nits, sum of about £12,000, they had disposed of it in a feet' minutes, and apparently without any discussieng They ought to have had an opportunity beforehand of inspecting all the plans and getting a thorough knowledge of what the Board proposed to do. It would cost £l2 for every house in the village, or £2 103. for each inhabitant.—After some further observations from the chairman the meeting con- cluded with a vote of thanks being accorded to Mr. Cameron for presiding.

GOVERNMENT INQUIRY. At the Waterworks' office, Lyrnm, on Wednesday, Mr. Harrison, Local Government Board inspector, held an in- quiry relative to the proposed sewerage scheme for Lvmm. There was a good attendance of members of the Local Boar.d, and also of ratepayers. The inspector beard evidence in favour of and against the scheme, and after a long inquiry Mr. Harrison expressed his approbation of the scheme, and said he thought the Board bad exercised a wise discretion in the selecfion of the site.

div.head: HALTON COURT LEET.
div.p: HALTON COURT LEET.

INTERESTING PROCEEDINGS. The ancient Court Lest of Halton was held at the Castle on Saturdav by the steward, Mr. Robert Davies, of War- rington, and the majority of the townships within the manor were represented. The proceedings were merely of a formal character, the functions ef the Court having become obselete. The proclamation having been read by the Higha Bailiff (Mr. Phillips), the following jurors answered to their names :—Messrs. Richard Coppock, Antrobus ; Henry Taylor, Barnton ; James Lowe, Bartington ; John Cooper and George Pennington, Daresbury; Thomas Wright, J. S. Jeacock, and William Fryer, Hatton; Thomas Bennett, IIC ekewick ;.William Brundritt, Millington; Philip Derby- shire, Newton-juxta-Daresbury ; Joseph Acton, Sutton; John Ellison, Stretton ; Peter Brocklehurst, Seven Oaks; William Beswick, Walton Superior; and William Turner, Walton Inferior. Mr: Thomas Wright was unanimously chosen foressan of the jury, and he and his fellows were then duly sworn, each jury being amereed in the sum of one shilling. This concluded, the STEWARD briefly Pfdressed the jury. He commented on the fact that the dugeons of the castle were now the ale cellars of their high bailiff, and were no longer used as a terror. In olden times dungeons were very terrible places, and imprisonment meant something very serious. It was customary to send prisoners from Chester to be tried and hanged at Halton. Unfortunately, their rolls were now at the Record Office, but the Court had been held for more than 600 years; and although it had to a certain extent been superseded by the County Court and other modern establishments of justice, yet they could take into acoonnt presentiments of offences, encroachments, tres- passes, and anything connected with the land within the manor. The Steward alluded to the oppressed condition of the English peasantry in remote times, and taid the Court was established to enable tenants of the land to get justice iwithin the manor. He (the steward) represented a long list of stewards, who in their generation were very important. Royal personages had been stewards of the manor. Cathe- rine of Braganza in her time was lady of the manor, and now it was held even by Her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen, uader whose seal he (the steward) held his appoint- ment. The steward referred to the jurisdiction of the minor in ancient times, and then said that in casually looking over the few rolls remaining at the castle he had found one which referred to an ancestor of his own, relating to the transfer of some land in Astmoor. There were many familiar names on the parchment, some being ancestors of several of the jurors then present. All the old powers sur- vived to the Court, but they had become obsolete, and he did hope that whatever Her Majesty might take it into her head to do she would never order the justice of the assizes to send any person from Chester to Halton to be hanged. If this happened to be the c7se, he should delegate his powers to his High Bailiff—(laughter)---who would have to do his best with the ease according to his skill and ability. (Renewed laughter.) The Court then appointed Mr. George Pennington and Mr. W. Fryer constables of Halton for the ensuing year. Mr. William Stokes and Mr. Joseph Astbury were appointed burleymen. The Court then adjourned for dinner. After the cloth was removed,
The STEWARD gave "The Queen," and said they were not only bound by their loyalty to drink his toast, but particularly because it was under her auspites that they were holding her Court.
The toast was honoured. The STEWARD gave the "Bishop and clergy of the diocese and the ministers of all denominations."

The Rev. J. LOCAWOOD, in responding, said he had at- tended the Court ior some five years at the kind invitation of Mr. Davies and it had always been a pleasure to meet the jury.. (Hear, hear.) Whatever denomination they 631onged it was a pleasure to meet at that Court. On the previous day he (the speaker) was at a meeting of the clergy in Chester, and a remark was made thaL perhaps one of the reasons why the masses of the people did not go to places of worship was that the clergy did not associate more with their people. Now, he did not think that was quite correct. He believed the clergy of the Church of England were a visiting clergy, and took a deep interest in all affairs of their parish. (Hear, hear.) Halton was a parish of 2,000 people, scattered over five miles by three, but it was impos- sible for a single person to do the duty required in a parish like that. What was wanted in the church was more lay help. (Hear. hear.) If they wanted workingmen to come to the church they must have workingmen to speak to them in their own way, and get them to come to church. They found that it was by this means the Salvation Army at- tained their great success. It was not the captain of the army that did the work. It was done by the members who, when at their daily toil,talked with their fellows, and brought them to the services. He thought if the clergy would get together a band of workingmen in every parish in the diocese, there would be less men and women idling their time and mis-spending their opportunities for good. He trusted there were better times in view, and that to them as a religious body there would be greater prosperity. Mr. ISENNEITT, of Kekewick, proposed "The health of the Steward." In whatever capacity they regarded Mr. Davies, whether as a gentleman, lawyer, or Steward of the Court, they always fornad him the same. He was a gentleman whom they all admired and respected. (Applause.) In Warrington there was not a gentleman more highly es- teemed, and he (Mr. Bennett) did not know how it was that he had never risen to the pinnacle of fame. (Hear, hear.) He was sure it was his own fault that he was not the Mayor of Warrington, and be felt sure, if he coveted Parliamentary honours, he would be the member of Parlia- ment for the borough. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with musical honours and ,three cheers.

Mr. DANIES responded, remarking that Mr. Bennett had spoken of him in too flattering a manner; but they were such old friends that he thought he exhibited a little ex- cusable partiality. He then proposed the health of the jury, coupling with the toast the name of Mr. Wright, the foreman, who responded. Other toasts followed.

An interesting part of the day's proceedings was the ceremony known as " colting." There were present several "colts "—persons who attend the Court for the first time— and they were according to custom "Shod with silver shoes," a ceremony which afforded considerable amusement. About five o'clock the High Bailiff read the proclamation for the adjournment of the Court, which is as follows :—"All manner of persons who have appeared here to-day at this Court may depart hence and give their attendance again upon a new summons. God save the Queen, the Duke of Lancaster and Lord of this Manor." The jurors then dispersed.

The Scotsman states that the name of Sir U. Kay-Shuttle- worth is mentioned in connection with the representation ef Edinburgh. Mr. Waddy. Q.C., who has, it is understood, abandoned all intention of again coutesting Sheffield, is also mentioned as a possible candidate, but the learned gentle- man will, of course, yield to the claims of Sir U. Kay- Shuttleworth, if the latter were preferred by the leaders of the Liberal party. On Thursday morning, Mrs. Cox, of East-street, Wolver- hampton, left her little boy George, three years of age, alone in the kitchen while she went a short errand. On returning, she found his dead body under a table burnt almost to a cinder. He only had his nightdress on, and it is supposed he set himself on fire and crouched under the table.

MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.

BAZIAR AT RUNCORN. A bazaar promoted by the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen, was opened in Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday afternoon. Its object was to raise fonds with which to build or purchase a .house for. the local missionary, Mr. W. Shaw. The propriety of providing a residence for the missionary was first .discussed in public at a meeting which was held in the Mission room, on the 12th October of last year, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A. A favourable decision was arrived at, and a committee was subsequently formed to give it effect. The chief difficulty encountered by the committee was, of course, how they were to raise the requisite amount of money, and it is not surprising that they should adopt that most popular and effective method of holding a bazaar, which they resolved should take place in spring. Various concurrent circumstances, however, prevented the carrying I out of this resolve, and, as the next more appropriate time, autumn was selected. As the person who will first receive the : benefit of the proposed residence, the interest of the occasion was, to a great extent, centred in Mr. Shaw, and it will not be out of place to refer briefly to the missions which are under ; his control. It was about midsummer of the year 1875, that Mr. Shaw commenced his labours amongst the seafaring population of Runcorn. A few years previous to that period a mission, established by the trustees of the Bridgewater Canal, had been at work, but when that waterway became vested in the Navigation Company its operations ceased, and the boatmen on the canal and also on the river were left without a special spiritual guide. Mr. Shaw, then, had, as it were, fresh ground to break—the raw material to mould. Describing at that time the people among whom it was his lot to labour, he said they were the most ignorant and neg. I lected in the country, and it was seldom any of them at- tended a place of worship. Some had never been in a church since they were married, and, the natural inference is, very seldom before that epoch in their lives. Some heads of families were so deaf to the calls of morality that they had even neglected to engage in that solemn rite. On board the flats the women worked the same as the men, and "at night when the work is done, both men and women go and drink until midnight, while the children are all the time playing in and about the public-house." The picture is not overdrawn —to a less extent, perhaps, the same depravity exists now— and it shows with what an Herculian labour Mr. Shaw was confronted. But Mr. Shaw has kindly followed the hard life of a sailor, and with that energy and earnestness which has characterised his conduct during 7 years he has been in the town, he commenced his mission of proclaiming the light and truth. Results had proved that those "ignorant people were not beyond the reach of the Gospel." The mis- sion has been rewarded with an abundant means of success. During the last six months of the year 1875, Mr. Shaw ad- dressed 3,492 persons, either in their houses or on their boats, and held 26 meetings in the mission room, which were attended by 2,001 persons, while 900 persoas attended 16 open-air meetings which were held. In the year 1881 he visited 6,791 boatmen in their houses, flats, and ships, and addressed 12,041 persons. He held 100 meetings in the mis- sion room and 15 in the open-air, the attendance being re- spectively 10,317 and 2,013. There was an average attendance at the Sunday school of 71, and the band of hope temperance meetings had been attended by 2,941 persons. Mr. Shaw is still zealously labouring, and by his genial disposition has made himself very popular in the town, and every success is wished for in the efforts that are being made to provide a residence for him and the future missionaries. The house when pur- chased or erected will be vested in the names of the follow- ing gentlemen as trustees :—Messrs. C. J. Bushell, president of the Mission, Liverpool; A. Ba Four, secretary, Liverpool; W. A. Tomlinson, treasurer, Liverpool; and the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., John Brundrit, J.P., C. W. Hazlehurat, J.P., J. Meadowcroft, John Simpson, all of Runcorn. The time fixed for the opening of the bazaar was two o'clock, but owing to the late arrival of Mr. Clarke Aspinall, of Liverpool, who was to perform the ceremony, it was half an- hour after that hour. Amongst those present were The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., Rev. T. M Ormson, Messrs. W. Shaw, J. Brundrit, J.P., John Simpsen, Wm. and Mrs. Whitaker, John and Mrs. Williams, H. and Mrs. White, Mrs. Hollingsworth, Mrs. Le Uourteur, Mrs. Gerard, Miss Wil- liams, Miss Hewitt, Mrs. R. Derbyshire, Miss Derbyshire,

The Rev. Canon Barclay introduced Mr. CLARBE Aspeeratn, who, after explaining the cause of his late arrival, said it was a great pleasure to him at all times to visit Runcorn. He did not care to indulge in any utterances that were not perfectly real and perfectly true, and therefore he said with perfect reality and perfect truth that he did not know that any previous visit to Runcorn had given him more satisfaction that the present one, because its purpose was of no ordinary kind. All occasions had been important and interesting. This was important and inter- esting, but it was special—it was almost unique in its character. What they apparently had in view was the establishment of a holm or reeidence—they could not quite call it a parsonage, a vicarage or a rectory—for Mr. Shaw and his successors in Mersey Mission work for all time to come, and he hoped that his successors would not occupy the premises yet awhile. (Applause.) He thought it in the interests of the mission that the first tenant should have a very long lease of the premises and continue there for many, many years to come. lie fancied be was not far astray when he said that likely, but for Mr. Shaw's deserved popularity in Runcorn—he used the word in its hest sense— that such an idea as having a residence for him and for his successors in the work in which he was so sympathetically and so successfully engaged would never have been thought of. He confessed that so far as he was concerned he was glad that in his (Mr. Shaw's) time he should have a sub- stantial residence placed at his disposal. He was glad partly because it meant an improved financial position to Mr. Shaw. And why not. The better people were paid ordinarily, for they were all human, the better they worked. But the compliment to Mr. Shaw' if he knew him aright, as he thought he did, would be much more valuable than any pounds, shillings, and pence considerations. (Applause.)l He would, naturally, if he was like the rest of them, feel sigularly pleased and grateful to God and to them that it should have entered into their hearts to do this thing, during, so to speak, his tenure of ofrare, because, naturally, he could not disguise from himself, though he was a modest retiring man, that his work had been sin done as to commend the work and the workers to the acceptability of the people of Runcorn. (Applause.) Might he trouble those present for a moment or two upon the subject of sea- men generally? Whether Runcorn was near the sea or far from it, its people, in common with all English people, were indebted beyond anything that his words could describe to the seafaring population of our land. Nobody valued the territorial and manufacterinfe greatness of England more than he did, and nobody could appreciate the manufacturing and seafaring position of England more than he did; and recollect it was the enterprise of our merchants and ship- owners which, in a very great degree, made England what she was—the envy and admiration of the world. "Ships, Colonies, and Commerce" was a cry they often heard of boastingly at election times. It was a cry we might justly hear of at all times. Ship% colonies, and commerce went far, very far, to place England in the forefront of the nations of the world. But where would ships, colonies, and com- merce be if we had no men before the nalet:? Recollect nothing more important than good capteins and good officers, and we were very well off in that respect :. but it was equally important that the men before the mast —the seamen of all ranks—should be true men, true Eng- lishmen, good navigators.and good in all their characteristics ' as citizens of the country. He believed that our men were improving. He was not a misanthropic person, and he did not really agree, after thoughtful consideration, with some persons who said we were all degenerating. That was a view of society which he thought was an absolutely delusive one. He, on the contrary, with a large connection with sea- faring people, with seafaring organisations, and with training ships—he deliberately gave it as his opinion, for. whatever that might be worth, that our seamen were improving rather than falling away in regard to all the characteristics which went to make sailors what we would wish them to be. Now, where should we be without sailors ? fie was a great believer in justice all round. He did not believe that one class could get on without another clase,and whenever he had to talk on social subjects he hoped he did it with the steady purpose in view of conscientiously proclaiming that we were all necessary, in our several stations, to the welfare of the community as a whole. That was a sound doctrine to teach. We could not get on without masters and officers; we could not get on without our seamen, our able-bodied. energetic, seafaring people. That being so, just think for a moment, they who dwelt on shore in comfortable homes and defied the storms, the tempests, and the raging billows of the ocean—just think for a moment, what a hard, ven- turesome, and dangerous life that sea life was after all. Pay them what we would, sympathise with them as we might— and sympathy was really what many of them wanted more than all—they could not make the forecastle of a ship and the foreign quarters of the sailor, when he was ashore, into an Englishman's home—the cottage home of our working folk (Applause.) They could not do it, and the seafaring life, though it suited some dispositions better than others, was a hard life. It was not absolutely without attractions to very many who pursued it, still hun- dreds of fine bold boys had gone to sea and stuck to it when men, who if they had had the experience of men nt the time when they elected to be sailors, would likely have never gone at all. And it was not because it had attractions, which the sea undoubtedly had, that it turned out quite so sunny a life as most young men think it when they embarked in the profession. "Those who go down to the sea in ships and do their business in the great waters" were generally not sorry when the time came for tern to live absolutely and entirely on shore again. Still it was a grand life, and fortunately for the greatness of this empire there always had teen and always would be men of the spirit which made them good sailors, and which made navigation an occupation which on the whole they liked perhaps as well, and did much better than anything else. But he would like for a moment to say to that audience, especially as there were many ladies present, was there not another aspect of the sailor's life out- side of what he had already mentioned? He thought there was. Of all comforts that men of all ranks looked forward to with the greatest interest and earnestness, the comforts of a home came the very first. A man did like at some time or other to have a permanent fireside of his very own —he did like to have a domestic circle—a family about him. It was music to his ears, it was sunshine in his path. He had spoken of the danger and hat dship of a sailor's life, but what of self-denial that a honest ;seafaring man's life involved in him? He signed articles in Liverpool to go may be to Calcutta or Bombay, or some other eastern pert in a sailine ship. He then went from there to California, and by the time he got home probably the round would have occupied 15 months, or thereabouts; and even if he Was

in a steamer it was everlasting from home. The great majority of seafaring men were away from home for very long periods of time in continuity, and very little at home. The best and most thrifty of them had to sign articles, and 'were gone just as home had begun to make itself more than ever attractive to them by the endearments that surrounded them. He did think people ought to put this and that to- gether, and to sympathise with our sailor population, aye, and their wives too, and their children too. Whatever else went undone, never treat in an unneighboarly, an unsym- pathetic, or unchristian way, the sailors' wives, for however steady, or good, or orderly' or modest she might be, it was a period of trial to many, and it was not 1 free from temptation to some, whilst they were left month after month with their husbands far, far away. He believed in the Seamen's Orphanage in Liverpool, in the annuity fund attached to that institution, which gave widows donations from time to time, but he would plead for the wives of living sailors, who lived here and there and al- most everywhere, and yet some of us could hardly tell, if we were put to it, where they lived, because we never asked and never cared to know. Yes, the seafaring population of England, ashore and afloat, deserved well of English people, and he hoped as time rolled on they would have more and more striking manifestations of our desire to do to them all that we ought to do, looking to the claims upon society. Coming back to the point which brought him there that day on such a pleasant and bright errand, he wished them God speed in their attempt to get a substantial dwelling for their friend Mr. Shaw. He hoped the donations and help from all sources would be very substantially added to by the bazaar or sale of work, call it what they would. Some people talked about bazaars in an unsympathetic sort of way, which he did not care to hear. He contended that a well- ordered bazaar was about as legitimate a way as be knew of of raising money for a good purpose like the one they had in view on that occasion (Applause.) Why, after all, what possible harm could a bazaar do, and could they offer anything much more likely to have a beneficial effect in the neighbourhood in which it took place. Had they any sort of comprehension of the ex- pense which somebody had been put to in arranging and furnishing those stalls as they now had them in view. Casual visitors to bazaars went in, they spent a shilling, walked out again, and thought that they had done good ser- vice. Well, in a way, they had, but they might have found a more substantial way of doing good often. The material on those stalls were the product of downright labour. He used the word advisedly, but he qualified it also advisedly. He knew it had been a labour of love. The work had been going on for months and months. It had filled up many a half hour that might have been listlessly spent but for the work in question. The talk they had bad with neighbours, the arrangement that had been going en—had not all this brought about a sympathetic interchange of feeling—had not it, as it were, brightened everybody up into activity and zeal, of which they might have known little or nothing had there been no bazaar to work for and no home for the missionary to be provided. He could not see any objection to a well-ordered bazaar. He thought the workingmen in favour of such a sale of work were very numerous indeed. In advocating that only a nominal charge should be made on the last day of the bazaar, in order that the workingmen might without difficulty attend, Mr. Asp:a all said they who were richer might talk about their increased obligations and expenditure, but they were better off, and had a firmer hold upon their incomes. The rich did not sympathise enough with the un- certainty of the working man's income, which he earned truly when he was in good employ and in good health. With all the fluctuations in the labour market he did not get more than enough to keep the wolf from the door, and to carry out all those social arrangements whim' they would like to see within the reach of every honest man in the realm. They might talk how they liked about the obligations of working people, but tbey must help them to fulfil them, and it ought to exercise the conscience as well as the heart of every man, to see that there were no men or women, flesh and blood like their own, struggling unduly, wading against the tide which in these days ran so fiercely. He did not believe this country would ever lose by the enlargement of the sympathies of the rich towards a class that was much more numerous than they were, and who, after all, formed the most important ingredient in all departments of wealth in the country, the chief part of which they enjoyed. Take this kindly from him; he did not care for a perfunctory opening of a bazaar or for formal cold and heartless truths at any meeting. (Applause.) When he did anything he liked to do it as his conscience dictated to the best of his ability,—(applause)—however limited that might be. He hoped the missionary home, which would soon rear its head amongst them, would be well built if it had to be built at all, and well bought if it only had to be purchased. (Applause.) Don't put up with an unsubstantial sort of place with 4,1,- feet inch inner walls and the ou'a- walls incapable of standing a breeze from the head of the Mersey. (Laughter and applause.) It was for the general public of Runcorn and surrounding villages to come in the bazaar and relieve the stall•keeper of the pro- ducts of their generosity and industry, and to do that in a cheerful, not in a growling, spirit. They had no right to go into a shop and hunt about for rep goods and bankrupt stocks. (Applause.) It was a condition of mind to live upon shipwrecked ships, or shipwrecked fortunes ashore ; and still less bad people a right to go into a bazaar where all glowed and glistened with Christian philanthropy to see what they could get at less than prime cost. (Applause.) The practice of ' going to the bazaar on the last day to buy goods cheap was like prowling about the markets to find decayed butchers' meatithat would not keep from Saturday to the opening day on Monday, and get it at such a price that if they had only been the only person 3 to help the breeder the cat- tle would have died when they were calved. (Lau4hter.) Mr. Aspinall announced that he would leave a trifle with Mr. Shaw towards the end, the consummation of which was so devoutly wished,—(applause)—and concluded by declaring the bazaar open. Mr. W. HEYS moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Aspinall for his kin:Ness in opening the bazaar in apprapriate terms. Mr. JOHN BRUNDRIT seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation, and Mr. Aspinall in responding, apologised for the absence of Mr. Charles J. Bushel, the president of the missions, Liverpool,who had been announced to appear. The bazaar was largely patronised on Thursday evening, and the various entertainments, including the waxwork, were very successful. The amount realised on Wednesday was £76, and on Thursday about £63. The sale was con- tinued last evening. e,ej

div.head: MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES,
div.p: MISSIONARY MEETING AT WIDNES,

The annual meeting in aid of the Wesleyan Home and Foreign Missiors was held in Oakland-street Chapel, Widnes, on Monday evening, and there was a large company present. In the absence of Mr. Win. Hartley, who was unable to be present through illness, Mr. Jones occupied the chair, and on the platform were the Rev. R. Harper, Rev. J. Tessyman, and Mr. Joseph Robinson. Mr. G. Proctor pre- sided at the harmonium. The proceedings were opened in the customary manner, after which

I The CHAIRMAN observed that although he could not say much about mission work across the ocean, he had actual experience of mission work at home, in Widnes and in West Bank. In some houses he found there was not that respect for religion manifested which he should like to see. There were too many destitute houses, houses where if the inmates were asked to go to the House of God, they replied that they had not decent clothes to go in. Here was a field of visitors to work upon! (Hear, hear.) Mr. Jones then dwelt upon the importance of out-door mission work, which he reminded the audience was zealously carried on in West Bank some years ago. The Rev. J. TEesTaraer read the annual report, which stated that the total amount received in the Widnes circuit on behalf of the Wesleyan Home and Foreign Missions was £ll7, which bad been raised as follows :—Victoria-road, £54 3s 6d ; Albert-road. £8 3s 10d; Farnworth, £1 us 9d; Ditton, £l2 Sc id; Halebank, £5 13s 7d; Moss Bank, £1 15s 10d; Cronton, £l9 Sc 6d ; Oakland-street. £ll 12s ld. Mr. Tesseyman observed that the debt on the fund had been liquidated, and the missions were consequently at present free from debt; but unless in all the circuits 5 per cent. more money was raised than last year, there would next year be a debt of £5,000. He urged them to strive to avert that result. Mr. JOSEPH ROBINSON, who was next called upon to address the meeting, said he lamented the falling off in the enthusiasm in mission work during the past few years. He thought there was one sad feature in their work. It would scarcely be denied that the one great opposing spirit to Christianity was Mahommedanism. It was a melancholy fact that in India more natives were annually converted to Mohammedanism than to Christianity, and at the present time the followers of the former religion were expecting a great deliverer to come and lead them back to power and glory. From several contemporary circumstances it was evident that the Sultan of Turkey was looked upon by some as this coming hero. There was, perhaps, some reason to fear a temporary revival and triumph, and it was to remove these evils that the Wesleyan home and foreign missions were working. (Applause.) The Rev. J. TESSYMAN then delivered a speech. He re• marked that he was glad that the time and necessity for defending Christian missions had passed away. Fifty years ago they were regarded as chimerical, and church members even were found ready to swear at them. Surely they for- got the command of the Master to go forth and preach the Gospel to all thee,world. But men were found ready to ehey that command—to go forth to fight the foe—the Prince of Darkness. The lines which Campbell haeLwritten of other heroes might be applied appropriately to them—
The battle ieepens I On ye brave Who rash to glory or the grave.

(Applaase.) And many of them did rush to the grave, and in many a sacred spot rested their remains. He regarded the mission scheme the greatest ever Inaugurated upon earth. There was something so self-denying in mission work ; and self-denial was the very soul and essence of mission work. The missionaries sacrificed their all for the sake of religion. Wide water rolled between them and those they left behind. And sometimes death hovered over the mission station ; and the wife the missionary had taken with him was snatchedaway, leaving him lonely—how lonely only those into whose hearts the arrow of bereavement had pierced could tell. Heathenism, he believed, was the strong- hold-of Satan, for, as Milton had put it,— Of this be sure: To do aught good will never be our task, But ever to do 11l our sole delight. Reason bad been tried as a substitute for religion, but bad it succeeded? Did the ancient Greek and Roman philoso- phers, who carried, perhaps, human reason to perfection, iucceed in finding a substitute? The Gospel alone was the pow er a God unto salTatiou. Christianity wherever it

went proved itself to be the want of the world. The Gospel had an universal application, and must gain an universal , victory; and Christ's command "Go forth and preach the ; Gospel to every creature" would be fulfilled. But not yet. At present society was torn with fend. Oppression, blood- shed, and avarice reigned. But this should pass away, and the complete triumph of Christianity ahonld come. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. R. MUMS, in a brief speech, pointed out that mission work, like charity, was twice blessed, and benefited both the giver and the receiver. Where the Gospel spread cultivation followed, and there was soon a demand for our products and manufactures. Ha did not agree with what previous :speakers had asserted in ;regard to Mahomme- danistn. In his opinion the power of Islam was doomed, and the time of its destruction was approaching. A collection was then taken, and the meeting closed with the singing of the doxology and the pronouncing of the benediction.

There was ' only one object which could have brought together those names, and that was to promote the welfare and good government of the town in the interests of the general body of the ratepayers. div.head: RUNCORN RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: RUNCORN RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIA- TION.
INAUGURAL MEETING.

With the object of establishing a Ratepayers' Association for Runcorn, about 70 ratepayers assembled in Bethesda School-room on Tues Jay evening. The meeting.was of a fairly representative character, and amongst those present were Messrs. H. Coleburn, J. R. Frith, T. Horsfall, W. H. Rogerson, George Moss, Wm. Littler, F. J. Adams, R. Wright, C. Cook, W. Mellor, H. Ainscow, Jos. Bridgewater, H. White, J. K. Digges, W. Croley, T. Stringfellow, T. Spender, J. Foulkes, Jno. Williams, A Campbell, J. Lunt, Wm. Handley, J. Roberts, Win. Cornea, W. R. Earp, J. Poole, R. Morris, T. Heeson, J. A. Smith, S. White, F. Rowles, S. Worrall, S. Yarwood, Toone, T. Faulkner, J. Much, W. Stanway, Price, T. H. Annett, Armstrong, J. Pritchard, J. Jones. Mr. W. H. ROGIIRSON took temporary possesssion of the chair, on the motion of Mr. Coleburn. He said he thought it was allowed on all sides that there was great need of a ratepayers' association, which they had met to form, in the town. (Hear, hear.) The ratepayers of Runcorn seemed to have at last awoke from their legarthy, And to have come to the conclusion that they had ben dictated to long enosigh ; that it was time they took the management of the town's affairs into their own hands—(hear, hear) ;—and that they would no longer permit to ex:it the farce into which the annual election of Commission.ls had generated. (Applause.) Finding a wide-spread feeling of this kind among their fellow-townsmen, a number of gentlemen met about a fortnight ago to discuss the feasibility of forming a ratepayers' association. From what took place at that meeting it was decided to endeavour to form one at once, and conse- quently those present had been invited to attend that evening to give their assent and support to the project. He was aware that this was not the first institulon of the kind that there had been in the town. There had been either two or three associations formed previous to this, but they had b3en unsuccessful, for reasons, perhaps, not hard to find. That, however, was no reason why those present should not try to inaugurate another, and that they intended to do. A list of names would shortly be submitted to them of gentle:nen whom it was proposed should form the executive committee of the association, and he thought they would ind the list a thorough representative one, comprising gentlemen in whom they could, he had no doubt, place every confidence and give every support. He called upon Mr. R. WRIGHT, who moved the first resolution, viz, "That this meeting forms itself into a ratepayers' associa- tion, to be known hereafter as the Runcorn Ratepayers' Association." _ Mr. H. Afxscow seconded the proposition. ' - • 11'

The CHAIRMAN read to the meeting the objects the association would be expected especially to undertake, and which have been published in The Examiner. They were greeted with applause, and the motion was carried unani- mously. Mr. Lirrusa then proposed that Mr. Henry Coleburn be elected president of the association—(hear, hear)—and in doing so said they could not rind a man in Runcorn who would fill the post better. The association ought to have as president a gentleman of independent principles as far as possible, and in Mr. Coleburn they had one who lie firmly believed would court no sympathies and fear no frowns. Mr. AINSCOW seconded the motion with great pleasure, and remarked upon the large experience of town's affairs pessessed by Mr. Coleburn.
Mr. Srmsrpatz was understood to say that he considered this a Liberal association.

The CHAIRMAN said it was not a Liberal association or a Conservative association. One of the objects of the associa- tion was to promote the return of representatives to the Board of Commissioners unbiassed by any political motives. He thought they would find when they heard the names of the committee that they comprised men of all shades of political and religious feeling. The motion was then carried by acclamation, and Mr. COLERIIRN took the chair. I He observed that he was very muctrobliged to the proposer and seconder of the reso- lution that he should become the president. He was sorry that it had devolved upon him to fill so important a position, but since he had been elected he presumed unanimously, he should have great pleasure in attending perhaps every meet- ing, if his health permitted. He always thought that if a thing was worth doing at all it was worth doing well—(hear, hear)—and he thought everything in connection with the Ratepayers' Association would be worth doing well. (Hear, hear.) As Mr. Rogerson had explained, there seemed to be a call for something to be done, and if those present would render him their assistance he would fill the chair as ably as he could. He begged to thank them for the honour they had conferred upon him. (Applause.) Mr. J. R. FRITH, who was greeted with applause on ris- ing, said he had been requested to move that Messrs. Fair- hurst and Mellor be the vice-presidents of the association, and he did so with very great pleasure. The office of vice-president of the association, he took it, would ha no sinecure. They wanted men in that position who would not be mere machines to do the bidding of others, but men who would have a mind of their own to think—(hear, hear) —and a will of their own to act upon what they thought was right. (Hear, hear, and applause.) In Runcorn, unfortu- nately, they were governed by those who had no mind of their own—(hear, hear)—and what was worse they had no will of their own. (Hear, hear, applause, and laughter.) It was very pitiful to think that they were governed by those who aspired to a position in life which ought to be an honourable one, but which he was sorry to say had become what might be called a zoological garden. (Laughter and applause.) The Board of Commissioners had been termed a hear garden, and that, he thought, was something near a zoological garden. In Runcorn they wanted men who would think before they lifted up their hand to vote, and not men who would look round when a resolution was put from the chair, and say, "How am I to vote ?" not men who would wait before putting up their hand to see how other people voted—not men who would vote, and when they had got out of the meeting ask what they had voted for. (Laughter and applause.) Such was the character of Ei3MO of their representatives in Runcorn. (Loud laughter and applause.) He did not say this from hearsay. (Hear, hear.) He was going to say unfortunately he had seen it. Unfortunately he did spend two years at the Board of Commissioners. But when a man sat there unaided by more than one or two who would strive to pro- mote the ratepayers' interests and not their own, it was very hard work, and especially when he saw such things going on as he had mentioned. The ratepayers did not want a mere minority of men who would devote themselves to the ratepayers' interests—they wanted a majority of them— (hear, hear,)—and it was no use the ratepayers being idle any longer, for if they wanted the work of the town to ba done in a satisfactory way they must pet their shoulders to the wheel, and strive to obtain that which they desired. He had heard many ratepayers complain about this or the other evil in the town. Why did not they as men go in September to the polling booth, and exercise an independent mind by voting for the men whom they thought would do their duty irrespective of place or person? (Hear, hear, and applause.) And until the ratepayers of Runcorn did combine and strive to serve their own interests irrespective of persons, they would have the same state of things going on year after year as they had had for many years past. He trusted this association would not be like former associations—spring up and bloom the "short-lived beauty of a day," but that it would exist until next September, and then show what it could and would do. He trusted what it would do next September would only be an impetus to the ratepayers to rally round it and help it on. (Hear, hear and applause.) The men he had proposed as vice-presidents of the associa- tion were men who could help themselves; men who had shown that they could help themselves, men who had worked and could pay a dividend to their own little body of shareholders at home. Most of them had got little share- holders about them, and if they could do well for their household and take care of it, they were likely to take care of the interests of ethers. The gentlemen he had proposed were men who had risen by their own labour and industry to the position they occupied, and who would strive to do their best for the interests of the ratepayers at large. As the chairman had said, they were not a political association— they were combined together, irrespective of creed or politics. ‘Hear, hear.) Mr. Fairhurst and Mr. Mellor differed in both religion and politics, and that circumstance showed the wisdom of the choice of the gentlemen who met together in fixing upon two such gentlemen to be the vice-presidents. (Applause.) Mr. HENRY WHITE seconded the motion. The CHAIRMAN read a letter, addressed to Mr. Cook, from Mr. Fairhurst, who expressed his regret that he was unable to attend the meeting and his sympathy with its object. It must, he added, be clear to anyone who took an interest in the welfare of the town that there was great need for the formation of a ratepayers' association or something of the kind.
The resolution was then carried unanimously. Mr. W. H. ROGERSOS proposed that Mr. Cook be elected secretary. - _

, Mr. MELLOR seconded, and, in doing so, begged to thank the meeting for the honour they had conferred upon him in electing him a vice-president of the association. He assured them that he should endeavour, as far as his abili- ties would allow him, to serve the interests of the ratepayers, and he considered that when he was doing that he wAs serving himself. (Applause.) Motion carried unanimously. On the proposition of Mr. MELLOR, seconded by Mr. Ltrrutrt, Mr, Henry White was appointed treasurer. Mr. Moss moved that a committee of 15 be appointed consisting of the following gentlemen :—Messrs. Thomas Horgan, W. H. Rogerson, J. R. Frith, William Handley, Richard Oldbury, Jol.n Williams, Joseph Jeffs, W. Mellor, H. Ainscow, J. J. Waterworth, Richard Roberts, Robert Wright, Charles Johnson, Joseph Pritchard, and G. MOSEL Mr. Moss remarked that it must be plain to the meeting

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

TIIIIRSDA.Y.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. CLAIM AGAINST TEA MERCHANTS.—ThiS was a case in which Mr. Charles Henry Cartwright claimed from Messrs. Crapon, Brine and Company the sum of £23 10s. for a quarter's rent ending September lst.—Mr. G. T. Moore appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Helmore, of London, for the defendants.—Mr. Moore said in 1877 the defendants became tenants of the plaintiff at the sum:of £llO a year. The defendants were noted N London for their tea, and for the extension of their business they opened premises in War- rington. The premises of the plaintiff were suitable, and they verbally agreed to pay £llO a year, payable quarterly in advance. Up to 1879 the rent was regularly paid in advance, but a request was made by defendants to plaintiff to reduce the rent on account of the badness of trade, as the shop did not, to a certain extent, answer their expectations. Plaintiff was good enough to reduce the rent from £llO to £9O a year. Without the sanction of the plaintiff, defendants, after having kept the shop shut for a certain length of time, sub-let it to an American butcher. The premises were suit- able no doubt for tea merchants, but they were anything but suitable, without doing a great deal of damage, for the business of a butcher. Defendants gave six months' notice to determine on the lit March, 1882, but they had sub-let the shop to this butcher, whose tenancy did not expire until the 24th of that month, and therefore the defendants were not in a position to give up possession.— His Honour asked why not? They could have turned the butcher out.—Mr. Moore said the plaintiff had nothing to do with the sub-tenant. On the 29th March an agreement was drawn up whereby the defendants agreed to give up possession to plaintiff on the Ist June this year. They bad paid £3O for damages done to the premises, and paid rent up te the Ist Jane, and undertook by that agreement to leave the shop in good and tenantable repair. That would keep alive the tenancy up to Ist June. On the Ist June possession was not given up. They still retain possession, the keys were still in their possession, and they had exercised by their agents occupation and use, and the premises were not in the original condition they were when defendant first entered into possession—in fact the premises, he was instructed to say, were more like a pigstye than anythingelse.—His Honour: When did you say you got possession ?—Mr. Moore: We have not got possession yet. Does not your Honour rule that agreement continues the tenancy ?—His Honour: No.—Mr. Moore: Well, then, I am out of court if that is the case.—His Honour: I think you have misconceived your action in suing for a quarter's rent up to Septernber.—Mr. Moore said he was not instructed when the action was commenced or he would have sued for use, occupation, and damages.— His Honour offered to allow Mr. Moore to amend the par- ticulars, but ultimately the plaintiff was nonsuited A DOCTOR'S CLAIM: EXTRAORDINARY CASE.—In this case Dr. James Cannell was plaintiff,and Joseph Wadsworth, loan agent, defendant.—Mr. G. T. Moore appeared on behalf of Dr. Cannel!, and Mr. Joseph Sims, of Manchester, repre- sented the defendant.—Mr. Moore said the [plaintiff was a medical gentleman practising in Warrington, and he sought to recover the sum of £2 17s. 6d., for medical attendance on defendant's wife. What the defence might be he was at a loss to conceive, but he understood from the whispering of a little bird that fluttered about him just now it would be that defendant did not live with his wife. It was perfectly true proceedings for divorce were instituted between defen- dant and his wife, but the Queen's proctor intervened, and a decree was not granted, and therefore the parties were man and wife. Defendant's wife was in receipt of parish relief to the extent of ss. a week, and proceedings wcre instituted by the Board of Guardians before the magistrates for the recovery of the money paid to the wife. The magistrates after hearing the evidence and counsel on behalf of Mr. Wadsworth, decided that he was still liable to the parish for what relief his wife had received. The present claim was for medical attend- ance upon the defendant's wife, and surely that was a neces- sary. Further than that, even if the parties did not live together, they were known to be man and wife, and there was no divorce, and he apprehended if his friend set up that defence he could not succeed in non-suiting him on that account. If the woman was still Wadsworth's wife, as no doubt she was, Wadsworth ought to pay the money to the doctor.—Mr. Sims: A judicial separation was grante 1 in this case.—Mr. Moore: No.—Mr. Sims: The wife was living in adultery, and I do not know whether I need go further.—Mr. Moore: All that was gone into in London; the Queen's proctor intervened, and the proceeding were declared null and void.—Mr. Sims said the wife contracted a bigamous marriage so late as 1874. Proceedings went on for divorce, and plaintiff must be well aware of that. The wife had been living in adultery ever since, and he would hand up to his Honour a certificate of the marriage in 1874 showing the wife had contracted a bigamous marriage, and since then they had lived apart. The doctor must have been well aware of that, and he submitted even were he not defendant would not be liable in a case where his wife was living in adultery, far the debts contracted by his wife. He thought his Honour would remember on appeal the magis- trates' decision was over-ruled, and Mr. Justice Hawkins ruled it would be a great hardship if a man had to pay his wife's debts.—His Honour: All that rests upon the Poor Law.—Mr. Sims put it before his Honour to refute Mr, Moore's statement. He submitted although there was no decree for divorce defendant was not liable for the debts of his wife.—Plaintiff was then called, and he said he attended Mrs. Wadsworth for chronic bron- chitis off and on from March 15th to June 6th, 1881. Mrs. Wadsworth came to his house herself and engaged him. He never saw the defendant.—This was plaintiff's case.—His Honour said Mr. Moore must show there was no blame at- taching to the wife, and that they did not separate by con- sent.—Mrs. Wadsworth was then called, and she said she lived with Mrs. Dcinkwater, Knight's Court, Winwie'r-road. She was living apart from her busband.—Mr. Moore: What was the cause of the separation? Witness: Through him living with another woman. She had been charged with adultery.—Mr. Moore: Is there any truth in the statement that von have committed adultery with anybody? Witness: Yes; I own to the truth.—Mr. Moore: How long is that since? Witness could not say. Defendant committed him- self before she did.—Did you tell Dr. Cannel! the cause of your separation? Yes, I told him.—You say you are still the wife of Joseph Wadsworth? Yes, sir.—His Honour said plaintiff could not receive from defendant, and he refused to allow costs.

div.head: RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY AND THE CORPORATION.
div.p: THE RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY AND THE CORPORATION.

At a m eting of the Paving and Sewerage Committee of the Corporation on the 9th October, a deputation of the Rural Sanitary Authority attended to ascertain the terms upon which the committee would permit the Authority to connect their sewers with those now in course of construction by the Corporation in Latchford. The committee recommended the following as the terms upon which such a connection may be made :- 1. That the Rural Authority pay to the Corporation annu- ally a rate equal to 41. in the pound, upon the rateable value of all property now erected or to he erected which drains into the said sewers as shown upon a plan to be pre- pared by the Surveyor of the Rural Authority, and also a rate equal to id in the pound for all land shown upon the plan, the value of such property to be given to the Corpora- tion by the Rural Authority annually. 2. The Rural Authority to pay to the Corporation annually their propor- tion of a sum equal to 10 per cent, on the total cost of the machinery and works in connection with the said sewerage wurks, and used for the purpose of lifting the sewage there- in, which sum of. 10 per cent. to be a charge upon the property draining into the said sewers, as well of the Corporation as of the Rural Authority, according to the rateable value of such property. •3. That no rain water he permitted to enter or run into the sewers excepting such as falls upon the roofs and yards of houses or buildings within the district shown on the said plan of the Rural Authority. 4. That no road gullies be connected with the sewers in the said district of the Rural Authority. 5. That plans of the system of sewers of the Rural Authority be submitted to the Corporation for their approval. 6. That the sewers of the Rural Authority and all private connections within their district, where formed in quicksand or wet ground, to be laid with Stamford's patent jointed pipes, and both the public pewers and pri- vate drain connections to be carried out under the super- vision of a clerk of the works, appointed by the Corporation, the wages of such clerk of the works, to be paid by the Rural Authority. 7. That all connections with the Corpora- tion sewers be made by Corporation workmen, under the supervision of the Borough Surveyor, the cost of such con- nections to be paid by the Rural Authority. 8. That the Rural Authority enter into an agreement as regards other clauses similar to the one entered into between such Authority and the Corporation relating to the drainage of their district near Liverpool and Winwick-roads.

div.head: TWO CANDIDATES SUCCESSFULLY OBJECTED
div.p: TWO CANDIDATES SUCCESSFULLY OBJECTED

TO. On Tuesday afternoon the Mayor (Mr. R. Pilkington), in his committee-room at the Town Hall, heard and decided on objections to nomination papers delivered on Monday, which was the last day on which they could be received. Besides the Mayor there were also present Aldermen Harrison and Cook, Councillors Baxter, Cook, Brook, Forster, and Belsher, Mr. P. McKinley, Mr. T. Brevris (town clerk), Mr. J. H. C. aik (deputy town clerk), and Mr. J. 0. Swift, who ap- peared on behalf of three of the candidates.—Mr. BRBWIS read the list of nominations, and said it was competent for any person nominated to take exception to the nomination papers of other persons nominated.—Mr. Bairan said that he maintained there was only one nomination for Parr Ward, and that was in favour of himself.—Mr. BREWIS said Mr. McKinley's nomination did not state what ward it was for; it could not be known whether it was for that ward or any other ward. He asked Mr. McKinley if the nomination paper was intenled for Parr Ward.—Mr. MCKINLEY replied that it was. The proposer, seconder, and assenter were per- sons who lived in Parr Ward.—Mr. BAXTER: We are now speaking within the Act of Parliament, and I take it that your Worship will decide according to the Act. I say that nomination is not for Parr Ward.—Mr. MCKINLEY: Mr. Craik said it was all right.—Mr. CRAIK : No, I did not.— Mr. BAXTER: It is not what Mr. Craik has said. The nomination paper is not correct.—Mr. BREW'S said the sub- section 2 of the Municipal Elections Act, 1875, required that a nomination paper should state the sur-name and other names of the person nominated, his place of abode and de- scription, and should be in the form No. 2as set forth by the schedule. He then read the form, which required that the name of the ward for which a person was nominated should be in the colnmn provided for the purpose. Mr. McKinley's nomination paper had not been made Out in conformity to the form in the Act, bat if there were any objections to it he should require them in writing. —Mr. BAXTER Mr. BAXTER maintained that it was not a nomination for Parr Ward; the borough was divided into eix.wards, and the nomination papers for these wards ought to be made out in accordance with the Act of Parliament. In this instance a nomination paper had been delivered, but the name of the ward for which the nominated person intended to be a can- didate had been omitted, and therefore it was only an assumption that this nomination paper was for Parr Ward. What right had they to hold that assumption?—Mr. BREWIS said he had asked Mr. McKinley what ward he in- tended to stand for, and he said Parr.—Mr. BAXTER, how- ever, contended tbat there was only his own nomination for Parr Ward.—Mr. BREWIS (to) Mr. Baxter) : The gentleman nominated says it is for Parr Ward, but as you are the only other person nominated for Parr, you can take objection to it formally.—Mr. BAXTER said he objected to the paper as being one for Parr Ward, seeing that the name of the ward was not mentioned In it.—Mr. BREWIS then said the paper was an informal one, as it was not in accordance with the form required by law. The borough was divided into six wards, and it seemed imposaible to conduct a ward election without the name of the ward being stated on the nomina- tion paper, as in some instances they would not be able.to say to what ward the nomination paper applied. He should therefore advise the Mayor that the paper was not in com- pliance with the form he had mentioned, and was therefore invalid.—Mr. MCKINLEY asked for Mr. Baxter's nomination paper, and after examining it he took objection to the address, which was stated as being Rainhill, but did not state where Rainhill wae.—Mr. BAXTER said that he received letters and telegrams from London and elsewhere addressed to Rainhill.—This objection was therefore disallowed.—Mr. Baxter then produced a written objection to Mr. McKin- ley's nomination, and the objection was allowed by the Mayor.

div.head: HARDSHAW WARD.
div.p: HARDSHAW WARD.

Mr. COOK said he had to raise an objection to the paper nominating Patrick Mclnerney on the ground that it wa s informal and did not comply with the requirements of the Act. It might seem to some to be ungracious on his part to raise a technical objection, but having regard to the interests of the borough and he believed the vsishes of the ratepayers generally, he thought he was justified in doing so. The objection he took was to the name of one of the assentors to the nomination. His Worship would find that there was the name of James Carney, 48, Atlas-street, as an assentor, his burgess roll No. being put down as 1807. He (Mr. Cook) found that in Hardshaw Ward there was no such number, the lowest number on that roll being 27011—8 y referring to the roll Mr. Brewis found that James Carney, living at the address mentioned, was registered under the number 2707, and therefore the number mentioned on the paper was wrong.—Mr. BREWIS then quoted a similar case decided upon by a higher court, and advised his worship to be guided by this ruling.—Mr. Mlncerney's nomination was therefore declared invalid.

div.head: ECCLESTON WARD.
div.p: ECCLESTON WARD.

Mr. J. 0. SWIFT, on behalf of Mr. W. H. Foster, objected to the nomination paper of Mr. John Hogan or Hagan, on the gronnd that the surname of the nominated party was not correctly stated, and further that the address was not correctly stated. He further objected on the ground that the names of the assentors were not correctly written.—These objections, however, were not allowed, and Mr. Hogan's nomination therefore remained good.

div.p: NEGLECT OP FAMILY. - At the instance of Mr. B. Shearer (relieving officer), John Warburton, a labourer, of no fixed residence, was brought up at Warrington Police- court, on Tuesday, before Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks, charged with neglecting to support his wife aad chil- dren, causing them to be chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Shearer said that the prisoner's wife and four children were admitted to the workhouse on the sth inst. He had endeavoured to find the prisoner, but could learn nothing whatever about him. The case was brought before the Board, and a warrant ordered to be taken out for the prisoner's apprehension. Prisoner had never made any enquiries about his family, and was a lazy, drunken fellow.—The prisoner said he was not fit to work as he had hurt his leg some time ago.— The Bench, however, oommitted him to gaol for a month with hard labotr.

At the Town Hall, Woolwich, yesterday, General Sir John Adye was presented with an address congratulating him upon the honours he had achieved in taking part in the brilliant and victorious Egyptian campaign. An explosion of fire-damp occurred yesterday at Brom- house Pit, Barleston, near Glasgow. Patrick Cavanah, Thomas Rennow, John Day, and an overman were seriously barnt, and are net expected to recover. Lord Charles Beresford arrived yesterday afternoon at Christchurch on a visit to the Marchioness of Waterford. A four-lined whip has been issued by the Conservative Whip yesterday. Two men named Byrne and Arnold, were walking from Stranoriar, county Donegal, on Thursday, when the former, it is alleged, shot Arnold with a revolver. Byrne has been arrested. The rain which fell in the neighbourhood of Windsor on Tuesday, caused the Thames to rise six inches, and conse- quently the inundations in the district between Staines and Oxford have become more extensive. Captain Liban and one seaman, the only survivors of the crew of the barque Victoria, of Rostock, were landed at Yarmouth yesterday; also the crew of the brig Sarah Louise, of Shoreham, which foundered during the gale. A Parliamentary return issued yesterday shows that in every County of the United Kingdom, depositors in the Post Office Saving's Banks increased during the year 1881. A young girl named Hope, employed in a millinery establishment in Durham, whilst proceeding to her work along the railway yesterday morning was knocked down by an express train and killed. The body was shockingly mutilated.

MILL FIRE NEAR OLDHAM. On Thursday evening, after the hands had left work, a .fire broke out in the MeMock Mill, Lees Brook, occupied by Mr. Edward Rye. The fire occurred in the top spinning room, and got into the room below. Two engines from Lees came to the scene, and the flames were extinguished after considerable difficulty. The damage will amount to nearly £l,OOO. The mill contained 15,000 spindles. REMARKABLE WEATHER IN SCOTLAND. The weather in Scotland on Thursday was very remark- able for its changes. Keen frost prevailed during the night, snow fell in the morning, and at noon there was a fog of extreme density, which stopped navigation on the Forth, Tay, and Clyde. About eight at night a thunderstorm burst over a wide area. The lightning was very bright, and hailstones of unusual size fell till the ground was quite white.

A NAVAL SCANDAL. A Court of Inquiry, which has had to deal with a grave naval scandal, closed at Aberdeen yesterday. The inquiry has extended over 10 days, and a report upon the subject will be submitted with the view to deciding upon a Court- martial. The inquiry has been held on board Her Majesty's ship Clyde. Statements by the accused parties have been heard, and the depositions will be forwarded to the Admiralty forthwith; and, if it is deemed necessary, a public Court- martial will be ordered at once. The news that has leaked out concerning this matter has created the greatest sensation in Aberdeen, where the parties concerned are held in the highest respect, and move in the most fashionable circles.

div.head: ALLEGED PERJURY AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED PERJURY AT WIDNES.

Yesterday, at Widnes Police-court, William Other, a labourer, was brought before Mr. John Brock, to answer a charge of having on the 18th inst. committed wilful an corrupt perjury in an affiliation case heard at the Widnes Petty Sessions.—lnspector Barnett said he merely proposed calling sufficient evidence to justify a remand.—Alice Wild, a young woman, said she was a single woman, and lived in Viaduct-street, Widnes. On the date named she summoned the prisoner, upon whom she made a claim for her child. She gave evidence that she was at Runcorn with the pri- soner on the 7th November, 1831.—The Clerk: You swore it was on the Bth November? Witness: No, it was on the 7th.—Did not the prisoner swear he never kept com- pany with you ? Yes, sir. And did not he also swear that he was never at Runcorn in his life ? Yes, sir.— Hadn't he been with you? Yes, sir.—Didn't the magis- trates dismiss the summons? Yes. The prisoner swore he had never walked me out —On this evidence the Bench granted a remand until Monday and bail was refused.

THE TREATMENT OF EGYPTIAN PRISONERS.—RepIy- ing to Mr. O'Kelly Mr. C. DILKE said the Home Government had no concern with the question that had arisen between Baker Pacha and the Sultan relative to former application to the command of the Egyptian Army. —Lord R. Cuuncumr. asked whether in the matter the Khedive acted independently.—Mr. C. DICKE said he stated so yesterday.
