ATTEMPT TO CUT A MAN'S THROAT AT ST. HELENS. Late on Saturday night last a middle-aged Irishms! named Thomas Gaffney was taken into custody on accoas' of haying attempted to cut the throat of a Welslitnan, haa named George Williams. It appeared that the two melt t been fellow-lodgers at a lodging-house in Liverpool-stree, and, both being somewhat under the influence of drink, entered into a somewhat warm controversy as to the met' h of their respective nationalities. Failing to convince e3C other with the legitimate weapon of debate—the tongsel they fell to ficticuffs, but after inflicting sundry knocks [IL bruises on each other they were separated by the 10'111'; and another lodger named McGill. Shortly after, howevei the Irishman, apparently thinking it was an argumt, which would not admit of a reply, drew his knife across other's throat, inflicting a severe but fortunately not a fa'„ wound. On Monday, at the Police Court, before Alderivel:4 Cook and Mcßryde, he was charged with unlawf6l wounding George Williams. The prosecutor said he was; present living with his brother at Sutton, but from T1311,,e' day to Saturday he had lived at McGovern's lodging-13° ~; ,rj- Liverpool-street. About 10-30 on Saturday night the r',;(l eoner asked him what countryman he was. and he answe,r;p 1 that he was a cross-bred—a mongrel—and also spoljes , words in the Welsh language. The prisoner said 3 lie words in reply, in what he (witness) thought to be Irish. a told prismer he could not tell what he was saying. Frin°„%e replied by calling prosecutor a Welshman, and said OP int° could beat any Welshman, and then got up and went %.,ci another room. Prosecutor followed and asked what he P:d been sa ping, at which prisoner turned round to strike s'.'ct made a blow but missed. On seeing this prosecutor struu4 the prisoner and both fell to the floor, where they strufgos A for a few seconds, but where at length separated bY 1.0, McGill, another lodger, and the landlady Mrs. McCrol'e , McGill took the prisoner into another room while the 10,,e lady took prosecutor into the bar. Whilst sitting there heard the prisoner swearing that he would cut his throst`o upon hearing which he opened the door and attemPtedthe get out. He met the prisoner in the doorway leading t° passage. He had an open pocket knife in his right Iwhich he drew across under prosecutor's chin naalii°g,4 wound three or four inches in length. Prosecutor ran P'pj out of the house, and went to the Town Hall and infolm:e the police of what had occurred. He then went back agtable to the :lodging-house with a policeman, and, after„p's prisoner had been apprehended, went to Dr. McNic'j.ily surgery where his wounds were stitched. He felt CO 2t and cold from his wound, and had not since been„.-ee work. Previous to Saturday night he had 12:the conversed with the prisoner. The prisoner was drunk Aipc) time of the quarrel, but he (prosecutor), although be had a little drink, was quite sober.--Dr. I%lcNicholl sa'' oa first saw the prosecutor about midnight on Saturdal _Abe stitched up his wound. The wound was about four in 46, in length, and had evidently been produced'by some instrument. Part of the wouui was what was calio ' superficial wound, bat the other part was deep into the Pile though not having touched the wind-pipe or arteries. tO had evidently lost some blood. He would probably be•Tbe reenme work in a week.—Jamem McCiill, a labourer, sal ()o- wes a lodger at McGovern's, and had separated the Pr the cutor and prisoner when fighting. After that he heard tbe prisoner cursing, but did not hear h'm threaten to cat tbe other's throat. He did not see what took place in_ io passage.—Mrs. McGovern, the landlady of the boodythe which the occurrence took place, said she believe srai prisoner came from County Mayor, and the prosecutor atia a Welsh man. She sew the quarrel between the tw'' saw the prosecutor strike the prisoner first. After thel been separated, she told prosecutor to remain in the bar 43, let the prisoner alone.—P.C. Bremner said that whilst btlli,°; ing the prisoner to the police office, he said, before litb ever bzen charged, "I did threaten to strike him poker, hut hut never used a knife." The two pocket knivesor be duce 4 were found on prisoner, one of them seemin!ttt„,f N . covered with blood.—The prisoner was then commit take his trial at the sessions.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. The Provisional Committee INVITE SUBSCRIPTIONS and Offers of Assistance to the £lOO 000 Fund now being raised to defray the expenses of en application to Parliament to carry out this scheme. Subscribers will have the following options allowed to them : (a) Of taking up twenty times the amount of their subscription in shares when the issue is autherised by law. (b) Or to receive fully paid-up shares equal to the amount of the subscription. (c) Or to leave the amount so subscribed as a 10 per cent, deposit on shares. (d) Or to have the amount returned In cash when the espital has been raised. Interest at the rate of 3 per cent, per annum will, provided the Act of Parliament is oetained, be allowed on all sums now subscribed from the date of payment of such subscriptions up to the date of allotment of shares, after which time further arrangements as to payment of interest will be made and duly advertised. As all classes in and round Manchester will materially benefit by the cheapening of transport by water, and by the creation of new industries and the enol3ragement of existing ones, it is hoped that everyone will feel it his duty to, share in the labours of promoting this great improvement. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH- EAST WARD, WARRINGTON. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, —Having been urgently requested by a large number of burgesses to allow my- self to be nominated as a candidate to represent you in the Town Council, I have accepted the invitation, and beg to place my services at your disposal. In appeal- ing for your suffrages, being a large ratepayer and property owner It will be as much my interest as yours to keep down the ra' es. Should you elect me as your representative in the Council Chamber I shall do my utmost to secure the economical expenditure of the rates, and further every effort for the prosperity of the borough. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, yours faith- fully. WILLIAM BOLTON, 84, Wilderspeol Causeway, Latchford, Oct. 24th, 1882. •

TO THE BURGESSES OF THE SOUTH- EAST WARD, WARRINGTON. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,----Being selected by the Council of the Conservative Association to stand for the South-East Ward, I ask your support and vote at the Election on Wednesday next. I have not had fair treatment from a clique, who, being defeated at a meeting of the Council, are now working very actively against me. I ought to be supported by the Council, instead of being left to contest the Ward alone; con- sequently, I have to come before you as an Independent , Candidate, and appeal to yo'l for fair play. If elected 41 I shall vete for Alderman Joseph Harrison as Mayor, and shall consider myself as the Workingmen's Candi- date, and study their interests. I may also state that I am a member ef the Ratepayers' Association, whose Interests are yours as well as mine. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, WM. TO THE ELECTORS OF THE SOUTH- EAST WARD OF THE BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON . LADIES AN]) GENTLEMEN, —As two vacancies are ose occurring in the above Ward, we have been requested by a large and influential number of our fellow rate- payers to allow ourselves to be n-minated to serve you on the Council of this Borough. We earnestly appeal to you for your support as we have been large rate- payers in the Ward for upwards of twenty years. If -f you do us the honour to elect us as your representa- tives in the Council, we promise you that our best attention shall be given to all questions affecting your interests. We are, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servants, ' ROBERT WILLIAM MARSH, THOMAS HUTCHINSON.

TO THE BURGESSES OF HARDSHAW WARD, BT. HELENS; LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I beg to thank you very sincerely for the honor you have conferred, and for the trust reposed in me, by returning me as your representative in the Council of this Borough, for the third time. I shall endeavour to serve you in the future, as I have done during the past six years, with all diligence and fidelity to your interests and those of the ratepayers generally. I am, yours faitfully, THOMAS COOK. Atlas Foundry, Bt. Helens, 24th October, 1882.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS. TO THE BURGESSES OF WEST SUTTON WARD, T. HELENS. LADIES AND Gforrimix,x,—The term for which you elected me to represent your Ward, three years ago, is just expiring. and I again venture to ask you for a renewal of your confidence. If I have pleased you in the past, it shall be my endeavour, if elected, to give you satisfaction in the future. During my term of office, it has always been my object to for- ward those schemes that tended to improve the sanitary, social, and moral condition of the Borough generally, and your ward in particular. All the questions that relate to good drainage, good ventilation, pure water, Baths, and Recreation Grounds, and pure air as far as is practicable, shall have my particular attention, as they have had hitherto, to endeavour as far as possible to banish disease and prolong life. I am. Ladies and Gentlemen. Your Obedient Servant, R. G. BROOK. Wolverhampton House, Bt. Helens, October 23rd, 1882.
